title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Big claims and words like FREE and NEW are so overused that today's prospects reject them on sight.
do: Cut stock hype words and giant claims from the first line of a hook; open with something specific and checkable.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Prospects meet every big promise with 'Yeah, sure', so a claim must never outrun its proof and the two must appear together.
do: In every hook, put the claim and its proof in the same breath (result plus who or what shows it) and never open on an unsupported claim.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Putting a big promise behind an easy IF requirement switches off the skeptic's alarm, and admitting it is only moderately easy is more believable.
do: Write a hook as 'If you have [small easy requirement], [strong promise]', then use the body to show how that small effort delivers it.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: The IF...THEN headline beat a strong control again on a second product, and exclamation marks add to the smell of hype.
do: Keep on-screen text and captions free of exclamation marks and hype punctuation; state the promise flatly.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: SCAMPER (substitute, combine, adapt, modify, put to other use, eliminate, rearrange) gives a quick list of ways to rework a stuck headline or offer, as Doubleday did by swapping niches into one winning offer.
do: When a hook or offer underperforms, run it through each SCAMPER word and write one variant per word.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Adapting a proven headline like 'Do You Make These Mistakes...' to a new product works, provided the body fills with common mistakes people make without it.
do: Draft a 'Do you make these mistakes with [category]?' hook and build the script as a quick list of the mistakes, with the product as the fix.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: The reliable way to predict which headline wins is to ask which offers more compelling proof, because readers ask both 'is this for me' and 'is it believable'.
do: When choosing between two hooks, pick the one that carries more proof and test that one first.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Adding a credible authority like doctors to a headline raised response 71% because it raised the level of proof.
do: Name a credible source in the hook line itself, such as an expert, a number of buyers or a review, rather than saving it for later.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Effective advertising is a believable promise to the right audience, and without belief nobody buys.
do: Check that every promise in a script has a matching proof beat before it is cut.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Read your own copy as a 'yeah, sure' skeptic and patch every hole with stronger proof until it would convince a fair jury.
do: Before sign-off, read each script line aloud as a skeptic and add proof wherever the answer is 'yeah, sure'.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Uncle Jim turned hail-marked apples into proof of mountain growth, and sold more with fewer refunds.
do: Where a product has a visible flaw or quirk, explain honestly what it proves and show it on screen as part of the pitch.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: The most persuasive tool is the reason why, and a sale needs reasons for three questions: why you, why true, why now.
do: Structure each script as three beats: why this product is better, why that is true, and why act today.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Slice won share in a crowded category by putting one small reason, 10-percent fruit juice, next to its better-taste claim.
do: Attach a concrete reason, such as an ingredient or a number, to the main claim in the first line.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: A discount gets believed and acted on when it carries a reason why, such as a fire sale, rather than just 'half off'.
do: Give every discount in a reel a real reason (stock clearance, anniversary, end of season) and say it in the same line as the price.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: The most profitable sales messages contain reasons the product is superior, reasons to believe it, and reasons to act today.
do: Run a checklist on every draft: one reason it is better, one reason to believe, one reason to act now.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: In Langer's queue test, asking with 'because' got about 93-94% compliance versus 60% without it, even when the reason said nothing new.
do: Phrase asks and calls to action with 'because' plus a reason.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: In writing, 'because' works best when followed by a genuinely compelling reason, since readers deliberate more.
do: Write key lines as 'X, because Y' with a real Y, in the voiceover or on-screen text.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Success depends on what others want, and marketers fail by launching products they want to sell rather than products people want to buy.
do: Open the script on the viewer's problem or desire, not on the product.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Markets are human wants, not demographics, and emotions are the flesh and blood of copy while logic is only the skeleton.
do: Name the buyer's specific want or pain in the first seconds, find it from best-seller lists or reviews, and name the emotion the scene should carry.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: The fear of loss motivates more than the desire for gain, and a test showed asking what it costs you not to act beat asking what you could save.
do: Try a version that states the daily cost of not buying or not acting alongside the version that states the gain.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: A boldly generous offer that only a fool would refuse can electrify a campaign and spark word of mouth.
do: Test one offer or guarantee that is more generous than competitors', and lead the reel with it.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Persistence wins: one top broker contacted prospects nine times where others quit after three or four.
do: Plan a sequence of several different videos for the same warm viewer rather than one video per product.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Research a product with who, what, why, how, where and when, bring back seven times more facts than you can use, and one fact outweighs 100 adjectives.
do: Before writing, collect at least seven times more facts than the reel can hold from the founder, product and customers, then keep the strongest few.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: People look for one specific product, so sell with a narrow rifle shot like Fuzzy Dice rather than a broad shotgun like Car Accessories.
do: Make each reel about one named product and one specific use, with the product named in the hook, instead of a brand-wide pitch.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Specific offers such as flood insurance for Hamptons homes find buyers faster than generic categories like insurance.
do: Write the hook around a specific person, place or situation, such as a particular occasion or scent, not the category.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Buyers who decide act within about 10 days and look first in the newspaper, so the dealer moved spend from TV to the place and time of intent.
do: Put the direct-offer cuts where buyers are ready (retargeting, search-style placements) and keep broad awareness cuts for cold feeds.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Free content should far outweigh sales copy, with only a light mention linking to a separate hard-sell page, or readers learn to ignore you.
do: Make organic reels mostly useful content with one soft mention and a link, keeping the hard offer for paid cuts.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: A gifted product beats a gifted pen: advertising can only convey a product advantage, not invent one.
do: Identify the product's real built-in advantage first and make it the spine of the script.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: The product is the star, so interrogate the client with ten questions about uniqueness and proof first, and resist clever, cute or entertaining execution that draws attention to the writer.
do: Ask the founder the ten questions before any script, and cut puns and clever lines that do not carry a product advantage.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: A product with a clear unique advantage and strong proof makes the ad nearly write itself and settles what to write about.
do: Choose which product to feature by its clearest proven advantage, and let that advantage decide the angle.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Separate strategy (the unique message) from tactics (the execution): decide the message first, then how to present it.
do: Write the one-line message of the reel before choosing a concept or format.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Execution should put the prospect front and center, but only after strategy settles which unique benefit the ad conveys.
do: Pick the single unique benefit first, then show the viewer's problem and wants leading to that benefit.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: An ad about what the prospect already wants sounds familiar and gets screened out, so research the product for a unique strength, like M&Ms melting in your mouth, not in your hand.
do: Find the one thing only this product does, such as how it is made, how long it lasts or what is in it, and build the hook on it instead of the obvious category benefit.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: M&Ms found their winning message by digging for what the product uniquely does (it doesn't melt in your hand), then built ads that demonstrated that one benefit visibly.
do: Before writing, list what the product does that rivals can't, pick one, and build the script as a visual demonstration of it (like the two closed fists test), ending on a one-line tagline.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: A strong ad is a unique product benefit plus an execution that shows how it improves the viewer's life, and what you say matters more than how you say it.
do: Write the script's one-sentence unique benefit first; if it could describe any rival product, redo it before shooting or cutting.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: The same discount worded as buy one get one free beat '50% off' and 'half price' by 40 percent in tests.
do: Where margins allow, word the offer in the video as a free extra item rather than a percentage or half-price discount.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Bogo works in nearly every market where discounts make sense, and creative versions (a cheap related freebie, or give one get one for gifting) work too.
do: Offer a cheap add-on free with purchase (a travel size, a sample) and for gifting season use 'buy one for a friend, get one for you'.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: A believable reason for a special offer lifts response, and each ad should sell one thing thoroughly.
do: State why the deal exists on screen (Black Friday, anniversary, overstock, new launch) and feature a single product per video.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Adding a deluxe or good-better-best option turns yes-or-no into A-or-B, and longer money-back guarantees raise response and reduce refunds.
do: Show two or three tiers in the offer card and give the guarantee its own beat with the longest term the client will honour.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Repeat business and subscriptions are where the money is, and real deadlines or limits boost response if you honour them.
do: Close with a genuine deadline or stock limit and a subscribe-and-save option, and never extend a limit you announced.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Announcing an upcoming price rise, offering a desirable premium (even unrelated to the product), and an early-bird bonus with a relative deadline all lift response.
do: Add a free gift for those who order within a set number of days and pick a gift people want, not one that merely relates to the product.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: A mystery early-bird gift described with teasing copy can pull better than naming the gift.
do: Tease a surprise bonus in the closing beat ('reveal it when you order in the next 7 days') and test it against naming the gift.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Free shipping, samples, trials, and similar 'free' offers cut perceived risk, and visible care for the customer makes people respond.
do: Put 'free' (shipping, sample or trial) in the offer line and let the speaker's warmth toward the viewer show in delivery.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Borden's formula says to imagine the audience shouting 'Ho hum!', 'Why bring that up!', 'For instance?' and 'So what?' and answer each in order.
do: Check each script against the four objections: does the opening beat ho-hum, is relevance clear, is there a concrete example, and is there a point?

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: A model talk opens with an intriguing fact, explains why it matters to the listener, then gives vivid concrete examples.
do: Structure a script as surprising fact, why it matters to you, two or three quick concrete examples, then the call to act.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Test every opening line by asking whether it would matter to someone shaken awake at 3 a.m., because that is what crashing the ho-hum barrier means.
do: Read each hook aloud as if to someone half asleep; if they wouldn't care, rewrite it, and write 30 to 50 hook options before choosing.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Most people are effectively asleep, so the headline must electrify them, and about five times more people read the headline than the body.
do: Spend most of your scripting time on the first two seconds and put real selling (the benefit or offer) into the hook itself.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: A good metaphor instantly transfers one thing's qualities onto another and bypasses critical resistance.
do: Express the main point as one compact comparison line in the hook or voiceover instead of a feature description.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Short metaphors like 'a Goldilocks economy' or 'small leaks sink great ships' persuade more than long arguments.
do: Look for a short familiar image that makes the product's point in one line and use it as a caption or spoken line.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Metaphors from fairy tales, sports and movies trigger emotions the audience already holds, so you can persuade instantly.
do: Borrow a universally known story image (David and Goliath, Cinderella) to frame the product's transformation in one line.

title: Bencivenga Bullets
author: Gary Bencivenga
says: Familiar clichés are credible because people already believe them, but exaggerated metaphors destroy credibility.
do: Use a plain, familiar comparison and cut any over-the-top simile that makes the claim sound unbelievable.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Each visual component is defined briefly, and movement is the first component to attract the eye.
do: Put the one moving thing in the frame on the product or the key action, and keep background movement low so the eye goes there first.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A colour or look means whatever you teach the audience it means, by repeating it with the same event, but borrowed stereotypes are the weakest option.
do: Pick one colour or frame treatment and use it only on the offer beat (price, deal, code) in every reel for a brand, so viewers learn to read it as 'the deal' without being told.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A visual progression moves from simple to complex, and strong sequences build in intensity this way.
do: Plan a reel so the visuals get busier across it, from one calm simple frame to denser, more complex frames at the climax, instead of holding one level throughout.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Progressions are as fundamental to visual structure as to story or music, and car ads make a car look fast through them.
do: Storyboard the reel's visual intensity as a rising curve so the build matches the claim, such as speed, transformation or result.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Visual intensity rises with contrast (difference) in any component and falls with affinity (similarity).
do: Make the hook frame high-contrast (size, brightness, colour, direction) and let calm beats use similar frames, so you control intensity by deliberately varying difference.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A film of nothing but alternating black and white frames is all contrast and becomes unwatchably intense.
do: Don't stack maximum contrast cut after cut, such as flashing colours and hard cuts with no rest; leave lower-contrast frames between the peaks.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A film of one unchanging gray frame is all affinity and so dull, meaning a piece needs both contrast and affinity.
do: If three or more shots in a row look alike (same angle, framing, brightness), change one visual component on the next cut to restore energy.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Vanishing points attract attention, more vanishing points mean more depth, and viewers can't tell more than three.
do: Put the speaker or product at or near where the lines in the frame converge, such as a table edge or shelf, so the lines help guide the eye to it.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Staging subjects on foreground, midground and background planes creates depth through size difference.
do: Shoot product demos with a large hand or product in the foreground and the person smaller behind it, to give the frame depth.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Camera dollies, tracks and booms create depth because the foreground moves faster than the background.
do: For a product reveal, move the camera past a foreground object toward the product so the parallax gives depth; a simple screen punch-in will not.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Brighter objects usually look closer and darker ones farther away, even at the same size.
do: Light the product brighter than its surroundings so it comes forward in a vertical frame.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Warm colours seem closer and cool colours farther, and objects lower in the frame feel nearer than those higher up.
do: Put the product in a warm colour against a cool background, and place it low in frame when you want it to feel near.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: In flat space subjects move side to side, and pans, tilts and zooms keep it flat because there's no relative movement.
do: For a flat graphic look, such as text-led or flat-lay product shots, move side to side or zoom rather than pushing toward the camera.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A zoom enlarges everything at once and reduces depth of field, so it reads flat while a dolly reads deep.
do: Use a gentle zoom or punch-in when you want a flat, graphic emphasis on the product, and a real camera move when you want depth.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Ambiguous space, where size and position can't be read, creates tension and anxiety and ends the moment an object of known size appears.
do: Open a hook on an unrecognisable close-up of the product or texture, then reveal its scale with a hand or familiar object on a planned beat.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Deep space comes from longitudinal planes, staging toward or away from camera, and moving the camera.
do: For a deep, immersive shot, such as a store or kitchen walkthrough, shoot along a long wall or counter and move toward the subject.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A surface division makes viewers compare the two sides and can direct their eye to one part of the frame.
do: For before/after or us-versus-them proof, split the frame with a clear vertical line so viewers compare both sides on their own.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Surface divisions act like a fence that confines attention, and they can change the apparent aspect ratio of a fixed frame.
do: Use a split or a boxed panel in a vertical frame to hold attention on one area, such as a text box over footage, and to vary the frame shape.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Contrast and affinity of space can be used within a shot, from shot to shot and across sequences.
do: Cut a flat shot next to a deep one at the moment you want a jolt, and keep similar spaces together where you want calm.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Deep space is more intense because it is built from contrasts, and flat space is calmer because it is built from affinity.
do: Shoot the hook and payoff in deep space with big size and brightness differences, and the explanatory middle in flatter, calmer framing.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Squinting at a picture reveals its dominant lines, the linear motif, and you should judge lines on the screen, not in real life.
do: Squint at the paused frame before locking an edit to check that the dominant lines lead to the product or face.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Diagonal lines are the most intense, verticals less, horizontals least, and line orientation can contrast or match from shot to shot.
do: Choose diagonal compositions for high-energy beats and horizontal ones for calm beats, and change orientation between cuts to raise the energy.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Straight lines read as direct and strong, curved lines as soft, safe and natural, and these are general guides only.
do: Choose curved forms and lines for gentle, natural, safe-feeling products, and straight, angular ones for bold, technical products.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Circles feel friendly, squares stable and triangles dynamic, and a silhouette reveals an object's basic shape.
do: Check the silhouette of the product, packaging and presenter, and match its shape to the feeling you want, such as round for friendly or triangular for fast.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Triangles feel bold and menacing, and shape contrast or affinity works within a shot, between shots and across sequences.
do: Put contrasting shapes (triangle against square) in the key frame, and keep shapes matching in calm sections.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Squint, light for tonal contrast and plan line orientation shot to shot so intensity builds toward the biggest contrast.
do: Sketch the reel as a row of tiny frames showing line direction, and place the strongest contrast, a diagonal against a horizontal, at the climax.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Tone is brightness, and the brightest area of a frame draws the eye first, especially when nothing moves.
do: Light or grade so the product or face is the brightest spot in the opening frame, and dim bright distractions such as windows, white walls and screens.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A shot works only if its tonal organisation reveals its intended subject, so a face or product left in shadow fails.
do: For every shot, name the subject (face, product, label) and check that it is visibly lit, and reshoot or regrade if it isn't.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Hiding the subject through darkness or similar tonal control, rather than by physically blocking it, makes viewers anxious and makes them listen harder to sound.
do: For a tension or reveal beat, let the product sit in shadow or low tone and carry the moment with voice-over, sound effect or music, then bring it into clear light on the reveal.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Maximum tonal contrast needs pure black and white with no middle greys, while tonal affinity is easiest to hold by keeping a whole shot or sequence inside about a third of the grey scale.
do: For a punchy cut, grade or light for deep blacks and bright whites with few mids. For a calm or premium sequence, keep every shot inside one narrow tonal band.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Viewers look at the brightest area of a frame when nothing moves, and you judge tone best by ignoring colour and checking in black and white.
do: Check each hero frame in greyscale and make sure the product or face is the brightest area, or add a small brightness lift on it in the grade.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Words cannot pin down a colour, so only a swatch communicates it exactly, and hue is just the position on the wheel.
do: When briefing an editor, designer or creator on brand colour, send a swatch or hex value from the client, never a name like warm peach.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Saturated yellow is naturally the brightest colour and pulls the eye first, while saturated blue is dark and cannot match yellow's brightness without losing saturation.
do: Put a yellow or orange product or caption against darker, cooler surroundings to pull the eye to it, and do not expect a deep blue item to compete.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Colour can contrast or share brightness, saturation and warmth, and a single saturated item in a desaturated frame stands out strongly.
do: Grade the background and talent slightly desaturated and keep the product or one accent colour fully saturated so it is the thing the eye finds.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Attention goes to brightness before saturation, so bright saturated colours grab the eye while dark ones, even vivid, are ignored.
do: Check that the product is brighter than everything around it, not merely more colourful, and do not rely on a dark saturated pack to draw the eye.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Complementary colours placed next to each other look more saturated, and in a cut the second shot's colour is the one that shifts.
do: Cut into the product shot from a shot dominated by its complementary colour, such as a teal scene before a red product, so the product looks more vivid.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: You can make a colour look more saturated by placing its complement behind it in the frame or by running complementary shots before it.
do: Shoot the product against its complementary colour, and grade the shots before the product reveal toward that complement so the product looks richer on the cut.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A colour scheme can be one hue or a complementary pair, assigned to characters, locations or foreground and background, with blue and orange the most common.
do: Pick a brand-led pair, such as blue and orange, and assign one to the problem state and the other to the product or result so colour carries meaning.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Richer schemes use three or four hues, and a color script of actual swatches is the way to plan colour because words fail.
do: Before shooting, make a strip of swatches for the video's beats and give it to the creator, editor and colourist.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A color script of swatches per act or sequence lets you plan colour change across a story, and audiences respond to colour immediately and emotionally.
do: Plan one swatch strip per reel, such as cool and muted for the problem and warm and saturated for the payoff, and grade to it.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: The best way to control colour is to limit the palette of sets, props and clothes, and because audiences remember colour poorly, shot-to-shot colour shifts go unnoticed.
do: Put a palette rule in every shoot brief: only brand colours in frame, wrong-coloured props and clothing removed, and the product colour owned by the product.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: On screen, movement only shows when an object moves relative to the frame or to a visible background, so a panned subject on a bare background looks still.
do: If the product must feel like it is moving, such as a spin, run or reveal, include textured background elements or let it cross the frame instead of panning to keep it centred.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Straight tracks feel direct and aggressive while curved tracks feel soft and passive, and a director can give characters different movement shapes.
do: Direct performers to move in straight lines on the hard-sell or confident beats and in curves on the soft, comfort or lifestyle beats.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Slower camera moves create affinity and calm, faster camera moves create visual intensity, and the audience reads camera movement through how objects move in frame.
do: Use slow gentle moves on calm benefit or care beats and quick moves on energy or urgency beats, and match the move speed to the intensity of the line.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Pans, tilts and zooms move everything equally, while dolly, track and crane moves create relative movement between foreground and background and so feel more intense.
do: For an opening shot that must grab attention, push in or track past foreground objects rather than zooming or panning on a phone.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Attention goes first to movement, then to the brightest area, then to eyes, vanishing points and whatever contrasts most.
do: In the first frames, make the thing you want seen the only moving, brightest or most contrasting element, and keep competing movement out of frame.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: The strongest contrast to movement is no movement, so a single still shot or still moment stands out in a moving sequence.
do: Hold one locked, still frame on the key claim or product after fast-moving shots so it lands harder.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Horizontal movement is the least intense, vertical is more, diagonal is the most, and repeating the same direction keeps intensity low.
do: Move objects and camera in one consistent horizontal direction for calm sections, then switch to diagonal or opposing-direction moves for the peak or offer beat.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: One object moving at a different speed from the rest creates contrast and intensity, and parallel horizontals are the calmest pairing of mover and background.
do: To lift energy, have one element move faster or slower than the others, such as a fast hand against slow background action.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Tracking, cranes and dollies are more intense than pans, tilts and zooms, with the snap zoom the exception that adds sudden intensity.
do: Use a snap zoom on one punch beat, like a claim or reveal, and keep other moves gentle so it stands out.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Handheld and tilted cameras add diagonals and instability and so more intensity, and larger camera moves create more intensity than small ones.
do: Choose handheld or tilted framing for urgent, raw UGC-style beats and a locked-off level camera for calm, premium ones.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Slow motion shows action more clearly and fast motion adds energy, and audiences feel the intensity without noticing the speed change.
do: Slow a product hero move such as a pour or a fabric swish to show it, and nudge action footage slightly faster for energy without announcing it.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Cross-screen eye travel barely exists on phone-sized screens, though attention is still pulled by movement, brightness, saturation, eyes and contrast.
do: Do not plan reels around large eye jumps between screen corners, and focus instead on movement, brightness and eyes to direct attention in the small frame.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Keeping subjects in one screen region gives smooth attention, and the further apart they sit, the more the viewer's eye must jump.
do: In two-person or product-and-person frames, place them close together so the eye does not have to jump when the speaker changes.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: An object that begins moving where the previous one stopped hands the viewer's attention across smoothly, while a new mover in a different place forces a jump.
do: Stage action so the next movement starts where the last one ended, such as the hand picking up the product where the previous move stopped.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: If the focal point sits in the same screen region on both sides of a cut, the eye does not have to move, so the cut feels smooth.
do: When cutting wide to close-up or between angles, reframe or reposition so the face or product lands in the same screen region on both shots.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Cutting between shots where the attention point jumps to a new region every time produces much more intensity than matching positions, and the editor can control this.
do: For a high-energy edit, deliberately change the screen region of the key subject on each cut. For a calm edit, match regions.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Matching where the eye lands from shot to shot makes cuts invisible and can hide continuity errors, and contrast raises intensity.
do: On each cut, pause the frame, mark where your own eye lands and match it with the next shot. Use it to hide continuity gaps and mismatches.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Rhythm needs alternation, repetition and tempo, and a single beat or constant hum is not a rhythm.
do: Build rhythm by alternating contrasting beats such as loud and quiet, close and wide, and repeating the pattern at a set tempo.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Placing objects in a frame creates visual rhythm, and unequal divisions of the frame are more intense than equal ones.
do: Place the product or face off-centre to create unequal frame divisions for energy, and centre it for steady, calm shots.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: The more objects divide the frame into parts, the faster the visual tempo.
do: Fill the frame with more distinct objects for a fast-feeling shot, and use a single subject with open space for a slow one.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A moving object creates rhythm by entering and exiting frame, passing in front of or behind things, stopping and starting, and changing direction.
do: Time beats by having hands or products enter and exit frame in a repeating pattern that matches the voice-over or music.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Each object passing a foreground or background item adds a beat, and more such objects raise the tempo.
do: Add foreground elements the subject passes, such as shelves, rails or hands, to speed up the rhythm of a shot.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Every cut is a beat, the bigger the visual difference between two shots the harder the beat, and repeating the same shot weakens it.
do: Cut on the beat and make shots on either side of a key cut differ in tone, size or colour, and avoid cutting back and forth between the same two framings too many times.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Viewers feel cutting rhythm best when cuts come fast, and edits more than about ten seconds apart no longer read as a rhythm.
do: Keep cuts well under ten seconds apart in a 15 to 60 second reel so there is a felt rhythm, and vary the tempo deliberately.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Breaking any event into numbered subevents reveals its parts and the best way to shoot it, and it can be shot as one continuous take.
do: List every small step of a demo or routine, such as open, pour, apply or reveal, then choose which steps get their own shot.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Breaking an event into separate shots lets you control contrast and rhythm, and each style gains emphasis when it follows the other.
do: After a run of fast cuts, drop in one unbroken take for the key demo or proof moment so it stands out.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Fragmenting lets the editor reorder and re-time an event, while mixing continuous and fragmented sections keeps visuals from getting dull.
do: Shoot key actions in several angles so you can retime them, and mix in a few longer takes to avoid sameness.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Stories have different rhythm patterns that can be drawn as a flow line, and a metronome can set the beat, for example 120 beats a minute is two a second.
do: Sketch a flow line of the reel's peaks and valleys before editing, and set the cut tempo to a metronome count such as 60 or 120.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Regular, predictable rhythm is calm, while changing the tempo makes an irregular rhythm that raises intensity, and any tempo can be given any meaning.
do: Keep cut lengths steady for calm sections and vary them unpredictably for the high-energy parts and the offer.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Find the sound's rhythm first and let it define the visual rhythm, more lines in frame give a faster rhythm, and do not confuse movement with rhythm.
do: Lock the voice-over and music first, then cut visuals to their beats, and do not assume fast movement in a shot makes the shot rhythmic.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A story is exposition, conflict and resolution, and viewers cannot get involved until they have the facts they need.
do: Open every script by giving who, what and why-now within the first seconds, so viewers do not spend attention working it out.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Voice-over narration is a common quick way to deliver the opening facts and can continue through the story.
do: Use a short voice-over line at the start to set up the person, problem and situation, then carry on over the visuals.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Conflict can be internal, an emotional struggle, or external, a physical problem, and the best stories combine both.
do: Give each script an outside problem, such as a stain or a slow delivery, and an inside feeling, such as embarrassment or frustration, and let the product resolve both.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Conflict builds to a climax where the main character must choose and the conflict ends, followed by a resolution that gives time to recover.
do: Build the script toward one clear moment of choice, such as the offer or the call to action, then close with a short settling beat.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Every story, including a commercial, has exposition, conflict, climax and resolution, resolutions can be very short, and intensity can be charted on a graph.
do: Mark exposition, conflict, climax and resolution on every script and keep the resolution very short, even a few seconds.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Plotting each sequence on an intensity graph from 0 to 100 shows where a story builds and drops, and the same method works for a single sequence.
do: Rate each beat of a script from 0 to 100 and check the line builds toward the climax, then adjust the flat or backwards beats.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Visual structure mirrors story structure, so the opening must set the visual rules, such as colour, shape and space, at the same time as the story facts.
do: In the first seconds of a reel, establish the look, such as palette, framing and pace, together with the story setup, and keep to those rules until the story turns.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Rules for music, camera view and look set up early become fixed associations, so the audience feels the emotion without seeing the thing itself.
do: Pick one recurring sound or framing in the first seconds and tie it to one meaning (problem, relief, payoff), then reuse it unchanged later in the reel.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: More contrast between visual elements raises intensity, more similarity lowers it, and the visuals should rise and fall with the story.
do: Plan each reel's intensity curve: put the strongest contrast (size, brightness, angle, cut speed) at the payoff and calm, similar shots at the open and close.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Graphing visual intensity under the story intensity shows whether the visuals track the story: calm in setup, contrast in the climax, calm again in the resolution.
do: Sketch a two-line strip for each script, story tension on top and visual contrast beneath, and check the peaks line up before cutting.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Any visual element can be held constant for unity, progress gradually to show change, or spike with contrast to hit specific moments.
do: Hold one element constant (e.g. framing or colour grade) across a reel, and move a second one to show the before-to-after change.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Visual spikes should be motivated by story conflict moments, and the climax can alternate sharply between contrasting looks shot to shot.
do: At the problem moment or big reveal, cut between two clearly contrasting setups (wide vs tight, flat vs deep) and keep other beats calm.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Graphs can be redrawn after the edit to analyse the contrast in actual footage and fix a sequence that isn't working.
do: When a cut feels flat or messy, list each shot's size, brightness and movement and find where contrast is missing or random.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Even a 10-second spot with no story needs a beginning, middle and end structure, with intense opening spikes, a drop, then a contrast build to the end.
do: For a 15 second reel, open on a high-contrast hook, ease off in the middle, then build contrast again for the offer or call to action.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: When working from existing footage, analyse its contrast first and use camera movement and cutting speed to lower intensity at the start and raise it at the climax.
do: With raw creator or client clips, cut slower and calmer through the setup even if the clips are busy, and speed up toward the payoff.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: The point-of-view, how the audience should feel about the subject, is the main clue for every visual choice.
do: Before writing, state in one line how the viewer should feel about the product or problem, and test each shot against it.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Commercials each carry one strong point-of-view such as great taste, fun, athleticism or social desirability.
do: Choose one single feeling for each ad (e.g. fun, confidence, belonging) and build hook, offer and visuals around only that.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Any choice, even arbitrary, beats none, because uncontrolled visuals structure themselves and probably work against the story; building a reference scrapbook helps.
do: Make a quick reference board of frames the edit should resemble and share it with the editor rather than leaving looks to chance.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Research by watching films muted and commissioning concept drawings helps find visual structure, and your own emotional reaction to the text reveals the intended point-of-view.
do: Watch top-performing competitor ads with sound off to see their visual structure, and note how the script made you feel before deciding the look.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Slow, deliberate rhythm builds anxiety, and a sudden change of rhythm shocks the viewer.
do: Hold a slow, steady cut pace through the problem, then break it with a sharp change of pace at the reveal.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Ads must stand out, trend-driven visual tricks fade when overused, and in ads the visuals often are the content so they must be structured.
do: Don't lean on a trending effect for the hook; choose contrast in a basic element (size, angle, movement) and use it with purpose.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: The same product can look calm and elegant using affinity or fast and wild using contrast across space, line, tone, colour, movement and rhythm, and contrast can make a dull product feel dynamic.
do: For a plain product, deliberately add contrast (angle changes, size jumps, tone, cut pace) to give energy; for premium or calm brands use slow, regular, similar shots.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: When using still photos, plan crops, camera move direction and where attention lands in the next picture.
do: When animating product stills, choose each move's direction and crop so the eye lands where the next cut starts.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Even talking-head footage can be controlled through background, colour, lighting, lens and shapes, driven by how you want the audience to feel about the information.
do: For testimonial or founder-to-camera clips, pick background, light and lens deliberately to match the feeling (trust, excitement).

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: In unplanned footage most control comes in the edit, where contrast and affinity between clips shapes the viewer's emotions.
do: When cutting raw UGC, check each neighbouring pair of clips for contrast or similarity and adjust order to build the intended feeling.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: On small screens depth cues from size, texture, tone and subtle colour differences are lost, and blacks are weak in bright viewing conditions.
do: For phone viewing, separate subject from background with big differences in size and brightness, not subtle tone or colour.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Studio shows stay visually static, while location work uses deep space and movement toward and away from camera, which is more dynamic than sideways movement.
do: Stage action moving toward or away from the camera rather than across the frame when you want energy.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A show's recognisable look is a small set of fixed visual rules, which also keeps the look consistent when different people work on it.
do: Write a short visual rule sheet for each brand (framing, colour, cut pace, movement) so every editor produces the same look.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Keep visual control simple, but have rules, because without them there is no right or wrong choice.
do: Limit each reel to three or four visual rules and follow them.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Visual rules give unity and, with contrast and affinity, make the visuals follow the story, and audiences expect a structured ride even in 10 seconds.
do: Give even a 10 to 15 second reel a deliberate visual arc, not just a story beat sequence.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: A beat is a change in the relationship or intention between characters, and beats organise a scene's structure.
do: Break each script into beats and make sure every beat changes one thing (the problem, mood or intention).

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: An editor can mark beat changes by switching shot type or changing a visual component, and bigger changes mean stronger beats.
do: Change shot size or framing at each script beat, such as wide for setup and close for the reveal.

title: The Visual Story
author: Bruce Block
says: Ignoring beats gives long run-on sequences with no shape, while marking them gives scenes structure the audience can follow.
do: Check that every script beat has a visible change in the cut so nothing runs on unchanged.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Two otherwise identical ads differed 19.5 times in sales because one used the right appeal, so finding the right appeal matters more than polish.
do: Spend most of the effort finding the one appeal that sells before writing; shoot or cut several different appeals as separate reels and test them before polishing any.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Giving every ad a different key number or code lets you trace which ad produced each sale.
do: Give every reel variant its own tracked link or code so sales can be traced to the exact video.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Run all ads in the same place with the same offer prominence, because the ad with most inquiries usually gets most sales.
do: Test reel variants side by side in the same placement with the same offer shown the same way, then keep the winner.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A successful ad needs an irresistible headline, facts to back it up, and an unbeatable offer with a guarantee.
do: Structure a reel as a hook that promises a benefit, a few concrete facts, then a clear offer with the guarantee in the closing beat.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A highly praised essay-style ad failed because its headline promised no benefit and its picture offered no reward; judge ads by sales, not literary merit.
do: Check that the first line and first image promise a reward to the viewer, and drop poetic openings that do not.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Changing 'Are you afraid of making mistakes' to 'Do you make these mistakes' made the winning headline, because 'these' promises specific content to read.
do: Write hooks that point at specific things on screen ('these 3 mistakes') rather than asking vague questions.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The headline decides whether an ad works, so Caples now spends hours or days on it and little time on copy.
do: Spend the most writing time on the first three seconds and draft many hooks before scripting the body.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: If the headline does not stop people the copy goes unread, and the best headlines offer something the reader wants, then news, then curiosity.
do: Open every reel with what the viewer gets or a piece of news, and use curiosity only as a third choice.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A self-interest headline beat a curiosity headline by twice the inquiries and sales, partly because it delivers a message even to people who only read the big print.
do: Make the on-screen hook text and first line carry the whole benefit, since many viewers will never watch past it.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Headlines that give neither news, benefit nor curiosity are meaningless and give no reason to read on.
do: Test each hook by asking whether it gives news, a benefit or real curiosity; cut it if it gives none.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A headline must work alone because readers see it first and do not judge it by how it ties to the copy.
do: Judge a hook on its own, without the rest of the script, since the viewer meets it first.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: 'Corn Gone In 5 Days or Money Back' wins because it speaks plainly to one person with a problem, with a speed claim and a guarantee in a few words.
do: Write the hook as problem solved, time frame, guarantee, in plain short words a distracted scroller catches instantly.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: 'How a fool stunt made me a star salesman' works by combining curiosity with self-interest, and one tested ad lost because its headline attracted the wrong audience.
do: Pair a curious detail with a clear benefit in one hook line.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Strong headlines add a quick, easy route and a curiosity gap to the benefit.
do: Hint in the hook that the result is quick and easy, and make the viewer want to see the answer.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Headlines with a short time frame ('one evening', '5 days') and a stated benefit sold well.
do: Put a specific short time frame in the hook, like 'in 5 days'.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: News plus self-interest headlines, and the word 'Wanted', make readers stop and read.
do: Use 'announcing' or 'new' news framing with the benefit, or address the viewer directly as someone wanted.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Headlines with concrete figures, like $35,840 in 2 years, offer a benefit and spark curiosity.
do: Put a precise number in the hook rather than a round claim.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Good headlines carry self-interest, news, curiosity or a quick easy way, and specific figures make them believable.
do: Use specific figures in hooks and claims, such as exact days, rand amounts and counts.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Ad juries pick poor headlines because they read the copy, favour fine writing, and are not buyers; what you say matters more than how you say it.
do: Pick hooks on how clearly they say the benefit, not how clever they sound in the room.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Experienced ad people picked the best-selling ad wrongly about half the time, so opinion is unreliable.
do: Decide between hook variants by live results, not team opinion.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Ten failed headlines were all curiosity-only, gave no news or benefit, and most were negative.
do: Avoid hooks that are only a teaser or paint a gloomy picture.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Five rules: put self-interest and news in the headline, avoid pure curiosity, avoid the negative, and suggest a quick easy way.
do: Check every hook against five rules: benefit, news, not just curiosity, positive angle, quick and easy.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Write the reason you yourself would buy, and keep it believable, because 'work less and earn more' failed as too good to be true.
do: Write the hook from your own best reason to buy, and cut claims that sound too good to be true.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A long headline that tells a complete story beats a short vague one, and dead or too-clever headlines should be avoided.
do: Let the hook run long enough to give price, scope or outcome rather than trimming it to a slogan.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Put the big point in the headline to catch the right audience, and add curiosity to self-interest headlines.
do: State the main point and the product category in the hook so the right viewer stops.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The reader's attention is yours for only a single instant, so hard-to-grasp headlines get skipped.
do: Make the hook understandable in the first second without needing thought or the next shot to explain it.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Never run without a headline unless the picture itself is excellent, and write a dozen or twenty-five headlines then choose.
do: Write at least ten hook options per reel and choose the one that would stop you if bored.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Show headlines to a fresh person, because a line can have a second meaning you do not see.
do: Have someone unfamiliar read each hook cold before it is locked.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Emphasis in a long headline should fall on words that say something, not on words chosen for layout balance.
do: In on-screen text, enlarge or highlight the meaningful words, not the first or last ones.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Big type should carry the words that select the audience and deliver a brief message even at a glance.
do: Make the large caption words the audience-selecting benefit words so the message lands even when skimmed.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Mail order headlines are short, direct and clear, while general advertisers' are vague and clever.
do: Write hooks like telegraph lines naming the thing and the result.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A Carnegie ad headline about marriage failed because it attracted people wanting a marriage book rather than one about winning friends.
do: Make sure the hook attracts the people who actually want the product, not a broader wrong audience.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The Navy ad promising free training worth $1500 beat the romantic appeal, since recruits were practical-minded.
do: Lead with concrete free value or a practical gain over lifestyle imagery.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The 'Buy no desk until you've seen' ad stopped readers because it said the opposite of every other ad.
do: Try a hook that tells the viewer to wait or not buy yet until they have seen this.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Beginning with 'Announcing', 'New', 'Now' or 'At last' gives a headline a news flavour.
do: Open launch or restock reels with 'Now' or 'At last' plus the benefit.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Price matters hugely in a sale: readers skip big headlines to reach prices, and dates and news style add urgency.
do: Show the price clearly and early in the reel, since viewers actively look for it.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Headlines featuring price, reduced price, special offers, easy payments or a free offer lift sales.
do: Put the price, the saving, a payment plan or the free item in the hook or opening line.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Information-style and story headlines get high readership, and story hooks should contain the key word that selects the right audience.
do: Frame educational reels as helpful information, or open stories with the product word in the first line.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Starting with 'How to' forces the copy to deliver what readers want.
do: Start a script's hook with 'How to' and keep the whole reel on delivering that.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: 'How', 'Why' and 'Which' hooks work, and listing symptoms lets nearly every viewer find themselves.
do: Use a list of 3 to 4 symptoms or problems in the hook so most viewers recognise one.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: 'Who else', 'Wanted', 'This' and 'Advice' headlines each draw readers by implying a crowd, a need, specificity or free help.
do: Try 'Who else wants...' or 'Advice to...' as hook templates.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Testimonial-style headlines and offering the reader a test are proven formulas.
do: Open with a customer-voice line or a quick self-test question like 'Can you pass this test?'

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Short problem-word headlines, 'don't buy' warnings, direct address and callouts to a specific group select the right audience.
do: Call out the exact audience in the first line, for example 'To anyone who...'

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Old appeals like making money still work, but only if they are believable, and the appeal (the reason to buy) is the most important part of an ad and usually is the headline.
do: Open the reel with one plain reason to buy and make it believable with a specific, not a big vague promise.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: In a study of eleven ads, every winner had one particular appeal in its headline and no loser did, even though some losers had it in the body copy.
do: Put the winning appeal in the first line or on-screen text of the reel, not just somewhere in the voiceover.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Rank your ads by results, lay them side by side, find what the winners share, then do more of it; the basic appeal sways people more than how nicely it is presented.
do: Rank the client's past videos by sales or cost per result and note what the top ones share (appeal, length, opening) before writing new ones.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: An ad with specific facts and figures about results beats one that speaks generally, and what an ad says matters more than how it looks.
do: Put a real number or named result on screen (how much, how fast, how many) instead of a general claim.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A beautifully written, much-praised story ad (the wife's letter) failed to bring in any response, so praise from ad people is not proof it sells.
do: Judge a clever or touching concept by sales results, and don't keep it because the team likes it.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Copy that rambles in general terms before reaching the facts loses, and ads people don't understand actually annoy them.
do: Cut any vague warm-up and state the concrete facts in the first lines of the script.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: People often admire an ad but buy another brand, and an ad that goes unnoticed is the worst failure, so being noticed matters.
do: Judge a hook by whether it stops the scroll and sells, not by whether the team finds it artistic.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Used-car ads with specific bargains, make, year and price drew three times as many customers as polished general ads, and a winning appeal can be reworded many ways.
do: Name the exact product, price and deal in the opening, then make several hook variations around the one winning appeal.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Find a winning appeal by testing several, working out the winner from results, then featuring it in everything.
do: Make three versions of a reel, each with a different appeal in the first three seconds, then scale the winner.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The dog food ad built on 'keep your dog safe this summer' got 56% more sample requests than the one that pushed the free offer harder.
do: Lead with the strongest reason to care before the free or discount offer.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Offering several choices raises response and shows which choice people want most.
do: Let one reel point to two or three products or bundles, and track which gets the clicks.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Attention tests showed some ads stopped 34 people in 1,000 and others 9, and a famous name raised attention, dropping 50% when removed.
do: Use a recognised name or face as the authority behind the opening claim.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: If an ad doesn't get attention nothing else about it counts, so copy the tested, repeated direct-response ads.
do: Spend most of the effort on the first seconds and borrow structures from ads that run again and again.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Timely ads tied to seasons and holidays get extra attention.
do: Tie the hook to the live moment (Black Friday, Mother's Day, back to school) in South Africa.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Years of mail-order tests moved the club ad from a vague 'prospectus' offer to a concrete 'choose any 4 for $1' offer.
do: State the concrete deal (what you get, for how much) rather than offering information.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Write while you are still excited about something, because enthusiasm cools and the writing goes flat.
do: Write or record the script straight after using or unboxing the product, while the reaction is fresh.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A fat-reducer ad ends with send no money, a refund promise and 'you risk nothing', and writers should draft fast and ignore their critics, then cut later.
do: Close with a plain risk-free line (guarantee, returns) and write the first draft without the approvers in mind.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Emotional copy gets to fear, love and desire where reason-why copy only gets a nod, so write fast and with excitement.
do: Give each script an emotional beat as well as the reasons to buy.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Combine emotion and reason, write in white-hot enthusiasm, then rewrite carefully.
do: Write a hot first draft, then tighten it over several passes.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The pear ad works through the two brothers' own voice and a story that starts with long, enthusiastic copy.
do: Write founder-voice scripts that tell how they came to sell this to people, in their own plain words.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The pear ad closes with delivery, specific prices, a comparison to restaurant prices, a money-back guarantee, scarcity and an easy order step.
do: End the script with price, a guarantee line and a limited-stock reason to act now.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Testimonials from satisfied users sell, work best signed with real names, and carry more weight than the maker saying the same thing.
do: Use a named real customer or creator saying the claim on camera instead of the brand.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Many ads improve by simply deleting the writer's warm-up opening and starting where the copy gets going.
do: Cut the first sentence or two of every draft script and begin at the first useful line.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Reader's Digest uses 'interrupting idea' openers, startling statements that break through boredom.
do: Try an odd, surprising fact or image as the first line.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Other proven openers are the shocker, news, a preview and a quotation.
do: Write hook options as a shocking contrast, a news line, or a quote and test them.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Over half of Reader's Digest articles open with a short story or anecdote, even though it is a nonfiction magazine.
do: Open with a specific moment, who, where, what happened, then move to the product.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Strong openings are fact-packed, telegraphic, specific, light on adjectives and arouse curiosity, and if nothing fits, just continue the headline's thought.
do: Write hook lines as short, specific, fact-heavy statements with almost no adjectives.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The first paragraph should continue the headline's idea and get straight to selling points, like the stammering and piano ads.
do: Make the second line of the reel deliver what the first line promised, with several benefits packed fast.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Introducing a different idea right after the headline loses the reader; keep the first paragraph short, on the headline's thought, and stating the key benefits.
do: Make the first spoken line match the hook promise and state the main benefit.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: People read ads for benefits, 'what do I get, what will it do for me', and straightforward copy just states facts plainly.
do: Early in each script, say what the viewer gets, in plain words.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Story copy starts with a human situation in short paragraphs and ends on the moral 'buy the product'.
do: Use a short real-life scene, then land on the product as the answer.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: 'You and me' copy speaks in a friendly personal voice, and the fish letter ends with a free trial on approval; the ad ran seven years.
do: Write like a friend speaking, ending with a try-it, send-back-if-not-happy offer.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Retail ads that tell the most facts make the most sales, so pile one fact on another.
do: Pack the script with specific product facts (materials, features, numbers), not adjectives.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Superlative boasting works if you have the facts to back it up.
do: Make bold 'best' claims only when the script then shows the facts that prove them.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The 'neglected estate' ad admits the house needs work and still sells it, which makes the rest more believable.
do: Include one honest limitation of the product in the script to raise trust.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Tested best-selling book titles are brief, simple and full of human interest in three or four words.
do: Write on-screen hook text as three to four plain words about a human interest.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Teaser copy that challenges or seems to exclude the reader stands out because it is unusual.
do: Try a hook that says who the video is not for.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A comparison table against competitors works, but clever copy often misfires with obscure headlines.
do: Show a side-by-side on screen with real numbers, and keep hooks clear rather than smart.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Clever copy is a gamble; stick to simple presentation of benefits unless the headline still attracts readers.
do: Choose a plain benefit hook over a clever one unless the clever one clearly stops the scroll.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Humour limits your audience because everyone finds different things funny, so most writers should avoid it.
do: If a skit is funny, make sure it still carries a clear selling point.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Poetic, word-juggling copy fails, while a plain list of specific results was repeated dozens of times.
do: Replace flowery lines with concrete results and numbers.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Affected, extravagant and unbelievable claims no longer work with intelligent readers.
do: Avoid shouting, exaggerated promises and get-rich style claims in scripts.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Misleading ads, like a 'free' item that required selling, create lasting scepticism and damage trust.
do: Never headline 'free' unless it is free without conditions.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The World Review ad earned $54,923 on $15,711 of space because it looked like editorial, was signed by a famous editor, spoke 'you and me', and named the paper in the headline.
do: Make the ad feel native, personal and signed by a known face, and name the platform or place in the hook.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Harvard Classics ads about the joy of owning books got few leads, while a dramatic Marie Antoinette story ad pulled eight times as many coupons.
do: Hook with a dramatic story moment or question, not the joy of owning the product.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Humour should be used sparingly, but a skilled writer can combine it with a real selling point as in the Arrow shirts ad.
do: If using a comic story, build the product benefit into the punchline.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The Sherwin Cody English ad speaks directly to the reader's worries and offers a method.
do: Address the viewer's likely mistake or worry directly in the opening.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The 'Do you make these mistakes' ad paid for years while a copy about the maker failed; write in present tense, second person.
do: Write the script in 'you' and present tense and talk about the viewer, not the brand.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Keep hammering 'you', and use subheads that tell the whole story to skimmers and keep people reading.
do: Use on-screen subhead cards at each section turn so a muted viewer still gets the story.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Captions under pictures get read, and writing should be simple enough to take minimal effort to understand.
do: Put a short selling caption on each key shot and keep sentences easy to take in.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Use short simple words; masses understand them better and educated readers don't mind.
do: Swap long or fancy words in the script for short everyday ones.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Short words mean the same thing to speaker and listener, so the reader grasps the point in a split second, while pompous words make them stumble and turn away.
do: Write voiceover and on-screen text in one- and two-syllable words and cut any word a viewer would have to think about.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Put free useful information first and the sales talk second, written in an editorial style, so the reader reaches the value before the pitch.
do: Open a reel with the useful tip or fact, in a plain explainer voice, and hold the product pitch until after it has paid off.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Style copy makes unsupported flowery claims, while selling copy backs each claim with a concrete, provable fact, and advertisers who can trace sales use selling copy.
do: Replace each adjective in a script (soft, fresh, pure) with a concrete fact such as an ingredient, a count or an expert endorsement.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Arouse curiosity by telling enough of a situation to intrigue, but never reveal the outcome or the secret, because satisfying curiosity loses the sale.
do: Write the hook to state that a result or method exists and hold back how it works until the viewer commits to the offer or click.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A curiosity pitch can carry proof such as numbers of people who saw the book and ordered it, while still not explaining the method, which you only get by buying.
do: Pair a curiosity hook with a concrete social-proof number, then close on what the product reveals without giving the answer away.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Exact specific numbers read as fact while round general claims read as a copywriter's exaggeration.
do: Use the exact figure on screen and in voiceover (97,482 sold, 158 of 165 tests) rather than a rounded 'nearly 100,000'.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A precise figure (52.7%) drove strong sales and demand collapsed when it was softened to 'over 50%'; a single specific word like 'self-stirring' beats piles of generic adjectives.
do: Keep the exact number from the brand's data in the script and never round it down for tidiness; name one specific feature instead of stacking adjectives.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A mail-order seller grew sales by adding more copy, because long copy crams in more sales arguments, but only if it is not padding.
do: For direct-response reels, make room for several distinct selling arguments and testimonials rather than one thin claim, and cut anything that is filler.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Not everybody reads long copy, but the best prospects will, so put the brief message in headlines and subheads for glancers and the full detail for the interested.
do: Make the first seconds and on-screen captions carry the whole offer for skimmers, and put the detailed reasons later in the reel for those who stay.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Copy gets stronger when cut down, because unessential words and whole paragraphs drop out and every line becomes a selling argument.
do: Write the 60-second script first, then cut it to 30 and 15 seconds, keeping only the lines that sell, and use the shortest cut as the strongest version.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Write twice the copy you need and boil it down, as one retirement ad shrank from three paragraphs to a single sentence while keeping the key facts.
do: Draft a script at double the target length, then trim to the time slot, keeping the concrete numbers and dropping the warm-up lines.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Selling the general category (TVs, smoking) helps competitors, so sell your own brand's particular feature.
do: Name the product's own distinct feature or ingredient in the script rather than only the pleasure of the category.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: In a letter the first sentence is the headline and decides whether it is read, and the strong openers are a question, a story, a promise of saving, an admission of failure or a surprising fact.
do: Treat the first spoken line as the headline and test openers like 'Somehow we failed you', a curiosity question or 'Enclosed find $200'.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Understatement copy, blunt and plain with no hype, has pulled better than overstated big-pay promises.
do: Tone down the hype in scripts: speak plainly and bluntly, and even tell the wrong viewer they are not for us.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A free-booklet close that says 'we do not urge you to send for it' can outperform an excited overstatement close.
do: Try a calm, low-pressure call to action that tells viewers who it is for rather than pushing 'turning point in your life' hype.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Conservative, specific testimonials with explanatory comments beat overstated ones, and avoid even the appearance of overstatement by writing the offer like a news item.
