do: Choose modest, believable customer quotes and add a short caption explaining why each detail matters; present a new product as plain news with the key feature first.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Do not gild the lily: a plain news write-up, plus avoiding obviously untrue slogans, builds more belief, and testing with a critic works better when they compare two versions.
do: Cut any slogan a viewer knows is untrue and replace it with a real selling argument; when showing cuts to anyone for feedback, show two versions.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Show a critic two versions to get a true opinion, and do not mention a salesman will call because it cuts coupon returns by at least 75 percent.
do: When getting feedback on a hook or cut, always present two options; keep call-to-action lines free of anything that sounds like a sales follow-up.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Write every ad as a complete sales talk with every important selling point, because you cannot know which one the viewer cares about.
do: Make sure each reel has the main selling arguments and a defined audience, rather than one reel per single benefit.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: End every ad with a clear instruction to act, backed by a real reason for acting now.
do: Close each reel with one direct instruction plus a true urgency reason (price rising, limited stock, deadline).

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Quick response comes from a time limit, price-rise or limited-supply warnings, action words and a reward for promptness.
do: Add a dated deadline, a stock warning or a free bonus 'for those who order now' to the final seconds of the reel.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Giving helpful free information, such as recipes or tips, attracts readers and makes them more likely to buy.
do: Build a reel around a genuinely useful tip, recipe or how-to that naturally needs the product.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: An insurance ad of over 3,000 words made a complete sales talk with a coupon that works as an order form, removing the need for a salesman.
do: Make the reel's call to action a full order step with everything needed to buy, rather than a vague lead-in.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Dull products can be dramatized with story devices such as horror scenes, hidden-thoughts asides, overheard conversations and a 'shame on you' scene.
do: For a dull product, script a short scene: a hidden-thought aside, an overheard complaint or an embarrassing moment, and bring the product in after the drama.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A concrete benefit headline (a 12-page letter for one stamp) with a proof offer, and a domestic-drama angle opened a cruise to new prospects.
do: State the benefit as a concrete comparison in the hook and offer a sample as proof; try a husband-and-wife drama angle to reach non-obvious buyers.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Headlines can imply a benefit without a hard promise using price comparisons, questions, qualified testimonial forms and guarantees.
do: Frame the hook as a price comparison ('for the price of a new hat'), a question, or 'How I...' first-person result.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: When a claim can't be promised outright, use a question headline, a toned-down believable claim or a first-person testimonial headline.
do: Write hooks as questions or first-person results ('How I improved my memory in one evening') where an outright claim would be disbelieved or not allowed.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Qualify a promise with a money-back guarantee in the headline, and a coupon with a big discount drove store traffic from a small ad.
do: Put the guarantee into the hook line ('lovelier in 24 hours or your money back') and make the offer concrete with was/now prices and a limit.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Make an irresistible offer, print it on a coupon, and put it in as many hands as possible, because the coupon does the talking and reminds the customer.
do: Show the offer as a code or coupon graphic on screen that the viewer can screenshot or reuse, and make it the closing frame.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A mail order ad dramatized an emergency oxygen kit with a short headline, a risk-free 10-day trial and a clear order form.
do: Lead with the emergency scenario and finish on a risk-free trial with a money-back guarantee.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A book-club ad can sell profitably only by offering a lot for very little, such as any 6 of 99 books for 99 cents, with a short trial membership.
do: Lead with the bundle and the tiny entry price ('any 6 for 99c'), and make clear nothing is paid up front.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Mentioning the offer in the headline, with the word free emphasised, increases response, as in 'Free booklet tells how...' or 'Free to Stout Women'.
do: Put the offer or free gift in the first line of the script and on screen text, and repeat the word free or its equivalent several times.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The speed with which an offer registers on the eye matters, so show the physical item with the word 'free' beside it, hold it up, and mention it both early and at the end.
do: Show the gift or product in hand within the first seconds, with 'FREE' beside it on screen, and mention the offer again at the close.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: An attractive title and a concrete list of contents or page-by-page benefits make a free offer more attractive.
do: Name the free guide or bonus with a benefit title and read out three or four concrete contents ('on page 3 you will find...').

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Famous-person forewords, testimonials from different types of people, and a free bonus sweeten an offer and raise replies.
do: Use testimonials from several different buyer types, each tied to a specific saving or result, and add a free bonus that is theirs even if they return the product.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: When a free booklet pulls too few replies, a richer free kit with a bonus gift, or a nominal charge framed as handling costs, increases response.
do: Upgrade a weak freebie into a named kit with a small extra gift in the offer segment.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Printing the value on the coupon and putting selling copy and a no-risk return promise inside the coupon improve response.
do: Show the value on the offer card ('worth R250, yours for R50') and restate the no-risk return line in the closing frame.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Phone callers convert at 1 in 2 versus 1 in 5 for mail inquiries, and a phone number adds quality inquiries.
do: Where it fits, offer a quick call or WhatsApp number as an alternative route to buy, since those who chat convert better.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Reduce friction with no-obligation phrasing, plain-envelope discretion, and a reward for acting immediately.
do: Say 'no obligation', 'no questions' or 'plain packaging' in the offer line, and add a bonus for acting at once.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Test several different offers against each other first, then test ads around the best offer, because food and soap samples pull well and drug samples poorly.
do: Run two or three different offers on the same reel to find the strongest before polishing the creative.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: After finding the best offer, test several ads, since one will often pull twice as many inquiries from a better headline or picture; test cheaply before spending big.
do: Cut several hook variants for the winning offer and test them with small spend first.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Once the right ad size is found, pack it with facts, since long copy full of product facts beats reminder slogans, and 'the more you tell, the more you sell'.
do: For considered purchases, let the reel run longer with more facts, and keep the copy interesting throughout.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A headline and its picture must tell the same story, because readers react to the picture first and pictures convey their message faster than words.
do: Make the opening image show exactly what the first spoken or on-screen line says, so frame one and hook one never contradict each other.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A picture matched to the headline (Marie Antoinette riding to her death) drew eight times the replies, and short paragraphs, sentences and words ease reading.
do: Pair a dramatic, specific image with a line describing that exact scene, and use short sentences and short on-screen text blocks.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A children's book became popular because a ten-year-old crossed out every word he did not understand, and contractions and exclamation marks can trip the eye.
do: Test a script with a non-expert reader and swap out any word they don't understand; keep on-screen text free of clutter.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Have someone read the copy aloud: any stumble will repeat across a million viewers, and sentences needing complicated punctuation should be rewritten.
do: Read every script aloud (or have someone else do so) and rewrite any line where the reader stumbles before recording.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Style-conscious copy leaves a sense of something brilliant but nothing remembered, and plain wording is strongest.
do: Choose the plainest version of each line ('To a $15,000 man who would like to be making $25,000') over clever phrasing.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Copy should be simple, not subtle, and worn words like 'exclusive' and 'guaranteed' should be spelled out.
do: Whenever a script says 'guaranteed' or 'exclusive', follow it with exactly what that means (replace within a year, or money back).

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Simplicity is vital in appealing to the masses, as shown by film, magazines and tabloids, and starting a sentence with the idea that ended the last makes it easier to follow.
do: Link lines by opening each with the idea the previous one ended on, so the script flows.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Ad copy is full of fancy words the average person does not know, and clever advertising impresses colleagues but not readers.
do: Strip words like 'distinctive' or 'sophisticated' from scripts and test lines on someone of average education.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Writers overestimate what ordinary people know: only one in ten women knew what a Pianola was, so use words from a fifth-grade reader.
do: Never assume the viewer knows a product category term, ingredient or brand word; explain it or use a simpler one.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Lazy viewers took a poster showing a motorboat as an ad for a motorboat, not a radio, so show the actual product, not a metaphor.
do: Put the real product on screen in the opening seconds and don't use a symbolic image that could be read as another product.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A clever headline, 'I will give you Bulldog Grit', was misread as dog food, and plain writing like a letter to a friend wins cases.
do: Show every hook to a friend with no context to check they read it as intended, and write as if to a friend.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Adding a selective opener like 'Car owners!' to an existing headline lifted sample requests by 20 percent, and adding a benefit promise ('Dry Up Hay Fever') lifted them 27 percent.
do: Name the target viewer in the first words of the hook and add a benefit verb to any bare topic label.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Making the headline specific to a person and a time frame, and more dramatic ('How a Man of 40 Can Retire in 15 Years'), improved response and lead quality.
do: Put the exact audience and the exact time frame or condition into the hook, such as age plus timescale.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Swapping one word for an easier one (Repair to Fix) raised orders 20 percent, and adding 'from Failure' to a title made it win.
do: Choose the verb that sounds quick and easy, and put the before state or struggle in the hook ('from failure to success').

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Magazine cover stickers sharpen titles by shortening, lengthening or reconstructing them into concrete benefits, such as 'How to Cut Fuel Bills' for 'Hot Tips on Heating Your Home'.
do: Rewrite each hook as a short concrete benefit or number-led promise ('3 Ways to Save a Marriage'), adding 'and what to do about it' where the problem needs a payoff.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Reconstructed titles turned vague topics into concrete numbered benefits, and a Frostilla ad was reworked with a story headline about a secretary caught with rough hands.
do: Turn topics into numbered, concrete promises and try a caught-in-the-act story hook for the same product copy.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: In a split-run test, the plain ad 'Hundreds are Changing to Fragrant Frostilla' got 89% more replies than the clever 'Popular Secretary Caught Red Handed', even though people voted the clever one the winner.
do: Do not pick a hook because the team finds it clever; put the plain, direct version up against it as a live ad test.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A first-person transformation story with a hard number in the headline ('I never stopped eating yet I lost 107 pounds') makes a testimonial that reads like a real story.
do: Open a testimonial reel with the customer's own line and one concrete number, then let them tell the story in their own voice.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The Ayds ad pulled high readership by looking like editorial: real people's photos, conversational first-person copy, a signed author and no logo.
do: Shape paid reels like native content: a real person talking in plain speech, held back from brand-style graphics and logo until late.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: An art director found that ordinary people picked plain Sears-style ads over his prize-winning artistic ones, so attention and a clear selling point matter more than artistry.
do: Before locking a cut, show two versions to people outside the creative team and go with the one that grabs attention and states the selling point, not the prettier one.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Ads should jar and stop the reader rather than blend in with their surroundings, and headline type must be big and copy type plain and easy to read.
do: Make the first frame contrast with the feed, and use plain, high-contrast, easy-to-read caption fonts instead of decorative ones.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Decorative type and artfully shaped text blocks stop people reading; plain, strong type copied from proven mail order ads works, and headlines should be big enough for the most careless glancer.
do: Set captions in a bold, plain face with generous size and spacing, and enlarge the key hook words on screen.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Big type makes a headline feel like news and gives it force, and in a long headline you can enlarge a few words as long as those words carry a complete message by themselves.
do: Make the on-screen hook text large, and when it runs long, enlarge only the words that carry the whole message.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Featured words in a headline should be meaningful on their own, and the featured phrase works best at the start of the headline.
do: Highlight the meaningful phrase at the start of the caption hook (e.g. 'BREAK UP A COLD') rather than a random word in the middle.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Readership surveys show certain pictures stop people (babies, animals, odd situations, story pictures), and people tend to look at pictures of their own sex, which act as labels.
do: Open on a person who looks like the target buyer, in an odd or story-driven moment, and avoid eye-candy that stops the wrong viewer.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A picture with high attention value does not sell unless it relates to the product, and the pictures that sell show the product, the product in use, the reward of using it, or the attainment of an ambition.
do: Make the opening shot the product, the product in use, or the reward, and cut any attention-grabbing shot that has nothing to do with what we sell.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Far-fetched or too-clever pictures confuse a glancer, who reads a picture of a compass as an ad for a compass, while detail close-ups and dramatic related pictures work.
do: Use literal visuals of the product and what it does, and drop metaphorical B-roll that a scrolling viewer could misread.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A picture of the product itself usually produces the most sales, and a lifelike photograph is more believable than a drawing.
do: Show real product footage on screen early and keep any graphics or renders as lifelike as possible.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Photographs convince because they carry real detail and show a true likeness, while idealised drawings prove nothing.
do: Use unpolished real footage with visible small details (texture, fit, packaging) as proof rather than glossy stylised shots.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Large photos of faces looking straight at the viewer stop people quickly and work well in tight space, especially when the face is a user of the product.
do: Open on a close face looking into the lens, of a real user, filling the frame.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Showing the face of the person who gave a testimonial adds confidence and intimacy because the reader can look at them as they read.
do: Keep the testimonial giver's face on screen while their words play or appear, rather than cutting away to product only.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Familiar brands are bought over unfamiliar ones, so repeating the name in broadcast, spoken and shown, builds a long-term advantage, and the logo can be dropped only when the product name is already in the headline.
do: Say the brand name aloud and show it on the pack at least twice in the reel.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A picture is not a must in every ad and should earn its cost; safe choices are the product, the product in use, people who use it, and the reward of using it.
do: Build the shot list from four buckets (product, in use, user, reward) and cut any shot that does not add selling value.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: An ad made to look like a magazine article pulled 81% more orders than identical copy set in ad style, though headline-only readers may not learn what the product is.
do: Shape paid reels like content (a story, a how-to, a news item) rather than an ad, and make sure the product is named in the hook for people who watch only a few seconds.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The big-print words in an ad should deliver a quick complete message to glancers and create desire to read more, as in the first-person 'Why Wall Street Journal readers live better' ad.
do: Make the big on-screen words alone sell the idea to someone watching on mute for two seconds.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Putting the product name in the headline lets the headline sell on its own and lets the ad look like a news item, and a dramatic real-incident photo (American Tourister) gets attention.
do: Name the product and its benefit in the hook line so the opener sells on its own.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A dramatic photo of a real incident arouses curiosity and pulls the reader into a sales talk, and an easy-to-explain product like a reducing belt can sell in a small ad.
do: Open on the dramatic result or incident, then explain how the product works; keep easy-to-explain products to a short 15 s cut.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Products that people are skeptical about, like hair treatments, need long explanation and many testimonials, so small ads fail for them, while easy-to-explain products work in short ads.
do: Give simple products a 15 s reel, and give skeptical or complex products a 45–60 s reel with the explanation and several customer proofs.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Small ads let you run a whole series cheaply, feature a different product or use in each, and appear more often.
do: Split a product with several uses into separate short reels, one use per reel.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Small ads work for narrow-market needs with a one-word call-out of the sufferer, and telegraphic language like 'Free Booklet' shows how far offer copy can be trimmed.
do: Call out the specific problem or buyer in the first word on screen, and cut the offer to two words.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: To make a good short ad, boil down a big one by cutting the introduction, weak sentences and unnecessary words, or write long today and cut it tomorrow.
do: Write the 60 s script first, then cut the intro and weakest lines to make the 15 s version.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Choose either the ad-style or the editorial-style approach and do not mix them, because ad devices in an editorial-looking ad give the game away.
do: If the reel is styled as UGC or editorial, strip out the ad tricks (stopper graphics, price bursts, coupon-style cards); if it is a loud ad, commit fully.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Successful small mail order ads follow a simple formula: the picture shows the product and the headline says what it does for you.
do: Show the product in frame at the start and caption it with what it does for the viewer.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Hail-damaged apples were sold by openly explaining the marks as proof of high-altitude growth, and not one customer complained.
do: Name a visible flaw or limitation up front and reframe it as proof of quality.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Reader's Digest raised newsstand sales with a series of small news-style ads, each promoting one specific article with one specific promise.
do: Make a series of reels that each promote one single feature or promise instead of one reel that tries to say it all.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The Wynn's ad turns a vague benefit into a concrete one ('save one gallon of gas in every ten') and backs it with a near-free trial offer.
do: State the benefit as a concrete ratio the viewer can picture and pair it with a low-cost first step.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Adding two words that select the prospect ('Car Owners') to an otherwise identical headline pulled 20% more responses.
do: Begin the hook by naming exactly who it is for (e.g. 'Dog owners', 'Mums') in the first words spoken and shown.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The most commented-on Wallachs ads were built from real incidents told by salespeople, and Murine became the best seller through repeated small tested ads.
do: Mine real moments from customers and staff for script stories, since true stories sound true.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A free ski guide offer produced 6,146 replies from 13 insertions, and a family of ads can share one headline theme while the supporting facts change.
do: Run a family of reels with one repeating theme line and a different fact or use in each.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A special small-space appeal to do-it-yourself men brought unusually high response, and the false teeth ad closes with send-no-money and a guarantee.
do: Make a separate reel aimed at one niche buyer, and close with a risk-free line such as 'pay on delivery' or 'money back'.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The Wall Street Journal ad answers the buyer's objection head on ('If you think The Journal is just for millionaires, you are WRONG!') and uses a low-priced trial offer.
do: Say the biggest objection out loud in the script and answer it, then offer a cheap trial.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The winning headline is specific, uses real money figures and a strong sign of increased earnings, and a hook that shows who it is for at a glance beats one that suggests the product might not work.
do: Put a specific figure and a result in the hook, and make sure the first frame signals the right audience.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Winning headlines promise a benefit and select the right audience, while pure curiosity headlines and cute or misleading ones lost.
do: Check each hook for a stated benefit; do not rely on curiosity alone or on a clever comparison.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Winning headlines imply a promised benefit, add curiosity, speak to 'you', or give a specific personal benefit, while a bare statement of fact loses.
do: Address the viewer as 'you' and attach a benefit to any curiosity hook.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Experts cannot judge in advance what will pull, so test copy on a small scale before spending big.
do: Run each new hook at small spend against a control before scaling any version.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Reread copy the next day with a cold mind and swap long words for short, cut needless phrases, split long sentences, drop the first paragraph, and write many headlines to choose from.
do: Write at least ten hooks, sleep on the script, then cut the first line and break long sentences.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Have someone else read your copy aloud to you cold, and treat any stumble or unclear idea as a fault in the copy that must be rewritten.
do: Hand the voiceover script to someone who has not seen it, listen with a pen, and rewrite every sentence they trip on.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: In an opinion test, always give people at least two options to choose between and keep each person's choices private, because people try to please and follow others.
do: When asking colleagues about cuts, give two versions and ask them to pick, and collect votes separately.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Opinion tests mislead because people avoid voting for appeals that reflect badly on themselves, favour pictures and clever ads, whereas sales tests often favour the uncomfortable, plain or simple one.
do: Do not drop an uncomfortable appeal (e.g. bad breath, embarrassment) because internal reviewers dislike it; test it live.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A three-way opinion test can reverse a two-way result through split votes, so test one variable at a time in separate stages.
do: Test hooks in pairs and change one thing per test instead of throwing many similar variants in at once.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Judge ads by sales and lead quality as well as by reply count, because a free offer featured in the headline brings lower-quality leads.
do: Judge a hook by purchases and customer quality, not just clicks, and be wary of leading with 'free' in the hook.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Requiring a small cash payment for a sample or booklet screens out curiosity seekers.
do: Use a small shipping or paid-sample charge in the offer to filter casual clickers.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A hidden, paid sample offer brought only two replies, and about a hundred replies per test ad is the right amount for dependable results.
do: Let each variant gather around 100 results before calling a winner.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Adding free gifts and bundling them as a named 'kit' lifted replies from under fifty to over four hundred per ad.
do: Bundle the offer with a free extra under a simple name (e.g. 'Free Starter Kit') and state it in the script.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Describing what is inside the free booklet in specific, attractive terms raised requests by more than 500%.
do: Spell out exactly what the viewer gets in the offer line (what is inside, how many, what it answers) instead of just 'get it free'.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: To raise hard-to-get replies, make the offer free, set a value on it, add a gift, describe it well and widen reach, but featuring the offer in the headline skews a copy test.
do: State the offer's worth ('regular R300 value') and keep the offer identical across hook tests so only the hook changes.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Alternating test ads over time averages out outside factors like weather.
do: Run variants at the same time, not one after another, so timing does not decide the winner.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The 'cool, quiet bedroom' headline drew two and a half times the calls of the 'get rid of humidity' feature headline, so the felt result beat the engineer's best feature.
do: Lead with the result the customer feels, not the technical feature, and test the two against each other.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A direct, concrete 'How you can get a loan of $100' headline drew two and a half times the calls of a philosophical one, because people in need want the thing, not reflection.
do: Make the hook state the concrete thing the viewer gets, and avoid reflective or philosophical openers.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: With the offer and body copy held constant, one headline appeal pulled nearly 50 per cent more replies than the others, and that appeal became the campaign theme.
do: Cut four or five reels with the same body and offer but a different opening appeal, and build the campaign on the winner.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A patent-medicine seller found his winning appeal by running a different ad each week in one town and counting packs on the shelves, until one week sold out.
do: For a new product, run a different angle each week and watch sales, then build on the week that clearly spikes.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: An ad that scores high on being noticed may be attention-getting without being a selling ad.
do: Judge reels by sales and add-to-carts, not just views or hold rate, so a scroll-stopper that does not sell is not mistaken for a winner.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Split-run testing shows two ads at the same time, in the same place, to equal halves of the audience, so the only difference is the one being tested.
do: Run the two reel versions in the same ad set at the same time, changing only one thing between them.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Split-run tests are accurate enough to show small changes matter, such as a smiling model beating a serious one by 25 per cent and a one-word audience call-out lifting replies by 20 per cent.
do: Test tiny edits one at a time, such as adding a plain audience call-out to the first line or choosing a smiling over a serious face on the opening frame.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Adding a plain 'Send for Free Booklet' line above the coupon lifted replies by 5 per cent.
do: Put a spoken or on-screen call to action directly before the buy moment in the reel's final seconds.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A set of ads can be tested in knockout rounds, pairing them off and then pitting the winners against each other.
do: Test hooks in pairs per week, then run the two winners head to head.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A winner can be run against a fresh challenger each week, which gives the writer a direction to follow and new ads that push the winning appeal.
do: Keep the current best reel running and each week test it against one new reel that pushes the appeal that is winning.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Run one fixed Control ad against each new ad every day and rank the new ads by the percentage they beat or lose to the control, which can find winners several hundred per cent better.
do: Pick one existing reel as the control and test every new hook against it in the same ad set, then rank by percentage over control.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Pulling power wears down as a test series goes on, but the percentage gap between two ads stays the same wherever they fall in the series.
do: Compare each new reel to the control in the same window and trust the relative gap, not absolute results across different days.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Thirty-six headlines on one body of copy were tested against a single control in two weeks, and the best beat the control by 300 per cent and the next by 200 per cent.
do: Write 20 or more openers for one body and offer, test them cheaply against one control, and build the campaign on the top two.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Copy, media, position and season can each swing results widely, with one ad pulling 19.5 times another and ads in a campaign differing by two or three times.
do: Expect a wide spread between reels at the same spend, so make many variants and cut the losers early.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Testing replaces opinion with facts, shows which appeals are hopeless, tracks changing trends, and the one rule that never changes is to test everything small before spending big.
do: Put every new angle through a small spend test before giving it a large budget.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The headline 'Girls! Want Quick Curls?' got two and a half times the replies of the other ad, and a 25-years-later test of a similar fast-permanent headline won again.
do: Open with a direct audience call-out plus a one-line question about the fast, simple result they want, and expect old basic appeals to keep working.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A sales manager and an engineer disagreed over whether cool-and-quiet or humidity would sell more air conditioners, and a test was run to settle it.
do: Do not settle hook arguments by opinion, put both versions into a test.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: In the New York Times test the ad about a cool, quiet bedroom produced two and a half times as many sales as the humidity ad.
do: Lead with the felt benefit in the customer's own life, such as a cool, quiet night, instead of the technical cause.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Two identical cookbook ads were split-tested with a one-time price versus monthly payments, to see which plan was more profitable in the long run.
do: Test the payment framing, such as pay in instalments versus one price, and judge it on profit, not only orders.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A magazine publisher offered a free choice of article summaries in an ad to learn in advance which titles are most promotable.
do: Before filming, post a cheap choose-your-topic offer or poll to see which angle the audience picks, then script that one.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Ten Rybutol ads were tested in ten days by running each against a control, with only the headlines and subheads changed.
do: Keep body and offer identical and change only the opening line for each test.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The copy was the same in every ad and each carried its own key number in the address so replies could be traced to the ad.
do: Give every reel variant its own code or tracking link so sales trace back to the opener.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: In the Rybutol test the best ad pulled 235 per cent more replies than the control and the worst pulled 24 per cent fewer, and the winning appeal drove a successful campaign.
do: Expect the best of ten hooks to be about double or triple the control, and build the full campaign on that winning appeal.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The Alexander Hamilton ad opens by selecting only the imaginative reader, then walks them through an imagined two-year trip meeting top bankers.
do: Open with a second-person walk-through of the experience, saying 'you will' step by step, and flatter the right viewer by selecting them.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The ad says the books and lectures are not the real course, the real product is the experience of successful men, and it ends with a free booklet.
do: Name the real product as the outcome or experience, not the physical item, and close on a free low-risk next step.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The Hathaway eye-patch image made almost everyone ask why the man wore it and also read the copy, and a good mail-order ad ran for seven years because repeating a winner pays.
do: Open on one odd, unexplained visual detail that makes viewers ask why, and pay it off in the copy; keep running proven winners.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Hopkins wrote with short paragraphs, short sentences and simple language, and said people will never know the benefit unless the headline or picture tells them.
do: Keep lines short and plain, and show the benefit in the first frame and first line.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: A short story of a client who could not tell a copied necklace from her own told the whole sales case in a few words.
do: Use a tiny anecdote or scene that demonstrates the product's quality in a few seconds.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The Dale Carnegie ad was tested first, then run widely and produced nearly 100,000 direct orders using a five-day free trial with no money sent now.
do: Offer a no-risk trial line, such as try it and keep it only if it does what we claim, and test the ad small before scaling.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The Sherwin Cody headline asks 'Do You Make These Mistakes in English?', making the reader check themselves against specific common errors.
do: Open with a question naming a mistake the viewer may be making, then list two or three specific examples.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The Travelers story ad ranked first in readership because of its sincerity, and the Hamilton watch ad, a list of thank-yous to a wife, was voted the ad writers' favorite.
do: Tell a short real story with a personal moment and a moral, or run a sincere list of specific thank-yous.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The French course ad opens on a scene where friends grin when the waiter speaks French to the narrator, with laughter turning to amazement at his reply.
do: Script a scene of doubt turning to surprise, with a person in company showing the skill they were thought to lack.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The narrator reveals he learned French with no teacher in minutes a day, with no tiresome rules, and the ad ends with a five-day free trial.
do: Use the reveal, then ease claims, such as just minutes a day with no hard rules, and finish on a free trial.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The French ad's tense moment drags out the suspense before the reply, and the Rolls-Royce headline opens with one concrete surprising fact about the clock being the loudest noise at 60 miles an hour.
do: Hold the reveal for a beat for suspense, and lead with one specific surprising fact as proof instead of a general claim.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Ogilvy's Rolls-Royce ad outsold vague puffery by using a very long headline and 719 words of pure fact, because the more you tell the more you sell.
do: In a 30 to 60 second reel, fill the script with specific, checkable facts about the product (materials, numbers, how it works) instead of general praise, and let the spoken lines carry one concrete fact after another.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: The Liberty Mutual ad sells by naming a special group (careful drivers), giving a selective reason to qualify, backing it with a dollar figure and years in business, and ending with a free, no-obligation booklet offer.
do: Open the script by addressing a specific kind of person ('if you're a careful driver'), give one hard number as proof, and close on a free, low-risk next step.

title: Tested Advertising Methods
author: John Caples
says: Localizing the ad with a panel headed 'If You Live in New York' increased coupon response, and offering lower cost to a selected group started a new school of insurance advertising.
do: Name the place or the group in the hook (for example 'Cape Town' or 'if you live in Joburg') and add a local delivery or availability line to lift response.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
chapter: Chapter 9: Instant Influence: Primitive Consent for an Automatic Age
says: Persuasion works in order: first make people feel warm toward you (reciprocation, liking, unity), then reduce their doubt (social proof, authority), then push them to act (consistency, scarcity).
do: Build the script in that order: a friendly or relatable opening, then proof and expert backing in the middle, and close with a reason to act now.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Giving a reason with a request, even a meaningless one, lifts compliance from 60 to about 94 percent because the word 'because' itself triggers agreement.
do: Put 'because' and a reason in every ask and call to action, for example 'Grab the 100ml because it lasts twice as long', rather than a bare instruction.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Buyers unsure of quality treat price as a sign of quality, so a higher price alone made the turquoise sell.
do: For premium products, don't lead with cheapness; let the price sit on screen as a quality cue and talk value only after.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A buyer rejected a $250 necklace as too cheap but loved it when it was shown at $500 and then discounted as a gift.
do: Show the full price first, then present the lower price as a gift or special reason rather than an everyday low price.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People who believed a drink or painkiller cost more expected it to work better, and it did, because price shapes expectations.
do: Avoid 'cheap' language in scripts; use words like 'affordable' or 'worth it' and show quality cues alongside the price.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People who care about an issue weigh the arguments, while uninvolved or distracted people go by shortcuts like the speaker's expertise.
do: Cold scrollers are low involvement, so lead with a quick cue like an expert, a number of buyers or a rating instead of a long argument.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Fake reviews lack concrete detail, use more 'I' and more verbs than nouns, and trust in reviewed businesses fell from 72 to 68 percent.
do: Write testimonial lines with concrete nouns and specifics, such as the bottle, the scent after hours or the delivery day, so they sound real rather than generic praise.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Contrast makes the second of two different things look more different than it is, as with the hot and cold water buckets.
do: Set up a contrast before the product shows, such as a drab or dear alternative first, then cut to your product.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Clothiers sell the costly suit first because later items, even pricey ones, then seem cheaper by comparison.
do: In bundles or upsells, show the big-ticket item or set first so the smaller add-ons feel small.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Showing the expensive item first makes later prices seem lower, while showing cheap first makes the expensive one look worse; estate agents even show bad 'setup' houses first.
do: Order price reveals big to small, and when comparing, show the poor alternative or old way first so your product looks better after it.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Car dealers add options after the main price is settled so small extras feel trivial, and an airline's $10,000 joke made a $200 offer look worthless.
do: Introduce add-ons after the main price is agreed and never anchor with a silly high number before the real one.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People feel they must repay what they are given: strangers returned Christmas cards, and bankers gave over twice as much after receiving a small packet of sweets.
do: Give something first in the video, such as a tip, a free sample or a useful fact, before making the ask.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A small favour wiped out the effect of disliking the requester, so even unwelcome people get yes after a gift.
do: Open with a small useful gift or freebie even when the brand is unknown or the viewer is cold.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Gifts given before the request beat rewards promised after: a $5 gift check with a survey did twice as well as a $50 payment, and a mint raised tips.
do: Put the free gift, bonus or sample up front in the offer, not as a reward for buying.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Giving children balloons on entry rather than exit raised the family's bill by 25 percent, including adult coffee.
do: Give the gift at the start of the interaction, such as the opening seconds of the video or first touch, and not after the purchase.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A free piece of candy made shoppers 42 percent more likely to buy, and they bought other candies, so the lift came from obligation and not from liking the taste.
do: Lead with a free sample or small gift such as a mini vial or travel size, because it lifts purchase even when the sample is not what they buy.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Free samples work both by informing and by indebting, and Amway leaves a bag of products free for one to three days.
do: Pitch a free or risk-free trial as a gift, such as 'try it for a week on us'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A gift personalised to the recipient's taste, like museum postcards for an art collector, cut a slow payer's delay and magnified the obligation.
do: Tailor any bonus to the specific audience, such as a scent note or occasion, instead of a generic freebie.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A gift matched to the customer's current need, yogurt for hungry diners, doubled the lift of an equal-value key ring.
do: Choose the freebie or bonus that matches the viewer's moment, such as a gift-ready box at gifting season, over a random extra.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Guests whose problem was fixed personally gave higher satisfaction and loyalty than guests who had no problem, because the fix felt like a customised gift.
do: Use a customer story where a mistake was quickly and personally put right as proof, for example a late order fixed with a handwritten note.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: An unrequested gift still creates a debt: adding free address labels nearly doubled donations from 18 to 35 percent.
do: Don't wait for the viewer to ask; include the free extra in the offer unprompted.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Charities frame their enclosed items as a gift rather than a product, because pressure to reciprocate a gift is stronger than pressure to buy.
do: Word the extra as 'a gift from us' in the script, not as a discount or bundle item.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Debt feels uncomfortable and being seen as a taker is shameful, so people give back more; two mints raised tips 14 percent against 3.3 for one.
do: Generosity beyond the minimum counts: add a second small extra rather than one grudging one.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: After refusing $5 circus tickets the author bought $1 chocolate bars he didn't want, because the smaller ask was presented as a retreat.
do: Offer a big option first, then step down to a smaller one as a concession in the same ad or sequence.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People feel obliged to concede when the other side concedes, so a smaller second request framed as a retreat gets a yes.
do: Structure the offer as a step down: show the big set first, then say 'or just start with the single bottle', worded as a concession.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Reciprocal concessions are how society handles compromise, which is why asking big, getting a no, then asking smaller works.
do: Sequence the pitch so the larger ask is declined first, either with two offers on screen or a follow-up ad, then present the real target.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Asking for a huge commitment first tripled agreement to a still-large second request, from 17 to 50 percent.
do: The second ask doesn't have to be small, only smaller than the first, so test a premium bundle ask before the single-item ask.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: The tactic backfires if the first request is so extreme it looks unreasonable, since then the retreat isn't seen as a real concession.
do: Keep the anchor offer believable, a pricey but real bundle, and not an absurd number.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Asking for a big thing first and then retreating to the smaller one you wanted makes the smaller ask feel smaller by contrast and feel like a concession to be repaid.
do: Show the biggest bundle or highest price first, then land on the real offer as the 'smaller' option.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Starting with a big request raised yes rates to the smaller one from 29 to 76 percent and show-up rates from 50 to 85 percent, and made people more willing to agree again later.
do: Anchor on the larger pack or longer commitment, then present the smaller one as the easy fallback.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: You cannot reason people out of feeling-based beliefs, but a widely liked person's endorsement shifted attitudes regardless of age, sex or religiosity, so liking is the lever for changing feelings.
do: Open with a face the viewer already likes or trusts reacting to the product, and use their feeling before any spec or argument.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A Tupperware sale works because the ask comes from a friend, and the strength of the social bond is twice as likely to decide the purchase as the product preference.
do: Have the ask come from someone who feels like a friend, such as a creator talking to camera, rather than a brand voiceover.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Mentioning a friend's name as the source of a recommendation makes refusal feel like rejecting the friend.
do: Frame testimonials and UGC as 'a friend told me', and use a real named person where possible.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: 92 percent of consumers trust recommendations from someone they know, more than any other source, and referred customers were 18 percent more loyal and 16 percent more profitable.
do: Shape testimonial-style reels as a friend-to-friend recommendation, not an ad pitch.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: We like people who are like us in opinions, background or lifestyle, and similarity was the best predictor of attraction across 421 million dating matches.
do: Cast on-camera people who look and sound like the target buyer, and say the shared trait early.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Even trivial similarities such as clothing, interests, or a near-matching name raise compliance, in one case nearly doubling survey response.
do: Open with a small shared detail the viewer will recognise, such as a shared setting, habit or local reference.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Using the words and slang of your audience builds liking, and the author endorses finding genuine parallels but not faking them.
do: Write scripts in the audience's own South African phrasing and avoid brand-speak the viewer would not say.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Compliments reliably increase liking and compliance, from restaurant tips to job offers.
do: Try a hook that compliments the viewer's taste or choice, as in 'you already know good fragrance'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Altercasting assigns a person a social role such as protector, and they then tend to act in line with it.
do: Address the viewer as a role, such as 'you're the one who always gets asked what you're wearing', so the buy fits who they are.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Praising someone's trait, like conscientiousness or helpfulness, makes them show more of it later.
do: Praise a trait in the viewer that the purchase expresses, such as being thoughtful or generous for a gift.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: The more often we are exposed to something, even without noticing, the more we like it and believe it.
do: Repeat the same face, product shot or sound across a campaign's variations so familiarity builds.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Placing a product beside attractive or positive things transfers their appeal to it, and viewers deny being influenced.
do: Cut the product beside desirable imagery, such as beautiful people, settings and textures, so the appeal rubs off.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: The mere presence of credit-card logos raised spending and giving, so positive symbols in view lift behaviour even when unrelated and unnoticed.
do: Keep trusted or positively loaded symbols, such as familiar payment marks and badges, visible in the frame during the offer.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A connection only needs to be positive, not logical, to lift sales, and SALE signs raise buying even without real savings.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People come to like the ideas, products and faces they meet while enjoying something pleasant like food, and unpleasant smells lowered approval of the same slogans.
do: Pair the key claim or offer line with a pleasant sensory moment on screen, such as food, warmth or satisfying sound, and keep it free of anything irritating.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Any pleasant thing can lend its warmth to whatever it is paired with, as with a jingle placed just before a hit song, and people avoid being linked to bad news.
do: Place the brand sound or logo right before the payoff beat so the lift lands on the brand.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Labelling a menu item the restaurant's 'most popular' lifted its sales 13 to 20 percent, and a pub's sign naming its most popular beer doubled that beer's sales, at no cost.
do: Open or label the hero product with a true popularity line ('our most popular', 'the one everyone reorders') on screen in the first seconds.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Telling customers a specific item is 'our visitors' favorite' raised McFlurry sales 55 percent, and naming the favorite topping added 48 percent more.
do: Name the best-selling variant or bundle in the offer beat, then name the favourite add-on as a second line.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Netflix found that telling members what was popular made those shows more popular, and 'fastest growing' or 'largest selling' claims work because they show many others think so.
do: Use a real count or rank (units sold, reorder rate, ranking) as the proof line instead of arguing the product is good.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Social proof is a useful shortcut that hustlers fake with planted crowds, seeded tip jars and paid reviews, and people tend to be moved more by what others do than by any argument.
do: Use only real numbers and real customers as proof, and show them plainly so the proof can't be mistaken for staged.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Telling people most others do something changes behaviour across many areas, such as Louisville's parking-fine letter raising payment 130 percent, and nearly all online shoppers say authentic reviews matter most.
do: Put real customer reviews or a 'most people do X' line on screen near the end of a reel, before the call to action.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Film clips showing many children with dogs worked best, and a car dealer's ad about heavy demand lifted sales 41.7 percent.
do: Show several customers using the product, not one, and mention demand ('we can't keep up') as a side line.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Social-proof information persuades more when people think it isn't meant to persuade them, as with demand slipped into a recruitment ad.
do: Let the proof arrive incidentally inside a scene, such as a boxes-stacking-up packing shot or a founder saying 'we're slammed', not as 'everyone is buying, get yours'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: With physical proof gone, the cult sought social proof, and social proof works best under uncertainty, from many people, and from people like us.
do: Check every proof moment for three things: is the viewer unsure, are there many voices, are they people like the viewer.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People who are unsure or unfamiliar lean hardest on others' choices, and an unfamiliar-looking shopping cart only took off once hired shoppers were seen using it.
do: For a new or odd-looking product, put a real person using it casually in the first seconds before explaining it.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Hired shoppers using the carts reduced customer uncertainty, and a London crowd shows how people follow others when no information is given.
do: Where the viewer doesn't know what to do with the product, show others doing it so the action reads as normal.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Pointing at one named person with a specific instruction removes the doubts that stop bystanders helping.
do: Make the call to action as specific as 'You, in the blue jacket, call 911': one named action, one place to tap, one thing to do now.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: The more people look up at an empty spot, the more passersby copy them, up to around twenty people.
do: In a proof shot, fill the frame with several people reacting or using the product, not one person.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Viewers judged debate candidates by how loudly the studio audience responded, even when that response was edited.
do: Keep real audience or crowd reactions (laughs, gasps, a live room) in the cut, since viewers read them as a verdict.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Canned laughter makes viewers laugh more and rate material funnier, and 'the many' works through validity, feasibility and social acceptance.
do: Cut to real reactions from real people to land a joke or claim, and avoid faking them.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A poster showing several people having an early lunch lifted early food-court traffic 75 percent, three times the lift from a poster showing one person.
do: Show multiple people taking the action in the proof shot, and use 'x out of y' style percentages where true.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Seeing many others do something tells us it's doable as well as sensible.
do: Show ordinary people doing the thing quickly and easily so the viewer thinks 'I could do that'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A message that most neighbours conserve energy produced 3.5 times the saving of messages about the environment, duty or money, because it makes the action feel achievable.
do: Lead with what most customers already do instead of the benefit, for example 'most people here already switched'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Going against the group causes real emotional pain, so being one of the many feels safe and accepted.
do: Frame the purchase as joining something people like the viewer already belong to, and show the group.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Social proof is strongest when it comes from people just like us, which the author calls peer-suasion.
do: Cast creators and testimonial voices who match the target buyer's age, look and situation.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People follow similar others, which is why advertisers use average-person testimonials to sell to ordinary viewers.
do: Prefer a customer who looks like the audience over a polished expert or celebrity for the proof beat.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Saying 'I'm a student here too' more than doubled donations, and comparing homes to nearby 'homes just like yours' drove large savings.
do: Open with a similarity line ('I'm a Cape Town mum too', 'same size flat as yours') before making the ask.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Same-age peers work better than adults as teachers or models for children, as the author's swimming story begins to show.
do: Choose the on-screen model who matches the viewer's exact situation.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A three-year-old dropped his swim ring after learning that another three-year-old could swim, though an adult instructor couldn't persuade him.
do: Use a closely matched peer to say 'I did it, so you can' rather than an expert telling the viewer.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A door-to-door seller raised sales 62 percent by citing past customers' names, then raised them further by only citing customers of the same type as the prospect.
do: Make versions of the proof for each segment (mums, men, couples) and match the testimonial speaker to the viewer.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: The seller credited social proof from similar others for a 119.67 percent improvement, and then the author turns to copycat suicide data.
do: Test a proof line that names someone like the buyer against a generic one in the same ad.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People's brand choices track the choices of similar people around them, and region explained about 80 percent of national brands' market share.
do: Name the place or the kind of person in the proof line, such as 'Cape Town moms are buying this', rather than a vague 'thousands of customers'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Campaigns that lament how many people do an unwanted thing end up signalling that everyone does it, which makes the behaviour worse.
do: Don't open a hook by saying that most people have the problem and nobody fixes it; that makes the bad habit look normal. Show the problem as something a few people are stuck with and the solution as what people like the viewer do.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A sign showing three thieves nearly tripled theft, while a sign showing one lone thief cut it below the baseline.
do: When a script has to show the problem, show one person with it (one dull-skinned friend, one bad purchase), never a crowd, and put the crowd in the solution shot.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Because fewer than 3 percent steal, the park missed the chance to use true social proof by telling visitors that the great majority are honourable.
do: Where the majority behaviour is the desired one, state it as a number: 'Most of our customers reorder in month two.'

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: If only a minority does something but the numbers are rising, people expect the trend to continue and join in.
do: For a young brand without big sales numbers, put the growth in a super in the first seconds: 'Orders doubled since June', rather than staying quiet about size.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Students told that only a minority conserve water used the most, but those told the minority was growing used the least, because trends read as where the majority is heading.
do: Do not say 'only a few people know about us'. Pair any small number with its direction: 'from 200 to 2,000 customers in a year'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: If a new product has honest evidence of growing popularity, make that growth the central feature of the messaging, and if it has none, rethink the product.
do: For launch-stage brands, build the proof beat around week-on-week or month-on-month growth, and only use it if the figure is real and can be checked.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Fake reviews tend to lack detail, overuse first-person pronouns and use more verbs than nouns, and the regular-people testimonial format works but only shows those who like the product.
do: Write testimonial lines with concrete nouns, such as the product, the day it arrived and what changed, so they read as real rather than as generic praise.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Social proof is strongest for people who are unsure, and simply pointing to an item's popularity raises its popularity.
do: For cold audiences who don't know the product, put the popularity line, such as number sold or reviews, near the top of the script.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Social proof is strongest when people are uncertain, when many others are doing it, and when those others are similar to them.
do: Cast and caption proof so that the viewer sees many people like them, in their own situation and area, instead of one polished model.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: In a bank donation test, a free gift plus a CEO's personal letter lifted compliance from 5 percent to 17 percent, well above either alone.
do: Stack a small free gift in the offer with a visible authority voice, such as a free sample with a founder or expert saying why.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: The look of authority (lab coat, stethoscope) can trigger compliance even without real credentials.
do: When the person on screen genuinely holds the credential, dress the frame to show it: coat, clinic or workspace visible in the first seconds.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A title changes how people treat a speaker, making them respectful and agreeable.
do: Put the expert's real title on a lower-third in the opening seconds, before they start making claims.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People obeyed an odd request far more often when the requester wore a guard uniform, 92 percent against 42 percent in street clothes.
do: Put the presenter in the clothing of their role (scrubs, apron, lab coat, chef whites) when the role is real, and show it in the first frame.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People dressed in prestige-labelled or higher quality clothing got far more survey compliance and donations and were judged more competent in under a second.
do: Check wardrobe on every person who speaks to camera: clean, well-made clothes, since viewers judge competence in under a second.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A set of experts is trusted more than any single expert, so citing several sources beats citing one.
do: In the proof beat, cite two or three independent voices, such as a dermatologist, a magazine and a stylist, rather than one.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Credible authority needs expertise and trustworthiness, and visible credentials create a halo that raises ratings of the expert's kindness as well.
do: Show diplomas or credentials on the wall or on screen behind the expert; it lifts how warm they seem too.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Mentioning a weakness early makes the speaker seem honest, so the strengths that follow are believed more.
do: Put the one honest drawback in the first third of the script, such as price, slower shipping or a small size, then go straight into the strongest benefit.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Admitting a drawback first wins more trials, votes and sales (Domino's), especially when the audience already knows the flaw.
do: If viewers already know the weakness, such as price, say it plainly in the opening lines instead of dodging it.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Average ratings above about 4.7 make shoppers suspect fake reviews, so 4.2 to 4.7 sells best.
do: Show real review screenshots around 4.5 with some mixed ones rather than a perfect 5.0 claim.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Negative reviews lift conversion by 67 percent, and the strongest argument should come right after the admission of a shortcoming.
do: Order the script as the honest flaw, then straight into the single best benefit, with no filler between them.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People trained to check credentials were less swayed by irrelevant spokespeople and more swayed by relevant ones.
do: Pick on-camera experts whose credentials match the product claim exactly, and state that credential on screen.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Experts who seem impartial persuade more than those who gain from our compliance, and arguing slightly against one's own interest signals sincerity.
do: Let the expert or founder say something that costs them, such as 'you may not need the big size', to signal impartiality.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A minor, easily outweighed drawback, as in Avis's 'We're #2' and L'Oréal's 'more expensive', establishes honesty so the main argument is believed.
do: Write the flaw as a line that flips into a strength, such as 'We're not the cheapest. Here's why people still reorder.'

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A waiter seen as knowledgeable and on your side got diners to ask him to choose, then upsold wine and dessert.
do: Have the expert say 'let me pick for you' and name a specific bundle or higher-priced option, rather than listing everything.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Owning up to failures helps companies and individuals, and seeming to argue against one's own financial interest served Vincent's interest very well.
do: If the brand has had a known problem like late deliveries or a bad batch, a short line owning it and saying what changed builds trust.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Ordering people creates resistance, while being seen as highly informed makes them willing to follow, and admitting a small flaw adds trust.
do: Write as a knowledgeable friend recommending ('here's what I'd pick'), not as a brand commanding ('buy now').

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Rewording the proposal as 'We have a deal' worked, and students liked cafeteria food more once they learned they would lose it.
do: Make availability visible and real, such as a restock date or end of a run, since losing access raises how much people value something.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People are more motivated to avoid losing something of value than to gain it, especially under risk and uncertainty.
do: Frame the offer and the hook around what the viewer stands to lose, such as price rise or sellout, more than what they might gain.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Wording that gives people possession of the thing first ('We have a deal') makes the alternative feel like a loss, which pushes them to close.
do: Write the CTA as something already theirs and at risk: 'Your bundle is reserved for the next 24 hours', not 'Get the bundle'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People are wired to fear loss more than they value gain, and anything rare or becoming rare is judged more valuable, even when the rarity comes from a flaw.
do: In an offer line, name what the viewer loses by missing out (the rare feature, the small batch) rather than only what they gain.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Potential loss moves people more than an equal gain, and messages framed around what stands to be lost work best when risk and uncertainty are present.
do: Write the hook or close as what the viewer stands to lose (the sale ending, the stock selling through) instead of what they could gain.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Telling shoppers how few units are left at a given price sharply raises purchases, as Booking.com found.
do: Put the real remaining count on screen in the offer beat (for example 'only 14 left in this colour') and cut to it right before the call to action.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Presenting an item in abundance lowers its perceived value, so abundant stock is better offered a piece at a time, and a 'sold to someone else' cue makes it more wanted.
do: Feature one product or bundle per video and drop releases in small batches rather than showing the full catalogue at once.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: If supply is unlimited, scarcity can still be used honestly by marketing a feature, or a unique combination of features, that can't be had elsewhere and what is lost if it is missed.
do: For brands with endless stock, find the one thing only they have (the founder's recipe, a local ingredient, the formula) and make the script's offer beat about losing that, not about units left.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Across 6,700 tests, low-stock notices, popularity badges and countdown timers were top performers, and limited-supply appeals generally beat limited-time ones.
do: Lead with a limited-supply cue (low stock, bestseller) and use a time limit as the second cue; show both as on-screen badges.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Deadlines make people want things they didn't much favour, and stacking several scarcity cues in a few words intensifies the effect.
do: Close the reel with a dated deadline line plus one more scarcity cue in the same breath, such as 'Ends Sunday, limited batch'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: When access to something is limited or threatened we want it more, which is psychological reactance.
do: Frame the hook around something the viewer is being kept from or might lose access to ('You can't get this in store') rather than a plain benefit.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: When something becomes less available, people want it more and then invent positive qualities to explain that desire, and banned information is likewise wanted and believed more.
do: Use 'banned', 'pulled' or 'can't get it anymore' angles for a product and let the viewer's desire carry the claim, with no need to over-list benefits.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Telling students a novel was restricted to adults made them want it and expect to like it more, and judges' instructions to ignore evidence often backfire.
do: Try a restriction-style hook ('Not for everyone', 'Only for people who...') to raise interest in a product.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Information is more persuasive when people believe they can't get it elsewhere, so the beef experiment tested scarce supply plus scarce news of that supply.
do: Frame the scarcity news as inside information ('here's what we're hearing from our supplier') in the script.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Customers told of a coming beef shortage bought twice as much, and those told it was exclusive information bought six times as much.
do: Deliver the scarcity news as a reveal only the viewer gets ('We haven't told anyone yet, but stock is running low'), as it doubles the effect of the shortage alone.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Adding 'but you are free to say no' to a request often more than doubled compliance, and admitting a drawback early lowers resistance and builds credibility.
do: End the call to action with a freedom line ('No pressure, you decide') and mention one honest drawback early in the script.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Something that has just become scarce is valued more than something always scarce, and a fall from abundance to scarcity feels strongest.
do: Show the supply shrinking (earlier abundant, now almost gone) rather than just stating it is limited.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Procter and Gamble's coupon removal caused a consumer revolt even though few used coupons, because long-held perks feel like rights.
do: Frame an ending discount or perk as something the viewer already had and is about to lose.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Cookies that became scarce because of other people's demand were rated most desirable, so showing competition for the item is stronger than plain scarcity or ordinary social proof.
do: Show other buyers taking the stock (orders coming in, 'selling fast', a crowd) and make it feel like the viewer is competing with them.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A rival bidder makes hesitant buyers eager, and competitive crowds drive frenzied wanting for items they would normally disdain.
do: Edit in fast cuts of other buyers or a live 'sold' counter to build rival pressure toward the end.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People want to stand out, especially in romantic moods and matters of taste, and an earned symbol loses value when it is handed to everyone.
do: For taste-driven products, pitch the item as setting the viewer apart and add a small visible detail they can choose to differ on.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
