says: The author's brother created competition by booking all car viewers for the same appointment time.
do: Create shared-slot urgency, such as a single drop time everyone is waiting for, in an organic or launch video.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Scarcity works best when it is new and when people compete for the item.
do: Announce the change as it happens ('as of today it's down to...') and show others competing for it.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People grow more certain about a choice once they have made it, such as horse-track bettors after placing a bet.
do: Get the viewer to pick a side early (a vote, comment or choice) so the later offer is consistent with their pick.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A small commitment ('watch my things') turned nineteen of twenty bystanders into thief-chasers, because people want to act consistently with what they've agreed to.
do: Open with a tiny yes-ask (a nod, a comment, a pick) that the call to action can later follow.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Toy makers advertise a toy before Christmas, undersupply it, then advertise again so parents buy to keep their promise.
do: Run a teaser campaign first and a stronger relaunch after, so viewers who 'promised themselves' come back.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Getting someone to take a stand or go on record sets up automatic consistency with it.
do: In scripts, ask the viewer to state or imagine their intention ('Tell me which one you'd pick') before the offer.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Asking people to predict what they'd do (volunteer) boosted actual volunteers sevenfold days later, and commitments made on paper control customers.
do: Open with a question that gets the viewer to say what they'd do ('Would you try this if it worked?') and have the call to action refer back to it.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A lofty stated commitment, or a polite 'how are you?' answered 'fine', makes later refusal feel inconsistent.
do: Start with a simple, easy-to-agree opening line or question to set the viewer saying yes before the ask.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Asking 'how are you feeling?' nearly doubled agreement (18 to 32 percent) and 89 percent of those who agreed then bought.
do: Lead with a 'how's your X going?' style question that gets a positive answer before presenting the ask.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Asking buyers to state the reasons for their choice commits them to those reasons, which lifted sales by 10 to 19 percent.
do: Put a question in the script that makes the viewer name their own reason, e.g. 'What do you want people to say when you walk past?'. Do not just list ours.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Salespeople start with a small order because its purpose is commitment, not profit, and larger purchases follow (the foot-in-the-door technique).
do: Make the first offer in the reel a small, low-risk entry step (a sample, a mini size, a discovery set) rather than the full-price buy.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Homeowners who had agreed to a tiny sign were 76 percent likely to accept a huge one, against 17 percent of those not asked first.
do: Sequence the ask: get a small yes (comment, tap, claim a sample) before the bigger purchase ask in a follow-up video.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Agreeing to a small unrelated request changed how people saw themselves, so about half then agreed to a much larger one.
do: Open with a small agreement that flatters the viewer's identity ('you're someone who notices good scent'), then make the ask.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Commitments work best when active, public, effortful and freely chosen, and cutting the first-page form fields from four to three raised completions 50 percent.
do: Make the first action in the funnel tiny and easy to finish, and show it in the video as one quick step.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People who actively opted in were far more likely to show up (74 percent) than those who passively failed to opt out, and they explained it as their own values.
do: End on an active ask the viewer does themselves, such as comment your pick or tap to choose, rather than a passive 'shop now'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Labelling shoppers with a flattering identity on the sign lifted purchases of the eco bananas from 32 to 51 percent, more than a price message did (46 percent).
do: Open the hook by naming the viewer's flattering identity ('Hey, you who actually reads ingredient lists') and show the product as what that kind of person picks. Test it against a price-led hook.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Testimonial contests get people to write praise for a product, and writing it makes them believe it.
do: Run a 'finish the sentence: I love it because...' prompt to gather customer lines for proof cuts, and invite viewers to write their own.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Changing 'Please call us if you change your plans' to a question that waits for a spoken yes cut no-shows from 30 to 10 percent.
do: Phrase the closing line as a question the viewer answers ('Will you grab yours before Friday?') and leave a beat of silence before the end card.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Big rewards or threats produce compliance but not inner commitment, and can undermine the sense of owning the action.
do: Do not make a deep discount the only reason to buy in a script; give the viewer a reason of their own so the choice sticks after the sale ends.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A sign reminding doctors of their commitment raised hand-hygiene use 45 percent, and a signed pledge poster cut bad antibiotic prescribing 27 percent.
do: In retargeting videos, remind the viewer of the step they already took ('You picked the oud last week') before the ask.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Unity comes from shared identity ('one of us'), not from similar tastes ('like us'), and people say yes to someone they consider one of them.
do: Pick the presenter and the opening line for shared identity (place, language, culture, role), not just similar taste. Say it in the first second, e.g. 'Cape Town mums, this one's for you'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Ali Reda out-sold Joe Girard by following Girard's method and adding ethnic membership of the community he sold to.
do: Cast creators and testimonial voices who visibly belong to the target audience's community, and have them speak as insiders.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: The unity effect strengthens when something makes the shared identity salient, like an election or a holiday.
do: Put a visible identity cue in the opening seconds (local landmark, language, season or holiday) so the 'we' is active when the pitch lands.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: In couples' arguments, only the 'we, our, us' appeal changed minds, while threats backfired and logic was ignored.
do: Open the script with the shared 'we' ('we're all tired of...') and make the ask only after that. Don't lead with a logical case or a scare line.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People act on whatever is most prominent in their mind at the moment of decision, so a reminder of a bond can change behaviour without any new argument.
do: Put the one connection you want in the viewer's head (a place, a community, a shared habit) in the first two seconds, since it will steer the decision more than a later feature list.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Shopping features built on friends' tastes lifted sales and order value, and the closer the friend, the stronger the pull.
do: For social proof, show a peer or close-friend style voice (a friend text, a mate recommending) ahead of a faceless review count.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Family words like brothers, heritage and legacy make people more willing to sacrifice for a group.
do: Use family language in brand talk (the family behind it, a heritage, 'our people') when the brand genuinely has that story.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Buffett made his case more convincing by saying he would tell shareholders what he would tell his family, and admitting up front where he could be wrong.
do: Frame the pitch as advice you'd give a family member ('what I'd tell my sister') and name one weakness first to earn the belief.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People trust and favour those who look like them or share core attitudes, and even a digitally morphed face resembling the viewer raises trust.
do: Cast creators and testimonial faces who resemble the target buyer in age, look and attitude, and match them to the audience of each ad.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Rescuers mostly said yes to relatives and neighbours asking on behalf of strangers, and the successful rescuer recruited through existing close ties.
do: Get the request to the viewer from someone in their own circle (a local, a neighbour, a mutual) rather than from the brand alone.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A rabbi saved his community by naming one shared identity with the listeners, and the Nazis were left outside it.
do: Find the single identity the viewer shares with the brand or creator (South African, Capetonian, mom, runner) and say it in the opening line before any product talk.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Doing things in unison (reading, speaking, dancing) makes people feel merged and cooperate better.
do: Cut movement to the beat and use chants, call-and-response or group actions so the viewer feels part of the rhythm.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Synchronised action raises liking and cut the bias in a test where people mirrored sipping water with out-group members.
do: Cut on matching gestures or mirrored motion, and let the viewer copy a simple action along with the creator.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Teams that marched in step were 50 percent more cooperative, and music is the practical way to create synchrony at scale.
do: Pick a track with a clear beat and land the key cuts and product reveals on it.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Appeals work better when matched to the buyer's mode: 'I feel this is for you' for emotional buyers, 'I think' for rational ones.
do: For feeling-led products like fragrance, write lines in 'feel' language; for spec-led products, write 'think' language with facts.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Music pushes people into feeling mode and makes analytical thinking hard.
do: Use music where the case rests on mood, not facts, but don't use it to cover a weak product case.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Match the message to the audience's mindset: emotional, hedonistic buyers get music, practical buyers get facts.
do: Decide per ad whether the buyer is in a feeling or a thinking mindset, then score it with music or build it on proof and numbers accordingly.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Music helps ads for familiar, feelings-based products but hurts ads for high-consideration products with strong arguments.
do: Drop or lower background music in videos selling considered purchases (tech, devices) so the claims can be heard.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Taking turns in escalating self-disclosure built strong closeness among strangers in 45 minutes.
do: Structure creator scripts as a back-and-forth that gets steadily more personal, starting light and ending with a real confession or story.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Shared pain bonds people more than a shared neutral activity does, as groups with hands in ice water cooperated more.
do: Open with a pain or annoyance the viewer and creator both live through ('load shedding again?') before offering the product.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Managers who helped create an ad rated the identical ad 50 percent higher.
do: Let the audience help shape the product or content (pick the next scent, vote on a colour) and show their input in the final ad.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Co-creation merges identities and brands win loyalty by inviting customers to co-create products.
do: Run content that asks customers for feature ideas and later show 'you asked, we made it'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Asking people for advice, not opinions, made them feel linked to the brand and more willing to buy from it.
do: Ask the audience for advice in captions and on-screen prompts ('What would you advise?'), not 'What do you think?'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Asking for advice puts people in a togetherness mindset and works even though they don't think it helped more.
do: End organic videos with a genuine advice question and answer the replies on camera.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Simply reminding people of a shared identity, enemy or common trait raises unity automatically.
do: Name a common identity or common enemy in the first line (a shared frustration, a shared nationality) and let it do the work.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Shared emotional reactions and taking another's perspective create self–other overlap and goodwill.
do: Script a moment where the creator takes the viewer's side and voices their exact feeling ('you know that moment when...').

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Whatever people focus on seems more important, so shifting attention to a shared link makes it count for more.
do: Direct the viewer's attention in the opening shot to the one thing you want them to weigh most, since focus alone raises its importance.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Importance judgments follow attention, as 9/11's rated importance rose and fell with media coverage.
do: Don't spread attention over many claims; give the one benefit that matters the most screen time.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: An image shown before shopping shifted what buyers valued: clouds made comfort matter more, coins made price matter more.
do: Make the opening visual stand for the one benefit you're selling (plush texture for comfort, coins for value), as it sets the buyer's criteria.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People say yes to someone they see as one of them, and shared identities such as nationality, family and place create that feeling of "we".
do: Open with a shared identity the viewer holds (a Cape Town shop owner, a South African mum, a local) so they read the speaker as one of their own before the pitch starts.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Unity comes from belonging together (kin, place) and from acting together (shared music, reciprocal exchange, co-creation).
do: Name the place in the first line (Joburg, Durbanville, Gqeberha) and put shared local music or a shared action in the cut, so viewers feel they are doing something together with the brand.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: When people are rushed, distracted, uncertain or tired, they decide on one good piece of evidence instead of weighing everything.
do: Scrollers are distracted, so build each reel around one clear trigger (one proof, one deal, one reason) rather than stacking several arguments.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Honest shortcut cues such as "largest selling" are useful evidence to buyers, and only faked cues are exploitation.
do: Use a true popularity claim (units sold, best-seller rank, number of reviews) as the single proof line, and make sure the number is real.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Staged "unrehearsed" testimonials, canned laughter and planted reviews counterfeit social proof and deserve retaliation from consumers.
do: Use only real customers, real reviews and real screenshots in proof sections, and never cast actors as customers.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Honest scarcity information is a gift to the buyer, while fabricated scarcity makes the seller a profiteer, and the author rewarded the honest salesman with a strong review.
do: State scarcity only when it is true (actual stock left, real end date) and show the evidence on screen, such as the stock count or the launch date.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People use "expensive equals good" most when they don't know a product, and a sale price can even weaken a product's perceived effect.
do: For an unfamiliar product, lead with quality and ingredients before the discount, so a price cut doesn't read as lower quality.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Tasters rated the same wine as more pleasurable, with more brain pleasure activity, when told it cost $45 instead of $5.
do: Show the full price or the premium cue (packaging, price tag, materials) so the product reads as valuable before any discount appears.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Marking an item as "Reduced from" a higher price works very well, and fake reviews are powerful because people look to what others say.
do: Show the original price struck through next to the sale price on screen, and only when the original price was genuinely charged.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Small favours lose their obligating power as time passes, so people feel the pull of a favour most when it is warm and fresh.
do: Give the free tip, sample or code right at the start of the reel, and put the ask directly after it, not at the end of a long video.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A gift that arrives before the request beats the same gift after compliance, in surveys, hotel towels and restaurant tips.
do: Give the discount code, free shipping or free guide up front, then ask for the purchase, instead of promising a reward after they buy.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A gift that fits the recipient's need and arrives unsolicited produces more giving back, and food-related gifts raised supermarket purchases more than a key ring.
do: Choose the free bonus because it fits what this buyer needs from the product (a sample of the hero item, a related add-on), not a generic freebie.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Asking big and retreating immediately to a smaller request increased orders, and the effect weakens if the retreat is delayed.
do: Present the larger bundle first and drop straight to the single item or starter size in the same breath, with no gap.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A liked celebrity moved opinion on evolution, but a prestigious professor's opinion had no significant effect, so a liked messenger beats an authority for changing minds.
do: For a sceptical or belief-driven topic, put a liked, relatable face on screen (a creator the audience already likes) ahead of a doctor or an expert.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Insincere flattery still works on the person flattered, but onlookers dislike the flatterer.
do: Keep praise of the viewer or the product specific and believable, and avoid gushing lines, because they read as manipulation.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Mere association transfers feeling, so a messenger is blamed for bad news and a product gains from liked music or nearby positive things.
do: Pair the product with liked music and positive imagery, and keep bad news (delays, price rises) out of the product's own shots.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Repeatedly pairing a brand with pleasant scenes made viewers like it more, without their noticing, and sale signs lift buying beyond the real savings.
do: In the edit, show the product or logo five or six times over pleasant footage (use, joy, nature), and add a visible Sale tag on offer shots.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Claiming a connection to a successful team raises how favourably others see you, and the effect reverses if the team is not liked.
do: Tie the brand to winners the audience likes (a local team, a respected stockist, a known name) as proof, and only where the audience actually admires them.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Labelling items as most popular lifts their choice, and a randomly-assigned popular song became more popular.
do: Put a "most popular" or "best seller" badge on the hero product in frame, and say it aloud once.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Social proof moves people most when they are unsure of their own preference, so it changed dessert choices but not burger choices.
do: Spend the social-proof line on products and categories the viewer has no firm view on (a new brand or an add-on), and for familiar items lead with something else.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People with low confidence in their opinion moved toward others' reviews more as they saw more reviews.
do: Stack several short real reviews in quick succession on screen, since each additional one adds to the push.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Ads citing a higher percentage of others preferring a brand work better, and wine that had sold two-thirds of its bottles was judged better quality.
do: Use a specific high number (percent who rebuy, units sold, "2 of 3 sold") instead of vague popularity.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Telling people to conserve with no reason did nothing, and the most persuasive reason was that most of their neighbours were doing it.
do: Never issue a bare "buy now" or "you should", and give a reason, preferably what people like them are already doing.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: A requester who says they are like the target ("I'm a student here, too") raised donations, and same-age peers are the most influential.
do: Cast the speaker as the same age, stage of life and situation as the buyer, and say the shared fact in the opening line.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Telling people a bad behaviour is common makes it more likely, as the Petrified Forest signs showed.
do: When explaining the problem, don't stress how many people suffer it or do the wrong thing, and instead stress how many are choosing the better option.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People expect a trend to continue, so a growing rising number moves them, and collectivist audiences follow friends' behaviour.
do: Use a rising-trend line ("more and more people are switching") with a real before-and-after figure, and show friends or groups choosing it.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Combining several influence principles in one message can alert people to the persuasion attempt and backfire.
do: Keep one or two levers per reel, and cut extra urgency or authority lines that make the ad feel heavy-handed.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Uniforms, titles, height and prestigious clothing each raise perceived authority and compliance, often without people noticing.
do: Dress the presenter in the right uniform for the claim (lab coat, apron, branded kit) and show the title as a lower third.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Admitting a weakness yourself raises trust, and DDB's Volkswagen and Avis ads did this and then countered with a strength.
do: Name one honest drawback up front ("it's not the cheapest") and follow straight away with the benefit it buys.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Admitting a negative works only when it comes before the positive, as in "It Tastes Awful. And It Works".
do: Write the line as flaw first, strength second, and put it in the hook or the first beat of the script.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Scarcity combined with exclusive information was far more persuasive to beef buyers than scarcity alone, and banning information raises its appeal.
do: Pair a real shortage with something that sounds like inside news ("we got word from our supplier"), and only when it is true.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Perceived intent to persuade creates reactance, and phrases that restore freedom or expect refusal, like "you will probably refuse but", raised donors from 25 to 39 percent.
do: Close the CTA with a freedom line ("you might not need this, but" or "totally up to you") instead of a pushy command.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People infer who they are from their own actions, and short forms with two or three fields and giving someone a label get more compliance.
do: Ask for a tiny first action (tap, comment, enter one field) and call the viewer a name worth living up to, such as "you're someone who reads labels".

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Making something take effort raises commitment, and an exclusive one-day-sale was valued more when access took effort.
do: Gate the offer behind a small step (comment a word, DM for the code) so winners value it more.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Small rewards for taking a stand create more commitment than large ones, and free choice strengthens commitment.
do: Keep referral and review rewards small and framed as a choice, since a big payout makes the loyalty feel bought.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Prospects were more willing to buy from a salesperson born in the same community.
do: Have the presenter state their home town or neighbourhood in the first seconds when it matches the audience.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Shared group identity produces favouritism across health, law, courts and education, even down to graders giving higher marks to matching nationalities.
do: Pick a presenter and voice that visibly match the target audience (accent, language, background), because match alone shifts how much they are trusted.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Hemingway's six-word story, 'For sale. Baby shoes. Never used.', shows that a tiny, spare line can carry a whole emotional story if the viewer fills in the gap.
do: Open a reel with one short, concrete line that implies a loss or a story and let the viewer complete it; cut the explanation and hold the image for a beat.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Local voices are more persuasive than distant ones, and calling customers a 'community' or 'family' recruits a sense of 'we'.
do: Use local South African voices, places and slang in scripts, and address viewers as 'our community' or by a shared local identity rather than as 'customers'.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Moving rhythmically and in sync with others creates a feeling of 'we', and attending to something together with someone you feel close to makes you give it more focus.
do: Cut on the beat of the music, and show people moving or reacting in unison with the viewer's likely peers so the viewer feels part of the group.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Marching and tapping in unison, and singing together, make people more cooperative and helpful toward fellow group members.
do: Use music with a clear shared beat and, where possible, a chant or sing-along moment so viewers join in before the ask.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Music and rhythm work outside rational thinking, and a guitar case tripled the success of a stranger asking for a phone number (31% against 14% with nothing).
do: Match the pitch to the viewer's mode: use feeling-based language and music for emotional products, reasoned language for rational ones, and put a music-led, feeling-first opening on emotional-product reels.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: People value what they help build or advise on, and paying them a lot for advice removes the bond; strong brand identification makes customers overlook the brand's product failures.
do: Run reels that ask customers for input, show customer-co-created products or flavours, and credit the people who helped, rather than paying them big for the input.

title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini
says: Shared identity, a common enemy, and taking the other person's perspective all increase felt unity, and realising someone has taken your perspective makes you feel closer to them.
do: Write the opening from the viewer's point of view ('you know that feeling when...') and name a shared frustration or common enemy the brand and viewer both oppose.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The Kidney Heist survives retelling because it has three concrete elements, while jargon-filled writing cannot be retold at all.
do: Boil each script down to about three concrete beats the viewer could retell to a friend, and cut anything they would forget.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A bare statistic means nothing to people, so the popcorn campaign turned it into a physical comparison with a whole day of greasy meals laid out on a table.
do: Replace any product number with a picture the viewer already understands, and show the comparison on screen rather than stating the figure.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The Halloween, popcorn and kidney stories all stuck because each pairs an unexpected danger with a vivid concrete image, a simple action and a strong emotion.
do: Give each script one concrete image, one simple action for the viewer, and one named emotion such as disgust or fear of missing out.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Simple means finding one core by excluding good points, and unexpected ideas win attention with surprise and hold it by opening and then filling gaps in knowledge.
do: Keep one core point per reel, and open a curiosity gap in the hook that the reel closes later.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Concrete sensory language makes ideas mean the same thing to everyone, and credibility comes from letting people test the claim themselves, as Reagan did with one question instead of statistics.
do: Prove a claim with a test the viewer can run themselves or a visible demo, not a pile of stats.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: People feel for individuals rather than abstractions, the right emotion is not always the obvious one, and stories work like a mental flight simulator.
do: Show one specific customer in one specific moment rather than a segment, and pick the emotion that moves that audience, which may be resentment rather than fear.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Tappers predicted listeners would guess the song 50 percent of the time but it happened 2.5 percent, because once you know something you cannot imagine not knowing it.
do: Test every script on someone who has never heard of the brand, and treat what the team finds obvious as unexplained.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The only way to beat the Curse of Knowledge is to transform the idea, and the six principles work as a checklist, which Kennedy's moon goal passes and maximize shareholder value fails.
do: Run each draft script through the checklist: simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, story.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Creativity can be learned: 89 percent of award-winning ads fit six basic templates.
do: Start scripts from a small set of proven ad templates rather than a blank page.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Great ads follow predictable templates, such as Extreme Consequences, while weak ads fail in their own varied ways.
do: Use the Extreme Consequences template to show an exaggerated, vivid result of the product's key attribute.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Novices who brainstormed freely made ads rated annoying or no more creative, and standard brainstorming training did not help.
do: Do not rely on open brainstorming to find concepts; work from a template and have an outsider pick the best.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Two hours of training on six ad templates made novices' ads clearly more creative and better liked, so working within proven rules beats a blank canvas.
do: Keep a short list of proven concept templates and make every new script start from one of them.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A one-line Commander's Intent stating the end goal lets people improvise correctly when the detailed plan breaks.
do: Put a single intent line at the top of every brief so the editor can improvise when footage differs from the plan.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Finding the core means dropping important ideas that are not the most important one, and you cannot have five most important goals.
do: Before writing, fill in: the single most important thing this reel must do is ___.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A single core idea works as a filter that tells staff what to reject, as with the chicken Caesar salad Southwest would not serve.
do: Use the reel's core as a cutting filter and drop any line or scene that does not serve it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Simple means prioritisation not dumbing down, and journalists put the most important information first in an inverted pyramid.
do: Put the single most important information in the first seconds of the reel.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Putting the most important information first means that whenever a reader stops, they have still got the main point, whereas a payoff at the end loses everyone who leaves early.
do: Structure reels so the key message lands in the first seconds, and treat any later seconds as bonus, since most viewers leave early.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Writers bury the lead because they are steeped in detail, and forced prioritisation, choosing the one thing you could send before the line is cut, is painful but necessary.
do: Ask what you would keep if the video were cut off after one line, and make that the lead.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Even when other points are valid, a message must be triaged down to one, because several points dilute into none.
do: Allow one claim per reel and move other benefits to other reels, even if the client insists they matter.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Adding a second good option made students half as likely to pick study, so extra choices reduce action, and a clear core message helps people choose.
do: Give the viewer one offer and one call to action, not a menu of options.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Do not open with something interesting but irrelevant to entertain people; unbury the core and make the core itself interesting.
do: Make the hook the core claim stated in a vivid way, not a side anecdote that has to be explained away later.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The phrase 'Names, names, and names' works because it is a core idea in concrete, compact words that guide many small decisions.
do: Give each reel a three-word concrete mantra the editor can use to decide every cut.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: People can hold only seven to ten letters at once, so a message must be compact because there is a limit to what we can juggle.
do: Limit each reel to a few pieces of information, and cap on-screen text accordingly.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Grouping letters into known things like JFK and NASA makes them easier to remember, because you plant one flag on a memory the audience already has.
do: Refer to things the viewer already knows, such as familiar brands or objects, so one short phrase carries a lot of meaning.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Explaining something new by pointing to something familiar and saying what changes, such as a supersized grapefruit, teaches faster than listing attributes.
do: Introduce an unfamiliar product as a known thing plus one change, in the first line.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The grapefruit explanation lets people infer properties and gives a lead that will still be remembered months later, unlike a list of attributes.
do: Choose the one comparison you want remembered as the lead, then add differences in order of importance.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A simple but slightly inaccurate analogy beats an accurate idea that cannot guide decisions, since an accurate but useless idea is still useless.
do: Prefer a claim the viewer can act on over a fully qualified one, and keep the caveats for the product page.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The Curse of Knowledge shows up as accuracy to the point of uselessness, so give people just enough to be useful, then a little more.
do: Layer information across the reel instead of explaining everything up front, and use an analogy to carry the first step.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A one-line analogy like 'Die Hard on a bus' settles many production decisions at once, from director to budget to tone.
do: Write each reel's concept as a one-line 'X on Y' and use it to decide casting, pace, set and music.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A flight attendant got people to listen to a dull mandatory safety announcement by using jokes that broke the generic spiel.
do: When a message is boilerplate, open with a line that breaks the generic version viewers expect.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: We cannot demand attention, so we attract it by breaking a pattern, because people tune out anything constant.
do: Open on a break from the feed's usual look or sound, and change something on screen whenever attention may drift.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Our brains notice change, so surprise gets attention and interest keeps it, and both are needed for complex messages.
do: Use a surprise to open and a question or open loop to hold viewers, and vary the picture or sound at intervals.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The Enclave ad surprises by breaking the schema of car commercials and of ordinary trips, and surprise happens when our guessing machine fails.
do: Find what a viewer expects from this product category's ads and break exactly that expectation.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Surprise makes us stop moving and take in new information, and the extra attention it forces sears the event into memory.
do: Place the key information right after the surprise beat, when the viewer has paused to take things in.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A big surprise that is unrelated to the message, like wolves attacking a marching band, is memorable but worthless for the brand.
do: Check that every shock or odd hook points straight at the product benefit, and cut it if it only draws attention.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Surprise without insight just frustrates, as with the made-up words HENSION and BARDLE, so surprise needs a satisfying resolution tied to the core.
do: Make sure each surprising hook is resolved by the end of the reel in a way that explains the product.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: To be satisfying a surprise must be postdictable, meaning it makes sense in hindsight from clues already shown, and should target an expectation tied to the core message.
do: Plant clues in the early shots so the twist or reveal feels earned, and avoid it-was-all-a-dream reveals.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: To make a message stick, find the counterintuitive implication of your core message and break the audience's expectation on exactly that point, then help them rebuild.
do: Before writing the hook, ask what the viewer would wrongly assume about this product or claim, and open on the line that contradicts that assumption.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Common sense slips past people, so a message needs an uncommon-sense element, such as Nordstrom's odd service stories, to be remembered.
do: Swap a generic claim like 'great quality' for one odd, specific true story about the brand (the tire-chains kind of detail) and lead with it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A surprising specific story, like gift-wrapping a competitor's purchase, teaches a value far better than a generic mission statement, as long as the surprise fits the core message.
do: Replace claims like 'best service' or 'premium quality' in a script with one specific, slightly absurd act or detail that proves it, and make sure it points back to the brand's actual promise.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A surprise only works when it is followed by insight that tells the audience what it means, otherwise it feels gimmicky.
do: Every shock or odd moment in a reel must land on the point within the next beat, so cut the surprises that do not lead to the offer or message.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Facts in order are not a story; the lead is the point of the facts, and a good teacher gets people to commit to a default view and then breaks it.
do: Open the script on the meaning of the facts (the 'no school next Thursday' line), not on the list of product features, and have the viewer expect the usual answer first before you flip it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The first foreign-aid message buried its strongest, schema-breaking fact at the end, so the reader never felt it.
do: Find the single most schema-breaking fact in the brief and put it in the first line of the script, not the last.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Huge numbers do not stick, but a comparison to something small, concrete and frivolous, like one soft drink a month, makes a figure graspable and emotional.
do: Turn any big or abstract number or price into a familiar everyday comparison on screen, such as per day cost against a coffee or a takeaway.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The best way to get attention is to break existing schemas directly, while longer messages need something more to keep attention.
do: State the belief the audience holds in the first second and break it in the same breath, then plan a second device to hold them through the body.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Cialdini found the most successful popular science writing all opened with a mystery that the reader is invited to solve.
do: Structure a 30 to 60 second script as a puzzle: open on something that seems to make no sense about the product or customer, then walk the viewer toward the answer.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Mysteries create a need for closure, and posing the question at the start, returning to it during the middle and answering at the end holds attention even when the material is dull.
do: Pose the question in the hook, reference it again around the midpoint, and hold the reveal (and the call to action tied to it) until the final seconds.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A schema violation gives a one-time jolt, while a mystery gives a journey with an unknown ending, which sustains interest rather than just surprise.
do: Use the surprising line as the hook, then keep an unanswered question running so the viewer stays for the ending instead of leaving after the jolt.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: McKee says a great script makes every scene a turning point that opens a new question, and the audience stays to get the answers.
do: End each scene or cut in a reel on a new question or reversal so every beat pulls into the next, and place the payoff last.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Loewenstein's gap theory says curiosity is the pain of a gap in knowledge, which people will sit through even bad content to close.
do: Treat the hook as creating an itch: show the viewer there is something they do not know and make them want it closed.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: People must first realise they are missing something before they will want your facts, so open a gap with a question, a puzzle, a prediction or something someone else knows.
do: Do not start with the product facts; start with a question, a claim to guess, or a thing the viewer does not know, then deliver the facts as the answer.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: News teasers work by making you care about something you did not know you did not know, whereas a plain summary of facts is safe and unsticky.
do: Write the hook as a teaser that names a specific unknown tied to the viewer's own life, in the style of 'it may be in your own medicine cabinet', without fake hype.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Reframing a summary as a puzzle with a theory and a test makes people care about the answer, and the gain comes from structure, not content.
do: Rewrite 'we did X and got Y' scripts as 'we wanted to know why Z, so we tried this', and delay the result.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Write by asking what questions you want the audience to ask, not what information you want to convey, although people's overconfidence can blunt the gap.
do: Before scripting, list the two questions the viewer should be asking by second three and build the hook to provoke them.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Getting people to commit to a prediction or exposing disagreement makes them more curious about the outcome, and knowing more makes people notice what they lack.
do: Ask the viewer to guess or pick a side in the hook (which of these is the real one?) and pay it off at the end of the reel.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: If the audience knows too little, you have an abyss rather than a gap, so supply enough context and backstory that they start caring about the unknown.
do: For a cold viewer who has never heard of the brand or problem, spend the first few seconds on a quick vivid piece of context (the place, the people, what is at stake) before asking them to care about the answer.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Prime interest with what people already know, then show what they are missing, and release information as a trail of clues rather than a dump.
do: Cut the reel as a sequence of clues: confirm something the viewer already knows, then drop one new piece per beat, each pulling toward the reveal.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Ibuka chose 'a pocketable radio', a vivid and seemingly preposterous image of the benefit, over technology talk or management themes like quality and competition.
do: Name the product's promise as a vivid, slightly improbable picture of the end result (the radio in your pocket) rather than a category claim like 'innovative' or 'premium'.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The gap should be big but not insurmountable: audacious goals like a man on the moon worked because people could start working out the first steps.
do: Make the promise bold but believable, so the viewer immediately imagines how it could happen for them, not so extreme they dismiss it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Concrete images preserve a message while abstract jargon and buzzwords fade, and life itself is concrete even when language is not.
do: Strip buzzwords from scripts and describe the real tangible action or object instead, such as what the customer does with the product.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A huge abstract goal becomes workable when you pick a unit people can picture, like fifty named landscapes rather than millions of acres.
do: State sizes, results and quantities in a unit the viewer can picture (three bottles, one parcel a week) and avoid raw totals.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Naming an unglamorous area the Mount Hamilton Wilderness made it tangible and got funders and groups to pay attention.
do: Give the unnamed feature, method or ingredient a clear name and use that name repeatedly on screen and in voiceover.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Something is concrete if you can examine it with your senses, and concreteness usually means specific people doing specific things, which is the only safe language for novices.
do: Rewrite every abstract line in a script as a specific person doing a specific visible thing, and drop lines that cannot be filmed.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Asian math teachers explained abstractions through familiar scenes like buying a notebook or playing ball, more often than American teachers did.
do: Explain a new idea through an everyday scene the viewer already knows, and show it, rather than describing it in the abstract.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Novices need a concrete picture first, such as 30 tiles removed from 50, and abstractions can then be built on it.
do: Show the thing physically on screen, like the amount, the before and after, the texture, before naming the concept, and show what the recipe's 'hearty' looks like.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Concrete, visualisable words and details are remembered better than abstract ones, and oral tales kept the concrete parts and lost the abstractions.
do: Choose a concrete visual noun (the ice-filled bathtub) over an abstract benefit word like 'confidence' wherever you can.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Memory works like Velcro, so an idea with more hooks, especially sensory and emotional ones, clings better, as Jane Elliott's lesson shows.
do: Load a key moment with several sensory hooks, such as a sound, a texture close-up or a physical action, rather than one line of copy.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Because Elliott made prejudice an experience with sights, feelings and consequences rather than a fact to learn, her students still remembered it decades later.
do: Let the viewer feel the problem through a short staged moment of it rather than telling them about the problem.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Experts naturally talk in abstractions and patterns, which causes the Curse of Knowledge when speaking to novices who see only concrete details.
do: Write for the novice viewer and check every line for expert shorthand, such as 'strategy' or 'formulation', and replace it with what is seen or done.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: When engineers tried to fix miscommunication with more elaborate drawings, it only worsened, and the fix was to solve it at the level of the physical machine everyone understands.
do: If an explanation is not landing, cut to the physical product in use rather than adding more explanatory graphics or text.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The answer to the Curse of Knowledge is not dumbing down but finding a universal concrete language, and concrete targets keep even experts aligned.
do: State the offer and the result in terms with one clear meaning, like a number, a product or a time, instead of vague words like 'best'.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Stone Yamashita replaced a presentation with a walk-through of a fictional family's Disney day using the technology, which turned abstract services into an experience that spread.
do: Show a specific person's day with the product in it (their morning, their kitchen), step by step, rather than listing features.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Concreteness mobilises and focuses the brain, which is why people list as many white things in their fridge as white things anywhere.
do: Ask about the viewer's own specific situation (your fridge, your child) rather than a general category.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Tossing his plain portfolio on the table as a model of the future computer made the investors touch it and start asking questions.
do: Put a physical prop or the product itself in the viewer's hand or on camera and let it be the demonstration instead of a description.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: James Grant pulled out a packet of salt and sugar and compared its cost to a cup of tea, which made leaders see the problem as solvable and start thinking about action.
do: Hold up the actual product on screen and say what it costs in a familiar everyday comparison and what it does in one concrete sentence.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A prop works better than a scientific description because it invites people to bring their knowledge, and General Mills started to ground decisions in real customers.
do: Open on the physical product or a prop rather than a spec list, and let it do the explaining.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Seeing real mothers cook in their homes revealed a need for predictability that the data binders had not, and simplifying the range lifted sales 11 percent.
do: Base the 'want' on a specific observed moment from a real customer, like the toddler on the hip, not on demographics or dashboards.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A vivid profile of one imagined person, like Saddleback Sam, gives a team a lens to judge decisions.
do: Write each script to one named, specific viewer with a job, a skeptical line and a taste, and check each line against what they would say.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A concrete picture of the audience aligns many people on whom to reach, and being concrete is the easiest trait because the barrier is only forgetting that others do not know what we know.
do: After drafting, mark each abstract word and swap it for something you could see or film, and reject any idea that the target viewer would dislike.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Authorities add credibility, either as experts or as celebrities and aspirational figures whom people want to be like.
do: Choose the person who speaks the claim for who the audience wants to be like, not just for credentials.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Antiauthorities such as Pam Laffin, an ordinary smoker with emphysema, are credible through lived experience, and real people telling stories were the most compelling approach.
do: Build proof around a real customer telling what happened to them in their own words and showing it, rather than an expert or brand voice.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Laffin's raw ads and the Doe Fund's formerly homeless driver Dennis let people who lived the problem act as living proof.
do: Have the person who lived the before state appear on camera, unpolished, and tell their own version.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: People distrust sources with something to gain, and a friend or someone with no stake earns more trust than a company, so honesty can matter more than status.
do: Choose real customers and plain testimony over brand claims, and show they have no stake, because a brand praising itself is the weakest proof in a reel.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Messages need internal credibility, and urban legends gain it from specific localized details like a named road or lake.
do: Put exact names, places, numbers and times into proof lines (the street, the order number, the day) rather than general statements.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Concrete details make a claim feel more real and believable, and they lend credibility to the idea itself, not just to the person telling it.
do: Back every claim in a script with one specific, visible detail (a named place, a number of days, a real object) instead of a general statement.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Mock jurors judged a mother as more fit when the arguments for her carried vivid details, even though the details were irrelevant, because vivid detail made the argument easier to picture and believe.
do: Add one small, vivid, picturable detail to the strongest benefit claim in a script, such as how the product looks in use.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The details we use should be true, human and symbolic of the core idea, like a 73-year-old dancer standing in for a dance company's claim to diversity.
do: Pick the one real customer or founder detail that symbolises the brand claim and show it instead of stating the claim.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A single concrete example (Thomas Dwyer) silenced a skeptical room because the credibility came from the example itself rather than from an outside source.
do: When a viewer is likely to doubt a claim, answer with one named, specific real example in the first few seconds instead of a general assurance.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Beyond War made a huge number felt by dropping one BB, then ten, then 5,000 into a bucket, turning an abstract statistic into a sound and a sensation.
do: Show a big number physically on camera (pour 5,000 items, stack the boxes shipped) and let the sound carry it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: People will not remember the statistic; they remember the relationship it showed, so a number should be used to show a comparison or gut-level scale, not to be recalled.
do: Pick the number that shows a relationship (many times more, a tiny fraction) and dramatise that, rather than reciting precise figures.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The same accuracy statistic was rated very impressive by 83 percent of people when expressed as New York to Los Angeles, against 58 percent when expressed as sun to earth, because the former is closer to human experience.
do: Restate any big or technical number in a distance, object or time the viewer already knows.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Covey turned dull survey percentages into a soccer team where only 2 of 11 players know their job, which gave the numbers drama and made the problem imaginable.
do: Translate a percentage into a familiar scene with people in it (out of ten customers, four do this) and let the viewer picture it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A cost or statistic only becomes useful when it is put at a scale people have intuition for, such as one to two minutes a day instead of $500 a year.
do: Break any price or saving into the smallest everyday unit (a coffee a day, minutes saved) in the offer line of a script.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Asking which is more likely to kill you, a shark or a deer, gives an unexpected, funny comparison that uses the audience's own lack of fear of deer as the proof.
do: Open with a two-option 'which is more X?' question where the surprising answer is the proof.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The Sinatra Test says one example that proves you can handle the hardest case in your field is enough to establish credibility across the field.
do: Lead with the single toughest or most impressive customer or job you have handled rather than a spread of average results.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Safexpress won a skeptical Bollywood studio by telling two hard-delivery stories (a Harry Potter launch and exam papers), one of which was chosen for the specific listener.
do: Choose the proof story that matches the viewer's own fear or situation and tell it in one concrete beat.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Concrete, hard-to-do examples gain their power from being concrete, more than from a percentage or a testimonial from a CEO.
do: Replace a generic '98% satisfied' line with the one hardest thing you delivered, told as a short story.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Wendy's made its claim credible by challenging the audience to see for themselves, outsourcing credibility to its customers, and it lifted revenue 31 percent.
do: Make a claim the viewer can check on screen in seconds, such as a side-by-side with the competitor.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A testable credential invites the audience to verify the claim themselves, which gives a large credibility boost, though it can backfire if the visible evidence is misread.
do: Build one 'see for yourself' moment into the script (a test, a comparison, a thing to try) rather than only asserting the claim.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Reagan's 'Are you better off now than four years ago?' and the Emotional Tank exercise both let the audience test the idea against their own experience.
do: Ask the viewer one question they can answer from their own life, so they supply the proof.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Asking readers to predict first which kills more people lets them botch the answer and discover the bias themselves, which beats being told.
do: Open with a quick guess-the-answer question where the viewer is likely to be wrong, then reveal.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Telling people the punch line first is less involving than letting them experience the effect for themselves.
do: Hold the reveal and let the viewer reach it, rather than giving away the answer in the first line.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The NBA made the AIDS risk credible by letting rookies flirt with women who then introduced themselves as HIV positive, so the players were fooled themselves rather than hearing about it.
do: Structure a script so the viewer is set up with an assumption, then the turn overturns it, instead of explaining the lesson.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Setting up a test of Mother Teresa's idea, researchers offered survey participants a donation request framed either as statistics about millions of children or as one girl, Rokia.
do: Choose a single named person for the story rather than a group.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: People gave more than twice as much to one named girl as to statistics, and adding the statistics to her story made giving drop.
do: Tell the story of one customer and leave the large totals off the page, or at most to a closing line.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Priming people to calculate before reading the Rokia letter cut their giving, showing that analytical thinking suppresses the emotional response that leads to action.
do: Do not put spec comparisons or maths ahead of the emotional beat in a reel; keep the viewer feeling until after the ask.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: People respond to an individual rather than an abstract cause, and making an idea emotional means making people care enough to act, not tugging at their heartstrings.
do: Frame the offer around a specific person or case instead of a category.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The Truth ad used rough documentary-style video and 1,800 physical body bags to make a death toll visible, and it made viewers angry.
do: Make a number visible by piling up real objects on camera, and keep the footage raw and documentary in feel.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: In a survey of 10,692 teenagers the emotional Truth campaign was remembered far more and cut intent to smoke, while the rational 'Think. Don't Smoke' ads raised it.
do: Choose the emotional angle over the rational-argument angle when testing two versions.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The rational campaign asked for thinking while the Truth campaign tapped teenage rebellion against authority, which is why it got people to act.
do: Find the emotion the audience already has, such as rebellion, pride or annoyance, and aim the script at it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Words that deliver an emotional kick get overused until they lose their power, as 'unique' did, so superlatives wear out.
do: Cut stock hype words such as 'unique', 'amazing' and 'game-changing' from scripts and use a specific detail instead.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The best direct-mail copywriter said every headline must carry self-interest, stressing benefits over features and the benefit of the benefit, since people buy the hole, not the drill bit.
do: Write the first line of the hook as what the viewer gets, and state the end result (the hole) rather than the product feature.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Spell out 'what's in it for you' explicitly, because a distracted audience will not connect a feature to its benefit before you have moved on.
do: After naming a feature on screen, say the benefit in the same line.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Self-interest copy should address the reader directly with 'you' rather than speaking about people in general.
do: Rewrite every benefit line in second person, in the viewer's own voice, not 'people' or 'customers'.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Homeowners who were asked to imagine themselves using cable subscribed at 47 percent, against 20 percent for those who just read the benefits.
do: Write a 'picture yourself' beat that walks the viewer through their own day with the product, in the second person.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: What makes people care is how tangible a benefit is, not how big it is, so reasonable benefits they can picture themselves enjoying are enough.
do: Describe a small, specific moment of use rather than promising a large transformation.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: People pursue many needs at once, and when asked what motivates them personally they choose esteem rather than money.
do: Consider an appeal to being recognised or feeling capable, not only to saving money.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: We think others are motivated by money and security while we are motivated by learning and esteem, so we underestimate higher motivations in our audience.
do: Test a script angle that appeals to pride, mastery or belonging instead of only price and safety.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Offering firefighters a free popcorn popper to review a safety film insulted them, because a self-interested gift can clash with their sense of who they are.
do: Do not attach a freebie to an offer aimed at an audience whose pride is in their seriousness.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: People decide by asking 'what's in it for my group' and by identity ('what do people like me do?'), not just by calculating personal gain.
do: Write the want beat as 'people like you do this' by naming the viewer's tribe.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Under the identity model people ask what someone like them would do, which explains why firefighters rejected a harmless gift.
do: Frame the product as the choice of a kind of person the viewer sees themselves as.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A teacher answers 'when will I use this?' with a surprising 'Never,' followed by a weight-lifting analogy for why it is still worth doing.
do: Open with a blunt line that contradicts what the viewer expects, then give a familiar analogy.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Don't Mess with Texas used famous Texans to set an identity that real Texans do not litter, rather than an authority telling them not to.
do: Use creators the target audience sees as one of them, and avoid the authority voice they resent.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The identity message was recalled by 73 percent and cut litter 29 percent in a year, making a planned enforcement programme unnecessary.
do: Choose an identity appeal ('people like us do this') over a fear or rational appeal.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Asked why it matters, the group found a line that worked: duo piano has the sound of the orchestra with the intimacy of chamber music.
do: Boil the offer down to a 'X but Y' contrast sentence that tells outsiders what it is.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Experts forget that outsiders have never heard of their thing, and asking 'why?' moved them from what they do to why it matters.
do: Before writing a script, ask 'why does this matter?' three times and use the last answer, not the product category.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: IDEO made hospital staff care by filming an emergency room visit from the patient's point of view, so they saw only ceilings and idle waiting.
do: Shoot the problem scene from the customer's first-person view so the viewer experiences it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Empathy comes from the particular rather than the pattern, so get audiences to feel for one individual and appeal to identity and higher motives.
do: Pick one individual and one specific moment to carry the whole reel.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A story of a nurse reading a baby's changing colour opens in a concrete scene with rising tension and a hunch that contradicts everyone else.
do: Start the script inside a specific moment with a visible detail and a problem about to go wrong.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A good story provides simulation (how to act) and inspiration (motivation to act), so stories are what make people act.
do: Choose stories where the viewer can see exactly what the person did and why it worked, so the viewer can copy it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A story with real detail lets listeners play along and test how they would have handled it, so it both entertains and teaches in a way a bare summary or punch line does not.
do: Don't give the result alone. Show the misleading step or wrong turn that came before it, so the viewer can try to solve it with you.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Replaying the steps of how events unfolded helped people far more than picturing a happy outcome, because mental simulation fires the same brain areas as real action.
do: Show the process of the problem and the fix, step by step, instead of only the glowing after-state. Give the viewer a short run of 'first this, then this' to live through.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Mental practice delivers about two thirds of the benefit of real practice, so a good story works as a flight simulator for the viewer.
do: Walk the viewer through using the product from first touch to result, so they feel they have already done it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A story shows the advice in action and delivers an unexpected, concrete solution, and we care about the person more than a bullet list.
do: Turn a tip list into one person's scene where the tips happen on screen, ending on the surprising fix.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Subway's statistic '7 Under 6' did not stick, but the story of Jared, a 425-pound student who lost weight eating Subway, did; resist skipping to the tips and leaving out the story.
do: Open on one named person with a concrete problem rather than a stat or a list of benefits.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The Jared ad simply introduced him by name, gave his before number and after number, added the diet and a doctor disclaimer, and the phones rang the next day.
do: Try a hook built as 'This is [name]. He used to [concrete before number]. Today [after number].' Keep an honest 'not for everyone' line.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: The Jared campaign lifted Subway sales 18 percent against flat sales the year before, because it inspired action as well as simulating it, where '7 Under 6' did not.
do: Use a hard-won personal transformation as the engine of an offer reel, because inspiration drives action.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Jared beat '7 Under 6' on every SUCCESs test because its core promise was a life change, while the other only listed a product feature.
do: Write the promise as the outcome in the buyer's life, not the product range or spec, and test the script against simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, story.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A number like 'under 6 grams of fat' isn't concrete, is barely credible because the bar is low, and doesn't move people.
do: Don't hang a hook on a bare spec number; pair it with a person or physical image.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Spotting sticky ideas is often easier and more useful than creating them, and ideas don't flag themselves, so you must look for them.
do: Mine customer reviews, DMs and unboxing clips for a real story with a surprising detail to build a reel around.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Inspirational stories fall into three plots, Challenge, Connection and Creativity, which cover over 80 percent of Chicken Soup stories.
do: Label each script idea as Challenge, Connection or Creativity before writing, and pick the plot that fits the goal.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A Challenge plot only works if the obstacle seems daunting to the protagonist, and it inspires people to act.
do: Choose customers or founders with a genuinely big obstacle and show how big it was before the win.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Connection plots bridge a gap between people, and Creativity plots show a mental breakthrough or an innovative fix, each inspiring a different action.
do: For gifting or community products, use a connection story; for hacks or clever product use, use a Creativity story.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Instead of arguing for knowledge management, Denning told one concrete story, and the executives adopted the idea as their own.
do: Replace a claim about the product category with one short story of one real person using it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: A direct argument invites the listener to judge and argue back, while a story engages their inner voice and gets them to participate.
do: Cut the hard-sell claim lines from the script and let a short story carry the argument, so the viewer reaches the conclusion themselves.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Stories beat the Curse of Knowledge and are naturally concrete, emotional and unexpected, but the hard part is keeping them simple and tied to your core message.
do: Before cutting a reel, write the one-line core message and drop any story beat that does not serve it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: In a Stanford exercise, polished speakers who leaned on statistics were forgotten, while 63 percent recalled the stories and only 5 percent recalled any statistic.
do: Cut stacked stats from the script; keep at most one number and make the story or emotional beat carry the memory.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Smart people bury the lead and focus on presentation over message, and charisma can't rescue a dense, unfocused message.
do: Put the single most important thing in the first two seconds and strip every fact that does not serve it.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Stress two or three points at most, and remember the expert's Curse of Knowledge makes them talk as if the audience already knows what they know.
do: Limit each reel to one point and write it for someone who has never heard of the product or category.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Sharing data is not communicating; an idea sticks only if it gets attention, is understood, believed, cared about and acted on.
do: Check each script against five questions: did it grab attention, can they follow it, do they believe it, do they care, do they know what to do next.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: To fix lost attention, break the viewer's guessing machine with something uncommon-sense, and to stop drop-off mid-way, open curiosity gaps.
do: Open with an unexpected claim, and plant an unanswered question early that the reel only resolves near the end.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: To be understood use concrete real-world examples, and to be believed use telling details and antiauthorities rather than more authorities and statistics.
do: Swap an expert quote for a vivid detail from an ordinary customer, and an abstract benefit for a specific example.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: People care more about one individual than abstractions, and identity appeals like 'Don't Mess with Texas' get action when apathy sets in.
do: Frame the offer as what people like the viewer do ('this is what Cape Town mums do') and show one person, not a crowd.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Ordinary people made ideas stick, such as Art Silverman laying a day's worth of fatty foods beside a tub of popcorn to show its saturated fat.
do: Show a claim as a physical side-by-side on screen, like the quantity of the thing laid out next to the product.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Winning ads come from a few templates, including Pictorial Analogy, Extreme Consequences, Extreme Situations, Competition, Interactive Experiments and Dimensionality Alteration.
do: Use these templates as hook formats, such as an extreme consequence of not using the product, and storyboard options from each.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Vivid details help only when they support the core message; irrelevant vivid details distract and weaken it.
do: Check every striking detail or shot against the core message and cut the ones that are merely eye-catching.

title: Made to Stick
author: Chip & Dan Heath
says: Things that are easy to visualise feel more emotional and are recalled better, and emotion sharpens memory of the central theme.
do: Pick the image the viewer can see most easily for each emotional beat, and cut to it on the line that carries the feeling.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Advertising is salesmanship multiplied, so judge it only by sales, and fine writing or a studied sales attempt creates resistance.
do: Write the script as a plain, sincere salesperson would speak it; cut polished lines that make the viewer notice the pitch.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Test every choice by asking whether it would help a salesman sell face to face, and do not cap the words a salesman may use.
do: Before keeping a line, slogan or clever beat, ask if a good salesperson would say it to a buyer in person; if not, cut it.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Only people already interested in the subject read ads, so give them enough to act and do not entertain, because entertainment seekers are not your buyers.
do: In skits and funny reels, make the laugh carry the product point, and cut any bit that earns applause without moving toward the sale.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
