says: Write to one typical buyer as if face to face, do not boast or try to amuse, and learn from real customers because the maker's interests are not the buyer's.
do: Name one real buyer before writing, script it as talking to her across a counter, and pull lines from customer reviews and DMs instead of brand talk.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: People are selfish, so the best ads offer service, information or a free trial instead of asking anyone to buy.
do: Open and close on what the viewer gets, such as a sample, a trial or useful information, and drop 'buy our brand' language.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Offering a free gift, trial or send-on-approval removes the buyer's risk and lifts sales sharply, because people can be coaxed but not driven.
do: Build the offer around a risk-free try, such as trial, returns or pay-after, and say that plainly in the CTA.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Proven mail order ads use every line, with no palaver, no boasting and no entertainment, and bigger type never paid.
do: Cut every second that does not sell; remove warm-up, logo sting intros and filler between claims.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Readers forget their decision to act within minutes, so the ad needs a reminder device, and pictures must earn their space as salesmen.
do: End on one clear action cue the viewer can use at once, and give each shot a selling job instead of decoration.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: A striking picture raised cost per reply by exactly its added cost and brought no added sales, while telling more sells more.
do: Do not add striking footage for its own sake; put the extra seconds into more reasons to buy.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: A headline's job is to hail only the people you can interest, even if a clever blind headline would attract more people who can never buy.
do: Make the first line or frame call out the specific buyer or situation, such as 'If your perfume vanishes by lunch', rather than a broad curiosity grab.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: People are hurried and decide at a glance, so the headline must show at once that the ad offers them something.
do: Show the benefit or subject in the first two seconds in picture and words, so the right viewer knows it is for them.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: The headline decides the return, with identical ads varying five to ten times by headline alone, so write many and test them.
do: Write at least ten hooks per script, run the same body under different hooks, and log which appeal wins.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: The appeals we prefer rarely win, so use varied ads with different approaches, and address only the people you seek.
do: Make several reels on one product, each leading with a different appeal such as beauty, durability or price, and let results rank them.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Human nature is fixed: curiosity is a strong incentive, shoppers want bargains but not cheapness, and a high stated price or cost raises perceived value.
do: Hook with a specific odd fact that sparks curiosity, and state what something cost or is worth instead of apologising for price.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Facts like what a formula cost, a neighbourly signed guarantee, and 'pay after trying' impress far more than a plain guarantee.
do: Offer 'try it, pay after' where possible, and add a concrete investment fact such as what the formula or sourcing cost.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: A buyer's own name on the product, or an offer limited to a defined group, makes people work harder to claim it.
do: Personalise the offer with a name or engraving, or restrict it to a named group, and say so in the hook.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Inviting comparison with rivals showed confidence and beat warnings, and sampling works better when the buyer asks for it after hearing the story than when it is thrown at them.
do: Show the product beside a rival or tell viewers to try the competition too, and let people ask for the sample.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Mental impression decides choices, and a warm, named human voice who understands the buyer beat a bare business offer.
do: Put a real named person, such as the founder, on camera speaking like a friend who knows the buyer's situation, and tell viewers what to notice.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Superlatives are discounted as selling talk, but specific claims and actual figures are taken at full weight.
do: Swap every 'best' or 'amazing' line for a measured figure or concrete fact on screen.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Exact numbers like '25 percent' or 'net profit 3 percent' beat common claims like 'lowest prices'.
do: Replace 'great value' with the exact saving, percentage or number, and show it as text.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Specific claims, even ordinary process facts every maker shares, won big when no rival had told them.
do: Show the ordinary making process with real numbers, such as steps, tests and hours, which competitors have never explained.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Each ad should tell a reasonably complete story with every strong claim, because people rarely read a series.
do: Put the top claims in every reel instead of one claim per episode, ordered strongest first.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Write only to new prospects, not existing users, and treat each viewer as a one-time reader who may never return.
do: Script every reel as a first meeting with someone who has never heard of the brand, and leave out content aimed at existing customers.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: There is no fixed brevity rule; a high-stakes purchase deserves a full story, and short ads leave buyers uninformed.
do: Set length by how much a doubtful buyer needs to know, so go longer for expensive or considered products.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Pictures cost a third to half of a campaign, so use them only when they sell better than the same space in type, and not for decoration.
do: Keep a shot only if it sells more than a text line would; skip expensive production.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Aspirational pictures of envied people in coveted settings sell, while eccentric or frivolous pictures steal attention from the main appeal and cost respect.
do: Show the outcome the buyer envies, with a reacting second person, and avoid gimmicky visuals that overshadow the hook.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: A picture must sell better than anything else in the same space, and the product itself pictured can awaken curiosity.
do: Test a tight, curious product close-up against a lifestyle shot, and keep the winner.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Repeating a picture is probably an economy, colour pays mainly for food-like products, and nothing should be done merely to attract.
do: Reuse proven footage across reels, and spend colour grading effort where the product's look is the appeal.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Changing people's habits is too costly, so don't spend ad lines educating people who don't already want the category.
do: Sell to people who already want the thing, and skip explainers about why the category matters.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Don't create a trend for the whole field; watch a rising popular desire and offer to satisfy it.
do: Hook to a trend or desire already circulating, such as a viral scent or look, and sell your product as the answer.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: People will pay to cure or beautify but not to prevent, and one claim can pull ten times what another does.
do: Lead with the attractive gain, such as looks, compliments or status, not the avoided problem.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: A claim that appeals to one in a hundred raises cost per result, so feature the broad appeal and keep niche claims secondary.
do: Lead hooks with the benefit most buyers want, and put niche uses later or in separate reels.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Deep reading on a subject often turns up one fact that reframes the product and wins the campaign.
do: Before scripting, read research, reviews and ingredient or process material to find one fact that reframes the product.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Surveying buyers showed only 4 percent used canned beans, so the real job was winning people away from home baking, not pushing a brand.
do: Find what most prospects do now instead of buying, and make the reel about switching from that habit.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Lab-tested exact figures and comparisons, like 425 calories equalling six eggs, make claims impressive and safer.
do: Turn a vague claim into a measured number plus a familiar comparison, and have claims checked.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Picture one user of a rival product and find what you could say to win that one person before addressing thousands, because there is nearly always something impressive rivals haven't told.
do: Write the script as a reply to one specific rival-brand user, and find the one true advantage competitors haven't stated.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Samples let you say 'Free', multiply responses, get action from half-convinced readers and capture an interested prospect.
do: Use 'free' sample or trial as the CTA and capture contact details for follow-up.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: A free sample works as a key to compare ads, and charging small amounts for it costs more in lost replies than it saves.
do: Make the sample or trial free rather than charging small shipping or a fee, and track which ad drove each request.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Putting a price on a sample or asking half price cuts replies by three-quarters or more, so don't make the seller's effort the buyer's cost.
do: Avoid 'pay shipping' or 'half price' trial offers in the CTA, and offer it free or risk-free.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Reducing effort in the response method raises replies sharply, such as coupons at a store, or a phone call instead of a letter.
do: Use the lowest-effort response method for your audience, such as a WhatsApp tap or one-click link, instead of forms.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Give samples only to interested people who show effort, and limit one per home, because scattered samples cheapen the product.
do: Gate free offers behind a small action and a limit per customer, instead of giving them to everyone.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Tell your story first to create respect and expectation, then the sample confirms your claims.
do: Order the reel as story and claims first, then the sample or trial offer at the end.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Small test campaigns answer questions cheaply and finally, because tastes differ and nobody's guess is reliable.
do: Test hook and offer variants on small spend before scaling, and let buyers decide.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Trying over fifty plans in five years cut selling cost by 75 percent, because constant testing of new methods against the proven one compounds.
do: Run a steady test pipeline where each new variant must beat the current best, and keep the winner live.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: A distinctive, becoming personality, often a named person who takes pride in the work, makes the product and the ad memorable.
do: Give the brand a recurring human voice, such as the founder or a named character, suited to the audience.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Keep the same tone every time so people come to know and trust you, since changing your manner makes friends re-acquaint.
do: Hold the same voice, pacing and look across reels for one brand so viewers recognise it.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Positive ads showing the desired result beat negative ones that show the problem, sometimes four to one, and attacking rivals backfires.
do: Show the after state and the happy, envied person, not the problem, and tell viewers what to do instead of what to avoid.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: Test letters, follow up on the exact interest created, and don't dress them up, since fine stationery lessens effect and people postpone action.
do: For conversion reels, keep production plain and honest instead of glossy, follow up on the same appeal, and give a reason to act now.

title: Scientific Advertising
author: Claude Hopkins
says: A deadline or a gift with a reason overcomes delay and pays for itself.
do: Put an expiry date or a limited gift in the offer line, and say what waiting costs.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Swapping a long webinar for a short screen-recorded case study showing the ads, page, script and real numbers made leads pour in.
do: Cut a reel that screen-records a real result from the brand, such as orders, reviews or a before and after, instead of explaining in the abstract.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A lead magnet is a complete solution to one narrow problem, given free or deeply discounted, and it should reveal the next problem that only your core offer solves.
do: Build the free hook of a video around one narrow problem fully solved, such as a single fix or tip, then point to the product as the next step.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: One type of free offer reveals a problem the person didn't know they had, and it carries built-in urgency when the problem gets worse while they wait.
do: Open a script by diagnosing a hidden problem that worsens with time, such as damage, wear or lost money, so the viewer feels urgency before the pitch.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A free giveaway only works if it leads naturally to the thing you actually sell, as free t-shirts don't lead to IT services.
do: When a script offers a freebie, sample or bonus, pick one that is close to the product so the viewer who wants it is already a buyer.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Redoing only the first five seconds of a flopped short video, with the core value unchanged, took it from 4,000 to 850,000 views.
do: When a reel underperforms, keep the body and re-cut or rewrite only the first five seconds with a new framing, then relaunch.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: How you frame and name the value decides how many people engage, so Hormozi tested book titles head to head and let the data pick the winner.
do: Write three or four alternative hook lines for each reel and test them against each other before picking one.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Because most people decide in the first five seconds, the headline sorts most of your traffic and deserves far more testing than it gets.
do: Spend disproportionate drafting time on the opening line and visual of each reel, and write several versions.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Removing a single word from a subheadline moved a poll from 30% to 70%, showing small wording changes can multiply clicks about two and a half times.
do: Test one-word edits to hook text and captions, and cut every word that doesn't earn its place.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: You can test names cheaply with about $50 of ads, a poll, a comment post or direct messages to friends.
do: Run two or three hook options as small ads or a quick poll to the client's audience before committing to the full production.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: People buy on a prediction of future value, and the easiest way to create that prediction is to give real value before they pay.
do: Put one genuinely useful tip, demo or result early in the reel, before the pitch, so the buy feels like a safe bet.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The call to action should be plain and direct, with a reason to act now built from scarcity (limited quantity), urgency (limited time), or both.
do: End every script on one plain action and add a real limit, either a deadline or a stock cap, stated in one line.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Any reason for a deadline or limit is more compelling than no reason, and better lead magnets attract better leads.
do: Give the offer a stated reason, such as clearing last season's stock or a small batch, rather than a bare limit.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The pitch names the struggle, the outcome and the timeframe, adds implied scarcity, a guarantee and two named case studies, one of them a beginner.
do: In an offer segment, name two customers like the viewer, including a first-timer, to prove it works for ordinary people.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Showing a person who struggled and still succeeded tells the viewer subconsciously that it is easy for them too, and the pitch covers all four value-equation parts.
do: Include a line showing someone with the viewer's exact objection succeeding, such as 'even someone who has never done X'.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The short pitch formula says you help an ideal customer get a dream outcome in a set time without effort and sacrifice, backed by examples.
do: Use this as the skeleton for a 15 to 30 second offer segment: who it's for, the outcome, how soon, no hassle, then real examples.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Proof of people just like the viewer getting the result is stronger than your own story, and a sheer volume of reviews adds to it.
do: Choose testimonials that match the target buyer and show a wall or scroll of five-star reviews on screen.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Certifications, stats and research, and borrowed authority from experts all raise belief, as long as you have permission.
do: Add one hard stat or credential on screen as a quick proof beat, and only use endorsements that were agreed.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A new mechanism that differs from what the buyer failed with before, plus a guarantee with real skin in the game, raises belief.
do: Name what's different about the product versus what the viewer has tried before, and state the guarantee with its consequence.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Describing the viewer's current pain in precise, specific detail makes them believe you can solve it, as if you were in their head.
do: Open with a concrete, almost uncomfortably accurate description of the viewer's daily frustration, then use feel, felt, found to bridge to the product.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Demonstrating the result live in real time, in about a minute, sent belief through the roof, and a video can stand in when you can't do it in person.
do: Show the product doing its job on camera in one unbroken take at the start or middle of the reel, with no cutaway before the result lands.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: For complex services, demonstrate in advance what receiving the result looks like, such as a real customer's lead call, then make a small easy-yes offer.
do: For services, show a real customer's actual output, such as a call recording or dashboard, in the reel to let the viewer picture the result.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Every piece of content, even a meme, runs on three steps: a hook to get noticed, retention to keep them watching, and a reward that satisfies why they came.
do: Write every script as three marked beats (hook, keep-watching device, payoff) and check each reel actually has all three before cutting.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A hook works by picking a topic the viewer finds interesting, a headline that gives a reason to watch, and a format they are used to, with life lessons as a prime topic source.
do: Open scripts with a 'I used to think X, then Y changed my mind' lesson from the brand or founder.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Interesting topics come from your recent past and real-time capture, and the audience's response shows which ones to repeat.
do: Build a topic list from the brand's last week of customer chats, orders and DMs, and make several short reels from it to see which one lands.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Comment on trends only where you have real expertise, and the easiest topic source is simply talking about what you actually do.
do: Tie hooks to a current trend only if the brand genuinely has a stake in it, otherwise show what the brand did this week.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Research on news headlines found seven traits of high performers, the first being recency: something that just happened beats something old.
do: Put recency in the hook ('just dropped', 'this week', 'new batch') and avoid undated claims.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Headlines convert better when they are personally relevant to the audience, feature a known person, or are geographically close to home.
do: Name the exact viewer in the first line (for example 'if you're a mom in Cape Town') and use local places or known faces in the hook.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Conflict between opposing ideas and anything unusual or rare make headlines more gripping.
do: Set up a versus in the hook (this versus that) or open on the oddest, rarest thing about the product.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Ongoing stories add pull, and a hook should also match the format people have been rewarded by on that platform.
do: Frame a series as 'part 2 of the story' to bring viewers back, and copy the look of top-performing native content on each platform.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Make your content resemble what already performs on each platform, because better-looking content will hook viewers before yours gets a chance.
do: Before cutting, study the top reels in the brand's niche on each platform and match their framing, captions and pacing in the first five seconds without copying them.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Lists and steps retain viewers, and stating the number of items in the headline or first seconds tells people what to expect.
do: Use a countdown hook like 'three things I'd do' and show the number on screen in the first seconds.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Steps are rigid with a clear payoff, lists are flexible with weaker payoff, and stories keep people watching because they want to know what happens next.
do: Choose the structure per concept: steps for how-to demos, a list for tips, a story arc for founder or customer pieces.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Stories, lists and steps can be woven together, but open loops that are never closed teach viewers not to come back.
do: Close every open loop in the same reel, and weave a quick story beat between list items to keep attention.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Length is not the problem, boredom is, because viewers have higher standards rather than shorter attention spans, so value per second is what counts.
do: Audit each cut second by second and remove any beat that does not give new information or reward, instead of just trimming to hit a duration.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The content must deliver exactly what the hook promised, because a broken promise means the viewer won't watch you again.
do: After writing the script, check the payoff against the hook line by line: if the hook says six ways, show six that are not obvious.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Start with short content and make everything for strangers, with no inside references a new viewer wouldn't understand.
do: Write every reel so a first-time viewer understands it cold, with brand jargon explained or removed and no references to earlier posts.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Treat the ask like a TV commercial that briefly interrupts your own value, then go straight back to giving.
do: Put the offer in one short beat after a valuable moment in the reel, then return to the content rather than ending in a hard sell throughout.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: You can ask inside every piece of content as long as the give-to-ask ratio stays high, such as a 30-second ask in a 60-minute piece.
do: Keep the pitch a small fraction of runtime: in a 30-second reel, deliver value for most of it and keep the offer to a few seconds.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Asking more and more often yields less and less per ask, so place the call to action after a valuable moment or at the end and offer with an open hand.
do: Put the call to action at the end or right after the payoff and test one placement before adding more.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: For short-form, do not squeeze an ask into every clip: make many pure-give pieces and occasionally one piece that still hooks, retains and rewards but carries an offer.
do: Plan a content calendar of roughly ten value reels to every one offer reel, and make the offer reel as watchable as the rest.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A call to action converts better when the lead magnet is directly relevant to the content that promoted it.
do: Match the freebie or CTA to the exact topic of the reel, for example a care guide offered on a how-to-clean reel.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Making the lead magnet relevant to the topic pre-selects viewers who have the problem and turns them into customers for life.
do: End a how-to reel with a free sample, guide or demo that solves the specific problem shown.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A direct offer inside content can name a small number of spots, the outcome, a guarantee, and a simple way to respond.
do: Close an offer reel with limited spots, the promised result, the guarantee, and one clear action (DM, comment or link).

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A single short video can be reformatted cheaply for each similar short-video platform so it looks native on each.
do: Export each edit in per-platform versions with the native caption style, safe zones and ratio rather than one file everywhere.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Platforms reward content people send to others, so aim to make something valuable enough that the viewer would share it.
do: Ask of every script whether a viewer would send it to a friend, and add one 'I didn't know that' fact to make it share-worthy.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Framing content as 'how I did it' rather than 'how you should' takes the ego out and makes viewers less likely to argue.
do: Write hooks and scripts as 'how I/we did it' or 'how our customers do it' rather than commands.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Audiences need reminding more than teaching, since one in six of his audience didn't know he had a book despite daily posts.
do: Run the same core message across many reel variants and assume most viewers have not seen the previous ones.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: You get sick of your message long before the audience knows it, so repeat yourself for years, and start by competing in a small pond.
do: Do not retire a working message because the team is bored of it; refresh the visuals instead.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A newcomer should narrow content to a small area where their credibility can't be questioned and expand outward over time.
do: Keep early scripts to a narrow, specific claim the brand can fully back up.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Credibility comes from talking about specific people you helped and what you did for them, which nobody can dispute.
do: Build proof reels around one named customer and what happened for them, not general claims.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Organic content that unexpectedly draws buying inquiries should be turned into ads, and sorted into a library matched to specific objections.
do: Check organic posts for ones that draw buying enquiries or DMs, re-cut them as paid ads, and tag each by the objection it overcomes.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Labelling content by the problem it solves lets sales send the right piece to beat a given objection, and free content retains paying customers.
do: Make short objection-handling clips (too slow, too complex, does it work for me) that the team can send to prospects.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Rewriting outreach scripts at below a third-grade reading level lifted email responses by fifty percent because one unknown word makes people stop reading.
do: Run every script and on-screen caption through a reading-level checker and rewrite anything above a simple level before filming.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Strangers give you seconds, so skip teasing and deliver mind-blowing value in under 30 seconds with an exceptional lead magnet.
do: Put the strongest, most concrete value or offer in the first seconds of the reel, not at the end.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Make the offer so good people feel stupid saying no, and keep scripts short because the action matters more than the script.
do: Keep the offer line to a sentence or two and rewrite it until the deal feels like an obvious yes.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Tripling responses came from giving away free something other people normally charge for, because buyers already have a price anchor for it.
do: Make the free or lead offer a product or service that competitors actually charge for, and state its usual price on screen.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A short, relevant message that names a familiar third party opens a loop and prompts curiosity-driven callbacks.
do: Write a hook that references something the viewer already knows (a competitor, a place, a known customer) and withholds the rest to pull them in.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Ads should be formatted to match the platform so they look like content, and your best-performing organic content is the best thing to run as an ad.
do: Shoot paid reels in the native look of the platform (vertical, handheld or phone-shot feel, no commercial polish) and re-cut our best organic video as the paid version.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Make the ad look like content your ideal buyer wants to consume so the wrong people scroll past, and copy the placements and formats your competitors already run before inventing your own.
do: Before writing, check which formats and placements the brand's category competitors are running, replicate that format first, then iterate.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Study the longest-running, most-engaged ads in the ad library, transcribe about 50 of them for how they hook, retain, reward and make the offer, then write 10 of your own versions.
do: For each new brand, pull 50 long-running ads from the Meta Ad Library in its category, transcribe them, tag hook, middle, reward and offer, then write 10 script variants.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Every ad has a callout, a value section and a call to action, which are the hook, retain and reward, and you should study the ads in your feed to learn them.
do: Write every script as three labelled blocks: callout in the first seconds, value in the middle, one next step as the reward at the end.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Look at the exact words competitors use to call out their buyer and describe the dream outcome, likelihood, speed and ease, and borrow that language rather than the ad itself.
do: Collect the exact words customers and competitors use to describe themselves and the result, and use those words in the first line of the hook.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Each second of an ad exists to sell the next section, so put about 80 percent of the effort into the first five seconds and record value and hooks separately.
do: Spend most of the writing and cutting time on the first five seconds, and shoot the main body once with several different openers recorded separately.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Pairing 30 hooks with 10 value bodies gives 300 variations, and ads fail to scale because too few creatives are tested.
do: Build each body as a reusable block and write and cut at least 3 to 5 alternate hooks per body, so we test hooks first and then which body wins.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The four callouts that work best are labels, yes questions, if-then statements and ridiculous results, and the first five seconds get most of the effort.
do: Write four hook options for every script, one per type: a label naming the buyer, a yes-question, an if-then line and an absurd-sounding result.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Callouts also work through contrast, such as colour, sound and movement in the first seconds, as well as through words.
do: Open the cut on something that contrasts with the feed, such as a bright colour, a sound or movement, and do not start on a still or dull frame.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Show the label instead of saying it: use people and backgrounds that look like the customer, and use visuals of the problem to call out the viewer.
do: Cast and set-dress to match the buyer, and open on a visual of their problem or a local landmark so they self-identify before any words.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: People value an offer when benefits look big and costs look small, and the four value elements plus their opposites give a checklist for ideas.
do: For each script list the dream, speed, ease and likelihood on the good side and the nightmare on the bad side, then pick which ones to show.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A good ad shows the dream outcome and also the worse life of not buying, plus lowers perceived risk with past-failure explanations, proof from people like them and guarantees.
do: Add a short beat showing the viewer's current painful path continuing, then the flip to the result, and one risk-reducer such as a guarantee.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Ease comes from showing that no heavy work or skill is needed, and an ad should disprove the assumption that you must give up things you love.
do: Demonstrate the product being used with almost no effort or skill, and say plainly what the buyer does not have to do.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Status comes from how other people react to us, so show each benefit through the eyes of a spouse, boss or rival rather than only the buyer.
do: Write the payoff beat as a reaction from someone else, such as a partner noticing or a friend commenting, instead of the buyer simply stating the result.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Because you do not know which status the viewer is hungry for, make many versions of one benefit from different people's perspectives and across past, present and future.
do: For one product benefit, script three variants with different reactors such as partner, colleague and rival, and keep them as separate hooks to test.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Negative visualization of the future if nothing changes, shown through other people's eyes, is very compelling.
do: Include a one-line future-cost beat such as 'five years from now' showing what the viewer loses if they keep doing what they do.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Make copy as specific as possible without getting long, and let visuals carry extra specificity that words cannot.
do: Replace vague claims with a specific visual detail on screen instead of lengthening the voiceover.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Viewers have high motivation for a short window, so tell them exactly what to do next in simple words at about a third-grade reading level.
do: End every script on one literal instruction (tap, shop, use code) with a short memorable web address, written in plain words a child could follow.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Most ads lose, so expect to test hundreds to find a few winners and one home run.
do: Plan creative in volume per brand, with many cheap variations per month rather than a few polished ads.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Build a system that gets customers to send testimonials and unboxing videos, and feed them straight into ads, creating a flywheel.
do: Ask each brand's customers for unboxing and testimonial clips as standard, and cut them into paid reels as the proof section.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Some of the best ads were organic videos that spread widely, and a video the platform already likes gets shown to even more people when run as an ad.
do: Check each brand's organic posts for ones that already earned shares or views and run those as ads before making new ones.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Make 30 hooks for 10 pieces of valuable content to get 300 variations to test with small budgets, and treat early losses as a learning budget.
do: Deliver each batch as modular body clips with several swappable openers so the buyer can test hooks cheaply.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The top 0.1 percent of advertisers test 11 times more creative, because you cannot scale a mediocre ad and the only way to find exceptional ones is to make many.
do: Set a creative volume target per brand per month well above current output and cut more variants per concept.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Test one change per week per platform, because changing several things at once hides what worked and the tests interfere with each other.
do: When making variants, change only one element (the hook, or the offer line) between versions so the result is readable.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Work on funnel steps front to back, because the early steps have the lowest conversion and give the biggest gain for small improvements, as fixing the first five seconds of a video got 200 times the views.
do: Review the first five seconds of every underperforming reel before touching anything later in the cut.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Marketing that says plainly who the product is for and who it is not for brings in better customers, which lifts average results and gives you better results to advertise.
do: Add one line to the hook or body that names who the product is for and who should skip it, instead of calling out everyone.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: State what customers actually got on average at set points in time, as a fact that has happened, rather than promising what will happen for the viewer.
do: Write the proof beat as 'customers get X by week N' using real averages, not the one best testimonial, and don't promise it for the viewer.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Find what the best customers did, make new customers do the same, and tie the guarantee to those actions so the guarantee sells and the conditions improve results.
do: Where a brand offers a guarantee, state the 'do this and we guarantee that' condition in the offer beat so it reads as reasonable, not as a pitch.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The same deliverable is worth much more when it arrives sooner, and breaking the result into small milestones that you report often makes it feel faster.
do: Lead the offer beat with how fast the result shows up (days or hours) and name the first quick win.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Frame the ask to bring a friend around the buyer's own gain, such as doubling their results, because people respond to what they get rather than to helping the friend.
do: End a script with 'double your results, do it with a friend' or 'send this to your mate' pitched as a benefit to the viewer.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Soft, constant language such as 'you're not in this alone, do it with someone' in all content lifted one event's signups by a third.
do: Slip a 'do it with a friend' line into the body or caption of regular posts instead of saving it for one referral ad.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A gift card with a seven or fourteen day expiry, personalised with the friend's name, feels like a bigger gift and forces quick use.
do: Offer a 'gift your friend R___ off, expires in 7 days' mechanic as the closing beat of an ecommerce reel.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Paying rewards in your own product feels worth the full retail value to the recipient while costing you only your cost.
do: When designing a bonus or reward in an offer beat, use product the viewer values at retail price over cash.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The first phase of a launch is a short, rare whisper that hints at how big the product is while keeping the product itself a mystery, like a movie trailer that shows only King Kong's foot and a release date.
do: For a new drop, cut a 10 to 15 second teaser reel that shows only a glimpse of the product (a detail, a shadow, a sound) with no name and no price. Post it well ahead of launch and space further teasers far apart.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: After the whisper comes the tease, which reveals the product, makes the launch date public and shows the elements of value, and then comes the shout, where bonuses, scarcity, urgency and guarantees are pushed hard and posting frequency rises in the last days.
do: Plan a launch as three reel waves: a reveal reel with the date and the value (what it is, who it is for, when they get the result), then a final-days run of reels (3 days, 2 days, 1 day, hours) built on the bonus, the limited stock and the guarantee.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Set a fixed learning budget that you give yourself full permission to lose on crazy ideas, because most do nothing but the occasional one takes off and spending on advertising teaches you faster than anything else.
do: Set aside a fixed slice of the monthly creative or ad budget for wild reel concepts that are allowed to flop, and judge them as learning spend rather than as normal ads.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Spend about 10% of content and ad effort on crazy ideas, such as monthly hackathon days where everyone makes one or two experimental pieces, which both finds new winners and keeps the team from burning out.
do: Run a monthly experiment day where each editor or writer makes one or two off-brief reels with no meetings. Keep roughly one in ten pieces experimental.

title: $100M Leads (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A test of 300 fliers is too small to show whether something works, since his mentor sent 5,000 to learn and then 5,000 a day, so the strategy was right and the volume was far too low.
do: Do not call a hook or angle dead after a few posts. Make several variations of each concept and give them enough volume or spend before deciding.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Better offers raise response rates, raise conversion and lower CPMs, so they are the biggest lever on acquisition cost.
do: When ads underperform, rework the offer in the first seconds before changing edit style or media spend.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The two most powerful words in advertising are free and new, and free offers aim to convert the largest share of the audience.
do: Test hooks that open on a free or new element (free gift, free shipping, a new drop) in the first line on screen.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Free beats even a one-cent price by a huge margin, so free value pulls far more takers than a tiny charge.
do: For a launch or gift-with-purchase reel, lead with the free item as the hook and show it on screen in the first two seconds.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: People respond to claims they believe, so a smaller believable promise can get more opt-ins than a bigger one.
do: Write the result claim at a level a stranger will believe, and back it with a real customer or a demo shot.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: If people do not want a free offer, the cause is the offer or its wording, disbelief, or the wrong audience, and each is useful feedback.
do: When a free-offer ad flops, test a new description and a new audience before killing the offer.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: In a 20-location test, free offers brought more sales than paid ones with the same close rate; only lead cost changed.
do: Do not hold back a free or heavily discounted offer in ads because of brand worry; compare the cost per sale instead.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Small discounts of 10 to 20 percent do not change behavior, so only deep discounts of 50 percent or more on known-value items move people.
do: If a reel's offer is a modest percent off, either raise it sharply on a limited item or make the reel about something else.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A discount can be shown as a percentage, an amount off, a relative equivalent, a portion free, or a crossed-out price, and each should be tested.
do: Make separate cuts of the same offer, one per framing (R200 off, 25% off, one free, was-now price).

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The same discount described in different ways keeps ads fresh while the real deal stays the same.
do: Rotate the discount framing on the on-screen text each month while keeping the underlying offer fixed.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A price-off only works when buyers already know the normal price; for unfamiliar products, percent off a stated retail value works better.
do: For a known category show the price against what people expect; for a new product anchor with a stated retail value or percent.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Do not discount the core product; split off one well-understood part or an extra and discount that heavily.
do: Build the hook around a single heavily discounted piece (a sample, the starter item) and let the main product be the second step.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Buyers go through short hyper-buying windows after a new decision, and sellers who do not make follow-on offers lose those sales to someone else.
do: In a reel for a main product, show the matching add-on in the same video (the bike, then the helmet).

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Letting a customer know about an offer that solves their problem is not hard selling, and nobody buys what they do not know exists.
do: State the offer and price plainly in the reel instead of hinting at it.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: An upsell fails when pitched after the customer's need is satisfied; create the next problem first, then offer the fix.
do: Script the add-on as the answer to a new problem the first purchase reveals, not as an afterthought.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: People buy when they feel the lack, not when they are satisfied, so offers should land at the moment of need.
do: Open a reel on the felt problem or craving and place the offer there, not after a satisfied ending.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Good upsell moments are right after the first sale, a day or two later, and after a big win, because a solved problem opens a new one.
do: Make follow-up videos for existing customers aimed at the next problem after a win.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Upsell mid-journey and not at the end, because pitching after the cycle finishes means reopening a closed purchase.
do: Time post-purchase content and flows to day-two and mid-use, not the end of the product's use.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Naming the cheapest tier 'minimum' makes it feel required, so nearly everyone takes it, unlike 'economy'.
do: Name the entry bundle or tier with a word that sounds like the sensible baseline (essentials, standard) in on-screen text.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Strangers cannot judge your claimed value but understand price, so a steep discount or free makes any offer an obvious deal.
do: Put the price and what is free or reduced on screen early, and stop leaning on claims of value alone.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A win-your-money-back offer, where the customer gets a refund for hitting a result, produced before-and-after proof that sold more customers.
do: Frame a reel around a customer who stands to win their money back, then use their real result as the follow-up proof reel.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Money-back offers can bet on a result, on actions taken, or both, and the actions should also advertise the business and help the result.
do: Tie required actions (post a photo, tag the brand) to the refund so each participant makes content for you.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The win-your-money-back offer works as a paid onboarding, since 78% hit the goal and he upsold during the programme rather than waiting for the end.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: An unconditional service guarantee alongside the performance guarantee closed more buyers and cut legal risk, and refunds on request are cheaper than angry customers.
do: Add a plain guarantee line to the offer section of a script, e.g. 'if you don't think it was worth it, you get your money back'.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Put a stated monetary value on the grand prize so it anchors the discounted offer, and a bigger discount makes a more compelling offer.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Each countdown update should sell a different benefit of the prize rather than just saying time is running out.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Pair each benefit with proof of that benefit, such as a customer saying it, every time you mention it.
do: Follow each benefit claim in a script with a customer clip or quote that backs that exact claim.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Compare the promo price to the full value or what it would cost elsewhere, so a small discount reads as a large one.
do: Show the 'value if bought separately' against the bundle price on screen, so the saving shown is larger than the percentage discount.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Explaining why the quick route fails (the turkey talk about not cooking faster at higher heat) makes customers see why they need the bigger plan.
do: Use a simple everyday analogy in the body of a script to explain why one purchase or one use will not do the job, and lead into the multi-pack or subscription.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Advertise the result rather than the vehicle, so you can choose the product and price in the sales conversation.
do: Write the hook around the result the customer wants and leave out product specs and price until after they are engaged.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Advertise benefits not features, a discount can be phrased four ways, and the gap between the free and premium option must be big.
do: Pick the strongest of four phrasings for a discount (percent off, amount off, months free, a total price) and test them in the hook.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Free stuff gets more attention than discounts, and a bundle can turn a one-third discount into a stronger 'buy two get one free' pitch.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Three shirts at $10 each and 'buy one, get two free' have identical economics, but the free framing gets far more attention.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: At the same price, the offer with the most free months looks the most compelling, so buy six get twelve free beats buy twelve get six free.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi

do: Check the margin before writing a free-item offer, and put the free items in bold on screen.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Several cheaper free items can beat one expensive free item, so test buy one shirt get three socks against buy one get one.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Promise a simple, measurable yes/no result, and measure before and after so progress is visible.
do: Show a before and after measurement in a reel, such as a rating or a count, so the result reads as a clear yes.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Free content only works as a selling tool if it teaches something and breaks the beliefs that stop people buying, like an FAQ on steroids.
do: List the top objections for a product and make each one the subject of a reel that answers it, ending in a call to action.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The time you need to sell grows with the price relative to the buyer's spending power, so a cheap item can sell in a seven second ad while a pricier one needs more.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The bigger the plane the longer the runway: the more expensive the thing is relative to the buyer's money, the more trust you must build first.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A multi-day sequence deals first with the audience's biggest fear, then the outside excuse, before pitching and repitching with proof.
do: Order a series of reels as fear or doubt about themselves, then the outside blocker, then the offer, then offer again with case studies.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Buyers say others (kids, spouse) will stop them, so reframe each objection as a reason the product helps those people.
do: In a script, name the common 'I can't because of X' excuse and show how the product helps X.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Break a belief in five beats (old belief, why it is wrong, what is right, why it is right, proof) and teach concepts that everyone can use rather than tactics only executors can use.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The next thing to sell is more of it (quantity), a better version (quality), or something complementary (different).
do: Build the post-purchase or bundle offer as a multipack, a premium version, or a complementary item.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Make the upsell the next natural thing the buyer needs, so the main product feels incomplete without it.
do: Pair the hero product in the offer with the item it needs to work well, framed as essential to results.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Detailed, personalised instructions on how to use the product after buying raise purchase likelihood because they assume the sale.
do: In the demo section, walk through exactly how and when they will use the product day to day, as if they already own it.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Crossing out products a customer doesn't need builds enough goodwill that they trust and buy what you do recommend.
do: Say plainly who or what in your range someone does not need, then recommend the one thing they do.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Unselling means telling the buyer what they don't need first, so they believe you about what they do need.
do: Open a product reel with what you should skip or not buy, then point to the one pick.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Prescribe the single solution by explaining how it fits what they already bought, then ask preference A or B instead of yes or no.
do: End on a choice between two ways to buy (size or colour or bundle) rather than 'buy now or not'.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Add a nudge to an A/B choice ('most people pick this') to give the illusion of choice while steering to the higher-margin or in-stock option.
do: On the offer card, label one option 'most popular' and give a one-line reason.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The Economist's digital-plus-print sales fell when digital was cheap, until they added a print-only decoy at the combined price.
do: Show three options where a decoy makes the bundle look like the obvious best value.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: To get people to buy both A and B, offer A, B and A+B, pricing A+B at the same price as the dearer single item.
do: Design a three-card bundle on screen: A, B, and A+B priced at the higher of the singles.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A very high first price recategorises everything after it, so the author spent five times his budget; Rolls-Royce shows cars next to jets and yachts for the same reason.
do: Show the pricey option or full set first so the hero item looks light by comparison.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Show a premium version at 5 to 10 times the price first, with the same primary features as the main offer, so the main offer looks like a steal.
do: In the offer segment, show the premium or full-price version first, then the real offer with the same core and fewer extras.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: An anchor must be an order of magnitude higher to make them gasp; then you rescue them by asking if they care about the premium extras.
do: Make the anchor price at least 5x the real offer, not 20% above it.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: An anchor only works if you treat it as a real offer, so the buyer seriously considers it and justifies the price in their head.
do: Spend real seconds selling the premium option with specifics before moving to the real offer.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The main offer should differ from the anchor only in secondary features so the buyer needn't re-evaluate value.
do: Keep core benefits identical between premium and main offer and only cut cosmetic extras.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A win-back message titled 'I owe you money' offers lapsed customers credit towards a new purchase.
do: Use 'I owe you' framing as the hook for win-back email, SMS or reel to past buyers.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A gift card play sells $200 cards for about $20 to be given to a friend, and the friend rolls it into a $2,000 product, effective around Black Friday.
do: For Black Friday, offer a limited, two-per-person discounted gift voucher that a friend can redeem toward a bigger item.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Cutting the price of the same product repeatedly destroys trust, whereas offering a different thing for less keeps it.
do: When a buyer hesitates or in a sale, change what is included rather than just shaving the price on the same item.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: People refuse because the price is too high today, not overall, so change the payment terms instead of cutting the price.
do: Show pay-in-instalments (e.g. a buy-now-pay-later option) on the offer card rather than a cheaper product.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A continuity bonus should be worth more than the first payment, and bonuses add good stuff while discounts remove bad stuff, both only if they join now.
do: In a subscription ad, make the free gift visibly worth more than the first month and say it is only for those who start today.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A pet-food subscription can open with a free $800 bundle of dog toys, plus a new toy every month to keep members.
do: For a subscribe-and-save ecommerce ad, lead with the free bundle gift and mention a monthly surprise as the reason to stay.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Advertise the free valuable bonus rather than the membership, and explain the subscription only once someone shows interest.
do: Open the reel on the free thing they receive, with the subscription revealed later in the video or on the landing page.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Keep bonuses related to the core offer and make them things you already do, or you attract the wrong customers.
do: Choose a bonus that fits the product the viewer is buying, such as a related accessory, not a random freebie.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A big value anchor makes a bonus compelling, but invented values destroy trust, so the anchor must be believable.
do: State the free gift's real retail price on screen and never inflate it.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Anchor bonuses on prices you actually charged before and show receipts, so the discount is real and believable.
do: Show a past price or receipt on screen beside the new free-gift or discount price.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Sell the bonus on its own first, then ask 'want to know how to get it free?', so people weigh it against the membership price.
do: Spend real time selling the bonus's benefits in the video, then reveal that it is free with the subscription.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Stacking several bonuses, each with its dollar value, pushes more people to choose the continuity option.
do: List two or three bonuses on screen with a price on each before the final price.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Sell the bonus seriously as a standalone offer before revealing it is free, because the anchor only works if people actually want it.
do: Don't rush through the bonus line; give it its own beat of value before the price reveal.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The same discount can be shown as free months, a dollar amount off, a percentage off or a comparison, and billing every four weeks yields 13 payments a year.
do: Test the same deal stated as months free, rand amount off and percent off in different reel versions.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: His fitness model chained a win-your-money-back front offer, a prepay buy-X-get-Y-free upsell, a continuity bonus, a free-trial-with-penalty downsell and a supplement menu upsell, so every 'no' had a next offer.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Once a customer is on a subscription, a buy-six-get-six-free offer can pull cash forward and double lifetime value, but only if the average customer would not stay longer than the prepaid period anyway.

title: $100M Money Models (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Start with a lower price to get yes answers and raise it in stages, keep the model as simple as possible, and a third-party affiliate product can serve as the buy-X-get-Y-free bonus without any operational load.
do: When a client lacks a strong bonus, suggest a complementary product from another brand as the free item in the offer, and keep the reel to one offer with one price rather than several.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The offer is the biggest driver of campaign success because a unique one stops buyers comparing prices and makes them decide on value.
do: Open the reel on what is distinctive about the offer, not the price, so the viewer has nothing to compare it against.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Swapping a commodity $99 membership for a defined six-week result with a money-back promise raised clicks, sales and price.
do: Pitch a defined result in a set time with a guarantee, not an open-ended product.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The service stayed the same; only how it was presented changed, with extras and a guarantee, and returns jumped to 30 to one.
do: Rework the reel's framing and bonuses before changing the product; stack the extras on screen.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Pick markets where customers are in absolute pain and need the product, not where it is merely nice to have.
do: Open on the buyer's desperate, specific pain rather than a convenience benefit.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Position yourself as helping one specific person solve one specific problem in a unique way that beats their biggest objection.
do: Write the hook so one named viewer hears it is for them, and let the body answer their biggest worry.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The same time-management course rose from $19 to about $2,000 purely by narrowing the audience and language.
do: Name the exact buyer in the first line of the script instead of speaking to everyone.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Copy works when the prospect feels understood, and describing their situation better than they can makes them trust you with the solution.
do: Spend the hook and first beat describing the viewer's situation in their own words before any pitch.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Cutting price is a path to failure; raise the value and perceived value instead, because average products earn no repeat buyers.
do: Do not lead with discounts; add proof, bonuses or a guarantee to raise the perceived value on screen.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Price itself communicates value, and in a blind taste test identical wine rated better when labelled more expensive.
do: Present the product with premium cues in the reel instead of cheap-deal framing, so the price reads as quality.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Perceived value rises with dream outcome and likelihood of success, and falls with time delay and effort or sacrifice.
do: Check every script against the four levers: say the outcome, show it will work, give a short timeframe, and cut the effort.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A more meaningful outcome is worth more, so solving a bigger or more expensive problem supports a higher price.
do: Frame the result as the meaningful end state the viewer wants, not the product feature.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Buyers pay more when they believe they will succeed, and repeated past success raises that belief.
do: Show a count of past results or repeat customers in the script, not just one testimonial.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Perceived likelihood must be communicated, and doing the established thing in half the time creates value.
do: Put the time-to-result in the hook and state it as a number.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Speed beats free, and showing progress on the way to a slow result raises the value buyers perceive.
do: Lead with how fast the result comes and show an early sign of progress in the first seconds of the demo.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: CoolSculpting commands high prices because the ad stresses high likelihood, no downtime and no change in lifestyle.
do: List what the buyer does not have to do or give up, on screen, as a quick run of lines.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The biggest companies win by driving time delay and effort to zero, and the buyer must perceive that ease.
do: Show the whole buying or using process as one or two taps in the demo, so the ease is seen not claimed.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: State the dream outcome as a specific result in a specific time without the buyer's biggest pain or fear, optionally naming the avatar.
do: Write the hook as outcome plus timeframe plus 'without' the dreaded thing, aimed at one named buyer.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Buyer objections map to the four value factors: not worth it, won't work for me, too hard, too slow.
do: List the viewer's likely objections and answer each in a line of the script body.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Solving obstacles nobody else mentions makes the prospect feel understood and more convinced you can deliver.
do: Name a small, specific obstacle competitors ignore and show how the product handles it.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Flip each objection into a plain 'how to' promise that removes it, such as quickly, for less, or with family.
do: Generate three hook options by turning each top objection into a 'how to X without Y' line and test them.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: One knife for $19 plus 38 free knives feels more valuable than 38 knives for $19, because splitting core from free extras changes the perceived value.
do: When a brand has a bundle, script it as one core product with the extras shown as free add-ons, not a single list of items for one price.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Instead of discounting, keep stacking one-time bonuses after the price anchor so people act now without the price dropping.
do: In the offer beat, name the price first, then add bonus after bonus ('and you also get...') rather than cutting the price.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Splitting one offer into a core item plus separate bonuses makes it feel like several things, and people count items far more easily than they judge intangible value.
do: List the offer on screen as a numbered count (1 core product, 2, 3, 4 free extras) with each item appearing as its own card or beat in the cut.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Bonuses work harder when they are scarce or time-limited, and each should carry a benefit in its name.
do: Name each free extra with its benefit ('Spend-Less Shopping Guide'), and add a limit such as 'only the last 3' to one of them in the script.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Each bonus should be sold: say what it does, give a stat or past customer as proof, paint life after using it, and put a price on it.
do: For every bonus in a script, give one line of what it does, one line of proof or a number, and its rand value.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Tools, checklists and shortcuts make better bonuses than extra hours of training because they sound easy and have sizzle.
do: Pick bonuses that sound instant (a template, a guide, a checklist) and describe them by the effort they save.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: People hold back when they fear it won't work for them, so free and guarantees convert better because they remove risk.
do: Put a risk-reversal line (return window, money-back, free trial) right before the call to action instead of leaving it in the fine print.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Frame the guarantee as 'I'm not asking you to decide yes or no, only to make an informed decision from the inside', like looking inside a house before buying.
do: Use the line 'try it, and if it's not for you, send it back' framed as an informed decision, as the closing line of a spoken script.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Show a money-back guarantee as two no-risk choices: walk away and certainly not get the result, or try it and likely get it.
do: Close a script with two options: do nothing and stay where you are, or try it with the return guarantee and risk nothing.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: A conditional guarantee must state both the condition and the penalty, like Domino's 30 minutes or free, and stay realistic.
do: Write guarantees as 'if X doesn't happen in Y time, we do Z' with all three parts spoken out loud.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Give your guarantee a vivid name, such as 'love it or leave it', because a plain 30-day money-back guarantee is forgettable.
do: Give the guarantee a named, imagery-led line in the script and say it as a hook-style line, not 'satisfaction guaranteed'.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Their best campaign showed customers a year on, which lets new prospects picture a long-term result and arrive with a long-term mindset.
do: Cut a reel of 'one year later' customer clips (reorders, still using it) stacked back to back, with the time gap shown on screen.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Long-term proof future-paces new customers so they expect steady growth instead of overnight rescue and become better customers.
do: Pair a customer's 'now' result with how long they've had it, and use before/after pairs spanning months.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: There are four honest ways to create urgency: the next group, the season, the promotion's price or bonuses, and a vanishing opportunity.
do: Choose one real deadline per script (batch closing, seasonal promo end, bonus leaving) and state the date.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Rolling start dates give a natural reason to decide today, because the next group starts soon.
do: Tie the call to action to a real cut-off such as the next dispatch date or the next batch.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Seasonal promotions create authentic urgency, and a similar offer under a new seasonal name keeps it fresh.
do: Rename the same offer for each season or event (Valentine's, Black Friday, Heritage Day) with an end date in the hook.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Rotate bonuses, names and starting prices each month so the same business model looks new and people act before the bonuses disappear.
do: Swap which free extras are included in each month's ads and say the current ones leave at month end.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Real capacity limits, such as the spots left, make people decide faster and also work as social proof.
do: State the real stock or capacity left ('only 40 left in this batch') on screen.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Limited physical bonuses, like a free item with the first X orders, make scarcity easy to grasp.
do: Offer a limited free gift for the first X orders and show the counter on screen.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: One-of-a-kind or limited drops sell out faster than permanent catalogues because scarcity drives purchasing.
do: Frame new product as a limited drop and say it won't be restocked.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Offers stall when prospects don't know it's for them, what problem it solves, or that it solves it the way they want.
do: Make the first line name who it's for and the problem, and describe the fix the way the viewer would say it.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: People who refuse the core product still want the bigger outcome, and offering a different route to it sold more.
do: Sell the bigger outcome (lose weight, look good) in the hook and treat the product as one route, with a lighter alternative for cold viewers.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The MAGIC naming formula: a magnetic reason, announce the avatar, a goal, a time interval, and a container word.
do: Write headline options with reason, who it's for, goal, time and a container word (kit, challenge, blueprint) in them.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Use the MAGIC formula to name programs, promotions and bonuses, fitting in at least three or four of the five parts.
do: Check each hook line has three or four of the parts: reason, who, goal, time, container.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Strong names pack the pieces together, such as '21 day mommy makeover', where one word does two jobs.
do: Pick words that call out the audience and the goal at once, like 'mommy makeover'.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
