says: A seasonal reason ('back to school', 'grand opening') plus a goal and a power word makes an effective headline.
do: Open with a time-bound real reason in the headline card and then the specific outcome.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: The whole program is measured in days or weeks while the sub-benefits are in seconds, minutes and hours, and small wins make the big one believable.
do: Describe each product benefit with a short time ('works in 60 seconds', 'ready in 10 minutes').

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Cutting the time makes the same thing far more valuable, so name speed in the offer to answer how long it will take.
do: Put the time in the first line and on screen ('10 seconds, not 10 minutes'), and show a timer or clock in the cut.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Value is the speed to the goal, not the amount of your time sold, and promotions fatigue and need refreshing in order of least effort.
do: Sell how fast they get the result, not how much is included.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: When an ad tires, first change only the creative, then the body copy, then the headline, keeping the offer the same.
do: When a reel fatigues, cut new first-3-second visuals for the same offer and script before rewriting the offer.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Refresh the wrapper by renaming it or changing the time unit (one month to four weeks, seven days to 164 hours) without changing the business.
do: Test the same offer with a reworded name and a different time unit in the headline.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: Mild 10% or 20% discounts don't change buyer behaviour; only free or massive discounts move people who were on the fence.
do: In offer tests, use free gift or a deep discount instead of 10% off, and say the offer plainly in the hook.

title: $100M Offers (free course)
author: Alex Hormozi
says: He changes creative weekly, copy and headline every two to three weeks, the enhancer and duration rarely, and the monetisation structure every few years.
do: Plan a refresh calendar: new creative weekly, new copy every two to three weeks, offer changes only occasionally.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: A copywriter cannot create desire; he can only take a want that millions already have and channel it onto one product.
do: Open each script by naming the want the viewer already has (for example, losing weight or looking put-together), then tie the product to that want. Do not invent a new need.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Only one mass desire can be channelled in a single ad, and no formula works twice because each product and market is a fresh problem.
do: Pick one desire per reel and cut every line that serves a second one. Brief each new script from the product and audience, not from a previous winner's template.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: People now spot advertising bunk in split-seconds because they have been trained by ad overload, not because attention spans shrank.
do: Make the first line specific and believable enough to survive that instant filter. Drop generic openers like 'Tired of X?'.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: First Action – Selecting A Mass Desire
says: A mass desire is a private want shared by many, and an ad's power comes from attaching to one that already exists, not from the words.
do: Before writing, state in one line the shared want your product serves and check that plenty of people already feel it.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: Three Dimensions of Any Mass Desire's Power
says: Every mass desire has urgency, staying power and scope, and only the dominant desire for the product gives the best return.
do: Rank the candidate desires for a product by urgency, staying power and number of people, and write the reel to the top one.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: To analyse a product, list its claims, then study how it works (physical and functional) to find the mechanisms that make the claims believable.
do: Before scripting a product, write a claims list and a how-it-works list. Pull the on-screen proof and the 'because' line from the mechanism list.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Each ad should align one desire, one key claim and one mechanism through headline and copy, and that alignment is the theme.
do: Write a one-line brief for every script (desire, claim, mechanism) and delete any shot or line that does not serve those three.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Body copy should sharpen the existing want and make the prospect picture, and feel, having it fulfilled.
do: Spend the middle of the script on the after-state (the relief, pride or satisfaction of having it), shown in a concrete scene, not just features.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: People also buy to define who they are (character roles), so a product can sell as the person they want to be.
do: Where the product is lifestyle or fashion, show the person the buyer wants to be using it, and let visuals carry that role without stating it.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: People accept ideas that match beliefs they already hold, and beliefs change only slowly, so don't fight them.
do: Write the claim so it fits what the viewer already believes. If a belief opposes the product, don't try to overturn it in a 30 s reel.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: A prospect who knows the product and wants it needs only the name, a good price and where to buy.
do: For retargeting and returning customers, cut a short reel with product, price, offer and link, and skip the persuasion.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: 2. Knows about the product but doesn't want it
says: Most advertising targets people who know the product but aren't convinced, so it must strengthen desire, sharpen the picture, add proof and announce a new mechanism.
do: For warm audiences, pick one lever: a new proof point, a new use scene, or a new mechanism, and build the reel around it.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: If the prospect wants the result but doesn't know your product does it, pinpoint the desire and show that your product is the solution.
do: Open on the exact desire or problem in the viewer's words, then reveal the product as the answer within the first few seconds.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: For a need rather than a want, name the need in the headline and dramatise it until the product is the inevitable fix.
do: For problem-solving products, open with the need named and shown vividly (the leak, the pain, the mess) before the product enters.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: When the prospect is unaware of the desire, lead with identification: the role they want, with the product as its symbol.
do: For cold audiences with no known need, open on the type of person or life the viewer aspires to, not on the product's function.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: When a product's claims are over-familiar and disbelieved, shift from what it does to who the buyer becomes, and carve out a narrower splinter market.
do: For crowded categories, stop repeating the standard benefit claim and find a narrower audience and identity to speak to.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: The best ideas come from listening to your market and the client; Schwartz's famous Boardroom ad was 70% the client's own words.
do: Record the founder or read customer reviews, and lift their exact phrases into hooks and lines instead of inventing ad-speak.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Schwartz won a crowded market with an extreme, oddly phrased headline ('71-year-old man has sexual congress five times a day') that pulled 9% on the first test.
do: When every competitor makes the same promise, push the claim to its extreme case and phrase it in an unusual, specific way for the hook.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Readers respond with the gut, not the logical brain, so copy should use very simple, vivid words.
do: Rewrite the hook and key lines in plain, vivid words a ten-year-old would follow, and cut abstract or clever phrasing.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Good copy is transparent like a shop window: the reader should see the product and react to it, not praise the writing.
do: Judge each draft by whether a viewer would say 'I need that' rather than 'nice line'. Cut any flourish, pun or edit trick that calls attention to itself.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: The headline has about ten seconds and one job: to get the reader to the next line, not to sell, prove or explain.
do: Write the first seconds of a reel only to earn the next beat. Move claims, proof and price to later lines.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Headline length is whatever it takes to stop the person, and each line exists only to sell the next line.
do: Check every line of a script by asking whether it makes the viewer want the next line. Cut any that does not.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Bold claims can be believed in the middle of an ad because the reader has been prepared, but the same claim at the top is thrown away.
do: Hold the boldest claim until after the hook and a proof beat, and open instead with something the viewer will accept.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: An envelope headline listing twenty specific tricks with page numbers ran as a control for fifteen years.
do: Use a hook or on-screen text with two or three very specific, concrete payoffs rather than one vague promise.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: You write to people who share a private want, addressing each as the only person in the world, and 'you' is the most powerful word.
do: Write in second person, name the viewer's specific want in the first line, and count the 'you's in the script.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: Headline Elements: Promise = Intrigue, Mechanism = Emotion
says: The 'Sneaky Little Arthritis Tricks' headline worked by using unexpected words that matched the readers' unspoken feeling of sneaking around doctors.
do: Find the unspoken feeling the buyer has about the problem and use an unexpected, unadvertisy word that names it in the hook.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: Headline Elements: Promise = Intrigue, Mechanism = Emotion
says: A strong opening stacks intrigue (promise), then a new mechanism, then proof from people like the reader, with emotion in the pictures.
do: Structure the opening 5 to 10 seconds as promise, then mechanism, then a person-like-you result, with a face that carries emotion.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: A headline can set a point of difference, include everyone ('both men and women'), and pair a strong claim with an easy mechanism.
do: State the claim and then the effortless way it happens in one line, and make sure the viewer can see they are included.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Putting the risk-free guarantee early makes the wild claims that follow more believable.
do: Mention the guarantee or free returns before the big claim, not only at the end of the reel.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: Prepare the Ground for Each Claim
says: Prepare each claim, and check adjectives, because they carry the feeling and change the meaning.
do: After drafting, do an adjective pass and swap flat words for gut words like 'effortless' or 'startling'. Line up a setup beat before each big claim.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Powerful claims need proof, and a detailed biography of the expert makes people believe, and they read every word of it.
do: Give the founder or expert a proper credentials moment with concrete detail (years, places, numbers) rather than a vague 'experts agree'.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: You’ve Got to Demonstrate the Product
says: Demonstration is powerful proof, and giving the reader something to do with the product convinces them in the moment.
do: Include a try-it-now beat, one simple action the viewer can see or do within seconds, shown step by step.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: You’ve Got to Demonstrate the Product
says: Build the ad as a mosaic where every sentence moves through claim, mechanism, proof, documentation and demonstration.
do: Check that each beat of a script is one of claim, mechanism, proof or demo, and cut beats that are none of these.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: You cannot create demand, only channel existing demand onto your product, and the bigger the demand the better the ad.
do: Choose products and angles where the demand is already visible (search volume, reviews, comments) before writing a script.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Beautiful layouts all look alike, while ugly ones are random and stand out, so being different in a sea of polish gets noticed.
do: When every competitor's ads look glossy, test a rawer, less polished look (phone footage, plain captions) for the cut.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Define the product by what it does for the buyer, not what it is, and use a different 'does' when an angle wears out.
do: List ten things the product does for the buyer and make a fresh reel around an unused one instead of re-editing the tired angle.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: One 'does' is bringing in an audience: show other people reacting, as in the flower ad where neighbours came to look.
do: Add a beat where friends, family or neighbours notice and react to the result.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Demonstration is proof at the present moment, so make the benefit something the reader can try or check immediately.
do: Give the viewer an instantly checkable proof (a visible before/after, a quick test) inside the reel.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Making benefits instantly accessible lets people prove the claim themselves, and nothing feels better than being proved right.
do: Offer something the viewer can check right away, like a simple self-test or a visible effect on screen.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Schwartz marks every claim in a long source manuscript and types them up into a short vocabulary before having any ideas.
do: Before scripting, mark every claim in the brand's site, reviews and founder notes and compile them into one page. Write only from that page.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Read the product itself from first page to last, without anyone else's summary, so its claims hit you fresh as surprises.
do: Before scripting, go through the brand's product page, reviews and founder material start to finish, and mark the claims that surprise you.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: When and How Your Writing Goes
says: Collect every claim first with no headline, then pick the most unusual and powerful ones, and know the source material better than its owner.
do: List every claim the product can make, then choose the single most unusual one to open the hook.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: When and How Your Writing Goes
says: Careful preparation beats raw talent because the selling power sits in the product, and the writer's job is to find it and express it.
do: Do the product homework (ingredients, reviews, founder story) before writing a line, and take the hook from something the product truly has.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Copy is assembled from building blocks of claims, images and desires, not written as prose.
do: Build each script from a bank of claims, images and desires, then arrange them, instead of drafting from a blank page.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: Assembling Words – Windows in a Store
says: Words must be see-through windows onto the product, so plain everyday words in a fresh combination beat pretty phrasing.
do: Cut any line the viewer would notice as a line; rewrite hooks in plain customer words that show the thing itself.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: Assembling Words – Windows in a Store
says: A hook lands when its words match the exact pain and failed attempts the audience already knows.
do: Write the hook in the words of someone who has already tried the usual fixes and been let down.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Creativity is joining two ideas that did not go together before, and a fresh verbal connection stops and moves the reader.
do: Pair two unrelated ideas from the audience's life to make a hook, such as the product and an unexpected situation.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: A hook line gives a wild claim, and the next line makes it believable and doable with proof.
do: Follow every hook with a second beat that names the how and who proved it, within the first seconds.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Every line has one job only: get the reader to the next line, so a headline should not try to sell.
do: Write each line of a reel only to earn the next second; make the first line a reason to keep watching, not a pitch.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: The envelope replaces the headline, needing only to tantalise enough to get opened, and the first line inside can be soft and conventional.
do: After a punchy teaser hook, open the body in a calm plain line so the hard hit is not repeated.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Pile belief upon belief with case histories, but give an escape route so anyone who leaves early can still try with a guarantee.
do: Put the offer and guarantee in a complete early beat so a viewer who leaves at 10 seconds has still seen how to try it.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Write to one person who shares a problem with a large mass, and use the word 'you' with their own specific hands, face or situation.
do: Pick one named viewer with one problem and speak to 'your' version of it, changing every 'the' into 'your'.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Using the audience's own technical terms makes copy feel full of 'you' because they have lived with those terms.
do: Lift the exact jargon and phrases from reviews and comments into the script voice-over.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Listening closely to the people with the problem lets you sound like their mirror image.
do: Read customer comments and DMs before writing and mirror their phrasing in the script.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Study tabloids, hit movies and the audience's own media, because those are their headlines, people and feelings.
do: Collect headlines from the magazines, shows and feeds your buyer actually consumes and borrow their emotional register.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Copy should deliver a fresh jolt every few minutes like a Joel Silver film, with each paragraph standing as its own headline.
do: Time a reel so there is a new punch beat every few seconds and each line could stand alone as a hook.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Frame the product as the way from hell to heaven and be dramatic, because the audience gives only part-attention.
do: Contrast the painful before with the vivid after in big, high-contrast terms in the opening seconds.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Pair a strong claim with a strange mechanism so the viewer has to find out how, and when claims all sound alike the mechanism carries the copy.
do: State a strong result, then tease an odd 'how' that is only explained later in the video.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: In crowded markets the claim can be modest if it implies a mechanism the reader wants to see.
do: Try hooks that state a small surprising fact and imply a hidden how, such as 'you can't X, right? Wrong.'

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Use a medium-sized believable claim paired with something that seems impossible, and people will seek the answer to prove you wrong.
do: Write a hook that says something can't be done, followed by the product doing it.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: A tired product is revived by finding a whole new set of benefits to lead with, because you sell bundles of news, not the product.
do: When a reel fatigues, keep the product but rebuild the hook around a different benefit or piece of news.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Offer at least one free premium with every product because it gets people to try and sets up the next sale.
do: Add a free bonus to the offer beat and say it out loud in the close.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: A copywriter must read the market's awareness, sophistication and driving desire, and prevention hooks work by picturing loved ones afflicted.
do: Before writing, note the viewer's stage of awareness; for a protective product try a hook that pictures their family at risk.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: B. How to align mass desire onto your product.
says: Each ad can tap only one mass desire at a time, and the reader gives a single glance so each thought must earn the next.
do: Choose one desire per reel and make the first line carry only one thought.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: C. What Your Prospect's State of Awareness Demands From Your Headline
says: The hook must change with the viewer's stage of awareness, from a bare price for those who already want it to dramatising a need for those who do not see one.
do: Tag each script with the audience's awareness stage and write the first line accordingly: price for aware, named solution for new, dramatised need for unaware.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: C. What Your Prospect's State of Awareness Demands From Your Headline
says: For a completely unaware market, use an identification hook that calls people together by naming what they are, since price, name and direct claims mean nothing yet.
do: For cold, unaware audiences open by describing a shared situation or attitude that picks out your person.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: D. Know the Stages of Sophistication of your Market
says: As a market gets crowded, move from simple claims to bigger claims to a new mechanism, and finally to identification.
do: If competitors already make the same promise, lead with how it works instead of repeating or inflating the promise.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Fill vague desires with concrete scenes of fulfilment, because the viewer takes away one dominant image and varying how you show it makes it stronger.
do: Pick one dominant image for the reel and show it from several angles instead of adding new messages.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Thirteen ways to build desire after the claim, including putting claims in action, showing the first day, tests, other voices, comparisons, ease, and a guarantee.
do: Use a checklist when building the middle: show first-day use, a test, an audience voice, the objection, then summarise and close with the guarantee.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: People buy products as instruments for roles they want to play, so build the product's personality from what they already believe about it.
do: Show who the buyer becomes by using the product, building from its existing image and appearance.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Never violate the viewer's existing beliefs, and one claim fully believed outsells many half-believed ones.
do: Cut weaker claims and let one believable claim carry the script, bridging from what the viewer already accepts.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Belief depends on structure, so start with an accepted statement and build a chain of acceptances before the main claim.
do: Open with something the viewer already agrees with, and hold the big claim until the second half.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Strengthen believability instead of piling on promises, using identification, contradiction of false beliefs, and promise-then-proof sequences.
do: Alternate each promise with a proof beat so the viewer never has room to doubt.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Redefine a product that is too complex, unimportant or pricey by simplifying, broadening its benefits, or comparing it to a costlier standard.
do: For a high price, compare cost to a more expensive alternative the viewer already accepts.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Mechanism copy must be loaded with promise and emotion, never dull, and be named, described or featured depending on what viewers already assume.
do: Explain how the product works in one vivid sentence tied to a benefit, not a spec list.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Only attack a competing option if you show at the same time how your product provides what the other lacks.
do: Any comparison shot must end on our product's fix for the flaw shown.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Borrow conviction through format and everyday phrasing, and avoid advertising language, using understatement and sincerity.
do: Shoot and speak in the plain format of a friend or customer, not in ad voice.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: F. Additional copywriting skills: Verification - Reinforcement – Interweaving
says: Place proof where it gains most acceptance, blend emotion, image and logic in each sentence, and anticipate the moment the reader wants to move on.
do: Put each proof right after the claim it supports and shift topic at the point viewers would drop.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: F. Additional copywriting skills: Verification - Reinforcement – Interweaving
says: Pull viewers deeper using incomplete statements that raise a question and imply an answer later, and set mood through words and rhythm.
do: Plant an open question early and pay it off late, and let the cut rhythm carry the mood.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Lists of triggers are not mass desires; find the real desire through research and learn what your audience calls it.
do: Take the desire's name from how customers talk about it, not from a trigger list.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: All marketing fits the hero's journey, and products are helpers or symbols at one stage of it.
do: Place the viewer at a stage of the journey (call, guide, trial, goal) and cast the product as the helper for that stage.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: What’s The Difference Between A Good And Bad Copywriter?
says: Features give the logical excuse, but the buy comes from the emotional benefit behind the want, as with wanting the hole not the drill.
do: For each feature in a script, ask what the viewer feels as a result and lead with that, then give the logic after.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: A story works by the emotion it carries, and a well-tuned one produces a physical reaction in the body.
do: Judge each cut by whether it causes a physical reaction like a tight throat, laugh or racing heart, and cut what only works intellectually.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Bad copy tells a story and then pitches something unrelated, while good copy ends in a sensible, surprising solution that triggers the 'ah-ha' and the sale.
do: Make the pitch the logical ending of the story just told, with no jump to an unrelated product.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: Versions of AIDA – the Song Sung Forever.
says: Bly's and Schwab's sales structures are all the same arc: attention, advantage, proof, credibility, action.
do: Check each script has attention, an advantage, proof and a clear call to action in order.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: Versions of AIDA – the Song Sung Forever.
says: Study proven headlines and vary them slightly to test, and only copy swipe files once you know why they work.
do: Take a proven winning hook, change one element, and test that version against the original.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: How to Use this Book to Get Everything You Could Possibly Want
says: Great advertising on a poor product kills the company, so the copywriter's job includes getting a flawed product fixed and choosing an honest client with a great product.
do: Before scripting a reel for a brand, check the product's real weak points and raise them with the client, and only promise what the product truly delivers.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
chapter: A Final Word from Eugene Schwartz
says: Every new market, product and ad is a fresh problem, past successes only give starting points, and the right headline comes out of the problem itself by asking the right questions before writing.
do: Do not copy a past winning hook for a new brand; before writing, answer the questions about this product's market (who wants it, what they already know, what they believe) and let the opening line come from those answers.

title: Masters of Copywriting
author: Masters of Copywriting (various)
says: Wheeler's tested philosophy is to think about what the prospect wants to hear rather than what you want to say, and the classic authors earned their results by testing against actual sales.
do: Write each reel's first line from what the viewer wants to hear, and test hook variants against actual sales, not likes.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 1: THE KEY TO BEING SEEN, HEARD, AND
says: The brain tunes out complicated messages because processing costs it energy, and simple, predictable story structure is easiest to digest.
do: Keep each reel to one idea in a predictable order so the viewer never has to work out what is going on.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 1: THE KEY TO BEING SEEN, HEARD, AND
says: People constantly scan messages for anything that helps them survive and thrive, so company facts like plant size do not register.
do: Open every script on what the viewer gains (time, status, money, belonging), never on how big or old the brand is.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 1: THE KEY TO BEING SEEN, HEARD, AND
says: Brands fail when they do not show how the offer helps people survive and thrive, because the brain discards everything else, like counting chairs instead of finding exits.
do: Cut every line in the first seconds that is not about the viewer's gain or relief, including founder backstory and brand facts, and put those after the hook if at all.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 1: THE KEY TO BEING SEEN, HEARD, AND
says: If viewers must burn mental effort to understand an offer, they tune out, so say something useful to them quickly.
do: Make the first line a usable benefit or problem the viewer instantly gets, and drop any setup that makes them decode it. Test by cutting the opening until nothing needs explaining.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 1: THE KEY TO BEING SEEN, HEARD, AND
says: An audience must always know who the hero is, what they want, what opposes them, and what is at stake, or they check out.
do: Before locking a script, check it answers: who is this for, what do they want, what blocks them, what happens if they win or lose.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 1: THE KEY TO BEING SEEN, HEARD, AND
says: Stripping a cluttered site to one plain statement of the service and a single button would grow the business.
do: State the offer in one blunt plain line and one action, and cut every side message from the reel.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 1: THE KEY TO BEING SEEN, HEARD, AND
says: Customers decide on what they hear, not what you meant, and good writing comes from cutting.
do: In the edit, cut every line, shot and graphic that does not serve the one message, then re-watch cold and ask what a stranger would say it was about.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 2: THE SECRET WEAPON THAT WILL
says: Like a film's final cut, a message should drop every scene or character that does not serve the plot, since overloaded information makes people click away.
do: Run a cutting-room pass on each reel: any shot or line that does not move the one story forward is removed, even if it looks good.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 2: THE SECRET WEAPON THAT WILL
says: Apple grew when it replaced a nine-page spec ad with two words and focused on what the customer wanted instead of the computer.
do: Lead with the customer's aspiration or identity, not product specs, and show specs only as a supporting beat.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 2: THE SECRET WEAPON THAT WILL
says: People buy the product they understand fastest, and the best brand casts itself as the tool in the customer's story.
do: Frame the product on screen as the tool the viewer uses to get what they want, with the viewer as the one doing the winning.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 2: THE SECRET WEAPON THAT WILL
says: Nearly every story is a character who wants something, hits a problem, meets a guide who gives a plan and calls them to action, avoiding failure and ending in success.
do: Use this as the default skeleton for a 15 to 60 second script: a viewer who wants something, the problem, the product as guide, a simple plan, a clear call to action, the stake, the success.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 2: THE SECRET WEAPON THAT WILL
says: Viewers must be able to answer three questions: what the hero wants, who or what opposes them, and what happens if they win or lose, and anything that does not serve that goes.
do: Pause the script at any point and check these three can be answered; if not, rewrite or cut.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 2: THE SECRET WEAPON THAT WILL
says: Within five seconds, a viewer should be able to answer what you offer, how it makes life better, and what to do to buy it.
do: Write a grunt-test line for every reel: in the first five seconds or on the last card, show the offer, the benefit and the next step, and test it on someone who has not seen the brand.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 2: THE SECRET WEAPON THAT WILL
says: Cutting 90 percent of the copy, swapping jargon for plain visual phrases and leading with life benefits took a repeat launch to the same list from $25,000 to $103,000.
do: Replace product jargon with what the viewer sees or gets (like 'blurry background pictures'), and lead with the life benefit over specs.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: The customer is the hero and the brand is the guide, and the story starts only once the customer wants something.
do: Put the viewer, not the brand, as the person on screen with a goal, and the product enters as help.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Customers buy solutions to internal problems (embarrassment, worry) more than external ones, and talking about the problem deepens interest.
do: Hook on the feeling the problem causes, such as embarrassment or worry, then show the product fixing the visible problem.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Brands that cast themselves as the hero compete with the customer, who is looking for a guide, not another hero.
do: Do not make the brand or founder the star of the reel; keep them as the helper, and the viewer or customer as the one who wins.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Customers want a clear plan or path that removes confusion about how to buy, and characters act only when challenged.
do: Give a short plan in the reel (order, it arrives, you use it) so the buyer sees the path.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: People do not engage without a clear and direct call to action, which can be direct (buy) or transitional.
do: End every reel with one explicit action and, for colder viewers, offer a softer second step.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: A message needs stakes, so show the cost of not buying, used sparingly like salt.
do: Include one beat that shows what the viewer loses or keeps suffering if they skip it, then move on to the gain.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Never assume people see how your brand changes their life, so tell them where you take them.
do: Close with an explicit picture of the success state (the after) instead of leaving it to be inferred.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: A story only starts once the hero wants something, and showing the desired outcome (a warm bath, a rocking chair) instead of the brand's buildings made the resort's message work.
do: Open on the image of what the customer wants (the result, the feeling), not the product, shop or team, and give it a short line like 'Find the luxury and rest you've been looking for.'

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Short, specific statements of what the customer wants (a hassle-free MBA, a yard better than your neighbor's) give a story direction.
do: Write the reel's want as one short customer-voice line in the vein of 'a yard better than your neighbor's'.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Showing the gap between a person and what they want makes viewers wait to see it close, like an unresolved musical note.
do: Open a gap in the first seconds (a want not yet met) and hold the payoff until near the end, opening small new gaps along the way.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: If no customer desire is defined there is no gap, so pick one single desire rather than listing many.
do: Pick one desire per reel and cut the other benefits to a later reel.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Focus on one simple desire at brand level and treat the others as subplots, and the desire must tie to survival and not be vague.
do: Run one desire per concept and make variants for each extra benefit.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: 'Inhale knowledge, exhale success' was vague, whereas 'become everyone's favorite leader' connects directly to survival and status.
do: Rewrite abstract hook lines into a concrete human outcome the viewer already wants.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Survival desires include saving money, saving time, belonging to a tribe, and gaining status.
do: Tag each script with which of these desires it taps (money, time, belonging, status) and write the hook straight at it.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Customers are like hitchhikers who only want to know where you are going, so say where you take them and not the mission or backstory.
do: Say in the first seconds where the product takes the viewer and skip the origin story.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: The problem is the hook of the story, and attention fades as soon as the conflict is resolved, so keep talking about the problem.
do: Spend real screen time on the problem before the product arrives and do not resolve it too early in the reel.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: A personified villain gives the problem a focus and makes the product a weapon to defeat it.
do: Name one villain (like distractions or dust) and show the product defeating it.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: A good villain is a root source, relatable, singular and real, and ads often personify the problem as a character.
do: Cast the problem as a single relatable character or object in the reel (a gang of dust bunnies, a nest in the drain), and keep it to one villain.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Most brands sell only external problem fixes, but the external problem exists to surface an internal one.
do: List the external problem and the feeling it creates before writing, and cover both.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: The wish to resolve an inner frustration (self-doubt, intimidation) motivates more than the external problem, as Apple found.
do: Hook on the doubt or frustration ('do I have what it takes?'), not the task.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Naming the frustration behind the external problem, like embarrassment about the ugliest house on the street, bonds the customer to the brand.
do: Write the headline for the feeling, like 'Paint That Will Make Your Neighbors Jealous', and let the visual show the product.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: National and CarMax won customers by advertising the relief from an irritation (no small talk, no haggling) rather than the product itself.
do: Build ads around the annoying part of the buying experience that you remove (returns, sizing, waiting, delivery) and show the character skipping it.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Framing a product as resolving both external and internal problems, as Starbucks did, increases perceived value and the price it can ask.
do: Describe the feeling the product gives, not just the function, when pricing is a hurdle.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: A philosophical problem frames why the story matters in terms of 'ought' and 'shouldn't', like 'pets deserve healthy food too'.
do: Add a one-line 'ought' stance to the hook or close (like 'You shouldn't have to X') to give the reel a bigger point.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Customers will adopt a brand's stance on a bigger cause and wear it, as with Tower Records' 'No music, no life'.
do: Look for a belief the brand stands for and put it in a short repeatable line for slogans and merch-style captions.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: The strongest brand promise resolves the external, internal and philosophical problem in one move, with the buy button as the action that closes the story.
do: Write the climax as one beat that resolves all three layers, with the buy call following directly.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Choose a single villain, a single external problem, how it feels, and why it is unjust, and resist stuffing in more.
do: Fill in four fields per script (villain, external problem, feeling, why unjust) and use one of each.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Heroes cannot solve their own problem, and brands that cast themselves as the hero lose.
do: Show the viewer as unable to fix it alone and the product as the equipment that helps.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Tidal failed because it served the artists, not customers, and never answered how it helps the customer win the day.
do: Check each script answers 'how does this help me win the day?' from the viewer's seat.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: The guide has authority but the story stays about the hero, who is often unsure and reluctant.
do: Keep the brand in the supporting role and the viewer as the focus of the scene.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: A guide must show empathy and authority together, and expressing understanding of the viewer's pain builds trust.
do: Put one empathy line ('I know how annoying that is') near the start and authority proof later.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Authority means competence, not bragging, and a guide who is just like you without experience is not trusted.
do: Show competence through results and experience, not self-praise or 'we are just like you'.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Add authority lightly with a few short testimonials (three is enough), one statistic and small award marks, because too many make you the hero.
do: Use at most three short testimonials or one number per reel, brief and quick, then move on.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Logos of known businesses give social proof, letting customers tick the trust box without bragging.
do: Flash a recognizable press or stockist logo briefly as a trust beat.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Empathy answers 'can I trust you' and competence answers 'can I respect you', and liking is still not enough to buy.
do: Put empathy first for trust and competence second for respect, then add a plan.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 7: WHO GIVES THEM A PLAN
says: A purchase is a commitment, and buyers hesitate over fear of being foolish, so they need a plan to reduce the risk.
do: Address the 'what if it doesn't work' worry directly in the offer beat.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 7: WHO GIVES THEM A PLAN
says: A plan is a set of stepping stones across a creek that makes the path look easy and gives hope.
do: Show the buying path as visible steps ('First, step here').

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 7: WHO GIVES THEM A PLAN
says: Without a plan customers use confusion as an excuse not to buy, so spell out easy steps like measure, order, install.
do: Add a three-step on-screen plan before the call to action in every reel (for example choose, order, receive), each a couple of words.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 7: WHO GIVES THEM A PLAN
says: A process plan with steps for buying or using the product removes confusion, and can cover steps before or after purchase.
do: Choose a buying or after-purchase set of steps and show it as a short list.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 7: WHO GIVES THEM A PLAN
says: A process plan should have three to six steps, and ideally about three or four, since more steps add confusion.
do: Cap the on-screen plan at three steps, and four at most.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 7: WHO GIVES THEM A PLAN
says: An agreement plan lists promises that remove fear of buying, like CarMax's no-haggle and quality-certified guarantees.
do: State the guarantee, returns promise or free shipping as a short on-screen promise list that answers the biggest fear.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 7: WHO GIVES THEM A PLAN
says: An agreement plan lists the buyer's worries and answers each with a promise, and a title for the plan raises its perceived value.
do: List the buyer's top three worries (fit, delivery, returns), answer each with a named promise such as 'the Fit Guarantee', and say it on screen in the offer beat.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 8: AND CALLS THEM TO ACTION
says: People, like story characters, do not act unless something challenges them to, so the brand has to issue the challenge.
do: End every reel with an explicit ask in words and on screen, never just a pretty product shot.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 8: AND CALLS THEM TO ACTION
says: Viewers are bombarded with thousands of messages a day, so soft calls to action go unnoticed and the winning move is to make them clear and repeat them.
do: State the call to action in the voiceover, as on-screen text and in the end card, and repeat it at least twice in a 30 to 60 second cut.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 8: AND CALLS THEM TO ACTION
says: Hardly anyone oversells; passive asks signal a lack of belief in the product and make the customer sense weakness.
do: Write the ask as a plain direct line ('Shop now, link below') and cut any hedged phrasing like 'check us out if you like'.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 8: AND CALLS THEM TO ACTION
says: Use a direct call to action to sell and a low-risk transitional one for people not ready, so you can keep deepening the relationship.
do: Give each ad a main ask (buy) and a softer second ask (free guide, quiz, sample or follow) for viewers who are not ready.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 8: AND CALLS THEM TO ACTION
says: The plainer site that named the buyer's worry and offered a free helpful PDF won over a more beautiful site with no clear ask.
do: Open the reel on the viewer's specific worry, then offer one free useful thing before the hard sell.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 8: AND CALLS THEM TO ACTION
says: Have one obvious direct call to action that stands out and keep repeating the same one everywhere.
do: Use identical call-to-action wording and button styling across all cuts of a campaign so it reads as one recurring ask.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 8: AND CALLS THEM TO ACTION
says: Testimonials, samples and free trials are low-risk on-ramps that let buyers see others reach a good ending or try before committing.
do: Lead with a risk-removal line in the offer beat (free returns, trial size, money-back) and cut in a customer result as the on-ramp.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 9: THAT HELPS THEM AVOID FAILURE
says: A story without stakes is boring, and every scene must move the hero toward or away from a bad outcome.
do: Name the bad outcome in the first five seconds and check that every beat after it moves the viewer toward or away from it, cutting any beat that does neither.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 9: THAT HELPS THEM AVOID FAILURE
says: Brands that never say what happens if you do not buy fail to answer the viewer's silent 'so what' question, as Allstate's Mayhem character answers it with a vivid disaster.
do: Dramatise the cost of not buying in one concrete, slightly funny scenario as the hook, then show the product as the safe state.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 9: THAT HELPS THEM AVOID FAILURE
says: Loss aversion means people are two to three times more motivated to avoid a loss than to gain, so most brands under-use the negative stakes.
do: Write the hook around what the viewer loses or keeps paying for without the product, and put the gain in the payoff.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 9: THAT HELPS THEM AVOID FAILURE
says: A fear appeal runs in four steps (you are vulnerable, act to reduce it, here is the specific fix, do it now), and only a moderate dose of fear changes behaviour.
do: Structure a problem-led script as threat, so you should act, our product as the fix, then the ask, and keep the scare to one pinch.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 9: THAT HELPS THEM AVOID FAILURE
says: List the concrete losses your product helps avoid (money, health, time, regret) and picture a tragic scene to make them felt.
do: List three things the buyer avoids by buying, pick the most vivid and open the script with that scene.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 9: THAT HELPS THEM AVOID FAILURE
says: A few negative stakes are enough, because too many resist and too few leave the product without a point.
do: Limit each script to one or two warnings and spend the remaining time on the better outcome.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 10: AND ENDS IN A SUCCESS
says: Never assume people see how you change their life; tell them where the brand is taking them.
do: Include one explicit line in every script that states the destination ('your mornings, sorted') rather than only features.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 10: AND ENDS IN A SUCCESS
says: A vague vision bores people, so the promised ending must be specific, and a before-and-after grid of life, feeling, daily routine and status helps find it.
do: Fill a before/after grid for the product and write the payoff line as one specific, visible change, not a lofty benefit.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 10: AND ENDS IN A SUCCESS
says: Tell customers plainly what life looks like after buying and show it with images of people happily using the product.
do: Make the final shot of the reel a person visibly enjoying the result, not a packshot alone.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 10: AND ENDS IN A SUCCESS
says: Most story endings give the hero status, union that makes them whole, or self-realisation, so a brand promise that matches one of these resonates.
do: Pick one of status, completeness or self-acceptance as the payoff of each script and write the closing line to it.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 10: AND ENDS IN A SUCCESS
says: Brands can offer status through access, scarcity, a premium tier or association with success.
do: Use scarcity or early access in the offer beat (limited drop, members first) and show it on screen.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 10: AND ENDS IN A SUCCESS
says: Products can offer completeness by reducing anxiety, reducing workload or giving time back.
do: Frame a product's benefit as relief, effort saved or time freed, and show the feeling of the problem easing in the demo.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 10: AND ENDS IN A SUCCESS
says: Brands can offer self-actualisation through inspiration, acceptance of real bodies or joining a larger cause like one-for-one giving.
do: If the brand has a cause or real-people stance, lead with it in the hook rather than burying it in the about page.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 10: AND ENDS IN A SUCCESS
says: Closing a story loop can be simple: show a happy outcome and say what the resolution looks like in basic terms.
do: Write the payoff as a plain, basic result in one line (a room that feels finished) and show it.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 11: PEOPLE WANT YOUR BRAND TO PARTICIPATE IN
says: The strongest buying motive is the wish to become someone better, so brands that join that change create fans.
do: Frame the product as part of who the buyer is becoming, not only what they get.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 11: PEOPLE WANT YOUR BRAND TO PARTICIPATE IN
says: Smart brands define an aspirational identity by asking who the customer wants to become.
do: Before scripting, write one line answering 'who does our buyer want to be?' and write the hook for that person.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 11: PEOPLE WANT YOUR BRAND TO PARTICIPATE IN
says: Gerber sells a kind of person, not a knife, and that associated identity is why a writer who never needs a knife still wanted one.
do: Write the script so the product is the badge of an identity (tough, organised, carefree) and show that person in action, with the hook speaking to that identity.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 11: PEOPLE WANT YOUR BRAND TO PARTICIPATE IN
says: Buyers pay for the identity as well as the item, and the way to find it is to ask how they want friends to describe them.
do: Ask 'how will their friends describe them after this?' and put that phrase in the script as the payoff.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 11: PEOPLE WANT YOUR BRAND TO PARTICIPATE IN
says: Dave Ramsey gives listeners an identity, a status symbol and a climactic scene (the debt-free scream) where the hero's win is celebrated.
do: Build a climactic payoff moment into the reel (the unboxing reaction, the finished result) and show someone celebrating it.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 11: PEOPLE WANT YOUR BRAND TO PARTICIPATE IN
says: Stories end with the guide telling the hero they have changed, because the hero often cannot see how far they have come.
do: End testimonial or UGC cuts with a before/after contrast and a line stating the change ('you're not the same person who started').

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 11: PEOPLE WANT YOUR BRAND TO PARTICIPATE IN
says: An aspirational identity is written as a from-to line (anxious and glum to carefree and radiant) that adds value to the product.
do: Write a from/to pair for each script and use the 'to' word as the on-screen payoff.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: The first date message must be short, enticing and entirely about the customer, and a cooking site lost people with an inside joke and a founder cartoon.
do: Spend the first seconds on what the viewer gets and leave the founder story for later or a separate cut.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: One short bold sentence ('we will make you a pro in the kitchen') beats confusion because customers must see what is in it for them immediately.
do: Write the opening line and first on-screen text as a single short promise of what the viewer gets, readable in under two seconds.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: The main call to action should be placed in expected spots, look identical and be a different colour from other buttons, and be repeated because people need many exposures.
do: Give the end card one distinctive call-to-action button style, use it identically in every cut and repeat it mid-video.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: Images of smiling, satisfied people using the product signal the emotional destination better than pictures of the building.
do: Choose shots of real customers happy with the product over brand or premises shots, and keep any softer second ask visually quieter than the main one.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: People scan rather than read, so copy should be 'Morse code': brief, punchy and relevant, such as bullet differentiators instead of a warm paragraph.
do: Cut on-screen text to three to six words per card and turn any sentence of explanation into a short bullet.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
says: The fewer words you use, the more likely they are read, and everything should come from the core message script.
do: Try cutting half the on-screen words from a draft, and drop any line that does not serve the script's core idea.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: Stories of how you transformed customers let prospects instantly see what the brand can do for them.
do: Build a series of reels around single customer transformations, framed as problem, change and result.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: A logline sells a film in one sentence through imagination and intrigue, and a one-liner should do the same for a brand.
do: Write a one-sentence logline for each reel before scripting and check it is both easy to picture and makes you want the next beat.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: A one-liner has four parts, character, problem, plan and success, and the viewer must be able to say 'that's me'.
do: Draft every hook and opening three lines from the four parts: who it is for, their problem, the plan, the outcome.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: Naming the problem makes the customer think 'yes, I struggle with that' and opens a story loop they want you to close.
do: Name the viewer's problem in the first line and hold the answer until the demo or payoff beat.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: A one-liner that names the buyer, problem, plan and success beats a bare description like 'I run a gym'.
do: Use the template 'We help [person] with [problem] through [plan] so they [result]' as the voiceover opener and test it against a plain description.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: Nobody wants to join a newsletter because it promises no value, so email is won with something valuable offered in return.
do: For email capture reels, offer one specific thing (a guide, a code, early access) rather than 'join our list'.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: A lead generator must give enormous value and establish authority, and separate ones for each product let you segment buyers.
do: Create one lead magnet per product line and point each reel's transitional ask at the one that matches it.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: The five best lead generators are a downloadable guide, a course or webinar, a demo or free trial, free samples, and live events, each trading something of value for an email address.
do: For a product brand, make the offer a free sample or a send-a-friend sample credit (the Blue Apron model), and say it plainly in the closing line of the reel.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: A helpful nurturing message follows three beats: talk about a problem, explain a plan to solve it, then describe life once it is solved, with a sales ask only every fourth message.
do: Cut an educational organic reel as problem, then plan, then life after, and keep the sell for every third or fourth post.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: An offer message states the problem, the product that solves it, the life after, and then a direct call to action, because being passive signals weakness.
do: End every paid reel on one direct, spoken action tied to the product, with no soft 'check it out' close.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: The sample offer email names the customer's pain, says why the company exists, and closes on a half-price one-time offer that adds scarcity.
do: Pair a concrete discount with a stated reason it is one-time, and show the guilt or fear relief ('no more...') in the final beat.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: Plain 'they're great' testimonials show no transformation, so you must ask structured questions to get specific results and what life is like now, in a form or a recorded interview.
do: Brief creators and customers with the five transformation questions, then cut the answers with b-roll rather than accepting a generic 'love this product' line.

title: Building a StoryBrand
author: Donald Miller
chapter: Chapter 13: HOW STORYBRAND CAN TRANSFORM A
says: Five questions (problem before, how the frustration felt, what was different, the moment it worked, life now) naturally produce a transformation story, and seeing transformation in others makes people want it.
do: Structure UGC and testimonial reels in that order: before problem, felt frustration, the difference, the moment it worked, then life now.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Cuts between two shots that are only slightly different, such as a wide to a marginally tighter framing, feel like a jarring jump, whereas a clearly different shot reads as a new context.
do: When cutting between shots of the same subject, make the change in size or angle obvious (wide to close-up, or a different angle) rather than a small punch-in or a near-match.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Do the most with the least: suggestion engages the audience more than exposition, and a good edit is judged by where it chooses not to cut.
do: In a 15 to 30 second cut, hold a shot until it has delivered its idea and drop any cut or on-screen element that does not add something new.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: An editor who changes shots too often is like a tour guide who never stops pointing, and viewers end up feeling controlled and resentful.
do: Check every cut in a reel and remove those that exist only to keep things moving; leave at least one beat where the viewer can look around the frame.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: A good cut satisfies six criteria in priority order (emotion, story, rhythm, eye-trace, planarity, spatial continuity), and emotion matters more than all the rest because people remember how they felt.
do: When two cut options conflict, pick the one that keeps the intended feeling and moves the story on, and give up spatial or continuity polish first.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: If a cut has the right emotion and story and rhythm, the audience will overlook flaws in lower-order items like eye-trace and spatial continuity, but not the reverse.
do: Do not reject a cut that feels right because of a continuity glitch such as a prop or position jump; fix only if the emotion or rhythm is also affected.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Emotion, story and rhythm are tightly bound together, while the lower criteria are weaker, so sacrifice them in order from the bottom and never give up emotion first.
do: Keep the order of priority as a checklist for each cut: emotion, story, rhythm, then eye-trace, and only then continuity.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: The editor's core job is to stand in for the audience and ask where they are looking and what they are thinking and feeling, directing their attention like a magician, and to judge the cut as it will look on the big screen, not the small editing monitor.
do: Before locking each cut, decide where the eye should be at the cut point and place the key element there; then check the cut on a phone at normal size rather than the large edit monitor.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: People who were on the shoot see around the edge of the frame and overvalue shots that were costly or hard to get, so they misjudge what is actually on screen.
do: When reviewing footage, judge only what is visible in the frame and cut shots that were hard to film but do not work; do not let effort decide what stays.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: The editor should see only what the audience will see and be their ombudsman, and the director should step away before editing to shed knowledge that is not on screen.
do: Have someone who was not on the shoot, or yourself after a break, watch the first cut cold and note where it is confusing or flat.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Pointing to a face in a still is a way around the language problem of describing nameless emotions, and the best frame of a shot is its distilled decisive moment, which usually sits near the cut point.
do: Pick a single hero frame that carries the feeling for each ad, share it as the reference for the edit, and cut around that moment.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Early notes marking takes as no good rely on script-driven first impressions, and shots you wrote off can become your salvation when you recut.
do: When a cut is not working, go back through rejected takes and unused footage rather than relying on first-pass notes.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: On the second viewing you see different things as the film evolves, and a scene is done when the shots seem to create each other and the editor feels invisible.
do: Re-watch all raw footage after the first assembly before refining, and keep working until each shot seems to lead naturally to the next.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Written audience feedback in the heat of the moment is skewed, but how you feel watching with fresh viewers is valuable, and calling people a day or two later gives better feedback.
do: Show a cut to a few people who have never seen it, watch their reactions instead of relying only on comments, and follow up a day later.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Audiences report where the pain is, not its source, so a scene most people dislike may be fine and the real problem is missing information earlier on.
do: When viewers say a part of the reel is weak or confusing, look at the 5 to 10 seconds before it for missing setup, instead of cutting or rewriting the weak part.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
chapter: Don't Worry, It's Only a Movie
says: People blink at the instant they grasp an idea, and a cut is the film's blink, marking the end of one idea and the start of another.
do: Cut when the viewer has just understood the point of the shot, not before or after; test by listening to a line and noting where you naturally blink.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
chapter: Don't Worry, It's Only a Movie
says: A well-placed cut ends one idea and begins another, and the bigger the visual change, the stronger the punctuation, so one cut per idea.
do: Make each shot carry one idea, and use a strong visual contrast, such as dark to bright, only where you want a hard stop between ideas.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Actors' blinks follow their character's thoughts, and Murch picks out-points by marking them live in real time, because inching frame by frame causes rhythmic tone deafness.
do: Pick cut points by playing the footage at speed and tapping the cut live, then only nudge if it is clearly wrong, rather than frame-peeping for the best match.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Cutting to whoever is speaking, as in Dragnet, is shallow, because real viewers look at the listener before the speaker finishes, so the question is when to turn.
do: In talking-head or testimonial reels, cut to a reaction, product or b-roll while the line is still being said, instead of cutting only when the speaker changes.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Each shot has a few natural cut points, like branches, and which one you pick decides what the audience thinks: cutting away early keeps them on the face value, while lingering lets them see the speaker is lying.
do: For each claim or testimonial line, decide whether you want it taken at face value (cut away mid-line) or doubted or felt (hold on the face after), and cut at that branch.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Cutting rate should match the thinking rate of the moment: action runs around 25 cuts a minute, while dialogue scenes average six or fewer, and cut points should be where you could comfortably blink.
do: Set pace by content: roughly 4 to 12 cuts in a 30 second reel for talking or explaining sections, and much faster for high-energy product or action sections.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Cut right with the viewer's thoughts, leading them ever so slightly, giving them what they want just before they have to ask for it, so it feels both surprising and self-evident.
do: Show the product, price or answer a beat before the viewer would wonder about it, rather than after the question has already formed.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: A coherent rhythm of emotion and thought earns audience trust, while a scattered, nervous edit makes them hold back from the film.
do: If a reel feels nervous, remove arbitrary cuts, effects and jumps so the pacing follows a clear line of thought from start to finish.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Cutting live on the fly and then seeing how many frames early or late you were turns a vague feeling into a measured one, which builds your sense of the film's rhythm.
do: Mark cut points while the clip plays at full speed, then replay and note how many frames early or late each cut felt, and use that offset to tune the rest of the reel.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Making the first assembly of a scene without sound is faster and lets picture stand on its own before sound is added.
do: Rough-cut the reel with the sound muted first, then switch audio on and adjust.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Notes taken at first viewing go stale as the film changes, so footage once marked no good must be re-reviewed because you recognise the right shot better than you can describe it.
do: Before cutting, rewatch the rejected takes with the finished idea in mind and pull any that now fit.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Instant search gives you only what you ask for, while scrubbing through material shows you what you actually need, and digital fast-forward skips most frames.
do: Scrub through whole clips at watchable speed instead of jumping to the take you expect.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Assistants act as a first audience whose feedback keeps the editor honest about what works.
do: Show every rough cut to one person who hasn't seen the footage before sending it on, and ask what they felt.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Normal-speed forward viewing is the only accurate check on rhythm, but seeing the film in reverse or upside-down reveals structure that straight viewing hides.
do: After the cut feels done, scrub it fast or flip it and look only at the alternation of shot sizes, colours and shapes.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Cut rates have roughly doubled over decades, but there is no right or wrong speed, only a mismatch if the pace doesn't suit the writing.
do: Set the cut rate from the script's own pace: fast narration gets fast cuts, slow lines get slower ones.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Compressed, low-detail footage lets the eye absorb a frame quickly so you cut too soon, and the final high-detail version then feels choppy.
do: Judge pace on the full-quality export on a real phone, not on a low-res proxy, and lengthen shots that feel rushed.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: On a small screen the eye takes everything in at once so you cut sooner, whereas on a big screen it takes sections at a time and needs longer.
do: Check every cut at the size viewers will actually see it, since screen size changes how long a shot needs.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Television is a look-at medium that must make things collide in a small frame to catch attention amid distractions, so quick cuts, jump cuts and swish pans suit it, while a theatre allows slower pacing.
do: Because social is look-at viewing among competing distractions, front-load collisions in the first seconds with a quick cut, jump cut or swish, and slow down only once attention is held.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Murch places small paper figures sized to scale beside the monitor so the small screen reads as a huge one and cutting problems are caught early.
do: Keep a real phone beside the edit timeline and check every reel on it at arm's length before approving.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: Easy undo makes editing feel consequence-free, but without a plan, a map and detailed notes you just slam images together for momentary effect.
do: Write a short plan and per-clip notes before opening the timeline, so every cut serves the whole reel.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: The close-up makes thought visible on a face and the cut mimics the jumping nature of thought, and collaboration gives film its multifaceted appeal.
do: Cut to the close-up at the moment the person reacts or realises something, so the viewer sees the thought land.

title: In the Blink of an Eye
author: Walter Murch
says: At home the viewer is king with a remote to chop off the jester's head, whereas going out commits you to stay and open up, so the same picture is watched in a different state of mind.
do: Write the opening assuming the viewer's thumb is on the swipe, and give a reason to stay in the first second because nothing forces them to.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
