says: Older techniques like demonstrations, talking heads and slice-of-life still sell, and consumers still respond to promises of value, beauty, relief and status.
do: Do not drop a demonstration or a talking-head format just because it looks old; use it when it shows the product doing its job.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Research, not opinion, shows that celebrity commercials persuade below average and that dark type on a light background is read by more people than the reverse.
do: Default to the brand's own customer or founder over a paid celebrity, and keep any on-screen text high-contrast and easy to read.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: Two ads with the same space, photos and care can differ nineteen-fold in sales purely because one used the right appeal and the other the wrong one.
do: For each product, write hooks on three or four different appeals (price, result, status, relief) and test them against each other before polishing any one cut.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: Study the product deeply before writing, because a specific real fact from that homework (the loudest noise is the clock) becomes the headline and the long factual copy sells.
do: Before scripting, read the product page, reviews and ingredients, and pull one surprising, specific fact to open the reel.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: After product homework, research how buyers think and talk about the category and which promise would make them buy, even through informal chats with a handful of customers.
do: Pull the exact words from reviews, comments and DMs and use them in the hook and the promise rather than brand-speak.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: Positioning means deciding what the product does and who it is for, and a narrow, specific choice (a bar for women with dry skin) can work for decades.
do: State in one line what the product does and for whom, and let the first three seconds of the script speak to that person only.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: A brand has a personality built from name, price, packaging and ad style, advertising should project the same image consistently, and cheap-looking ads rub off on the product.
do: Keep one consistent look, voice and quality bar across a brand's reels, and do not let a rushed edit look cheap.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: People choose between similar products by the image attached to them, not by comparing taste or features, so the image is most of what is being sold.
do: For parity products, build a clear personality in the reel's tone, setting and casting rather than leaning only on feature lists.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: A big idea is needed to get noticed, it comes from a mind stuffed with product knowledge, and rational fact-arguing fails for image products like liquor.
do: Feed yourself the brief and customer language first, then sleep on it before choosing the single idea a reel is built around.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: A good idea is hard to recognise, and five tests (gasp, envy, unique, fits the strategy, lasts) help identify one.
do: Run each concept through the five questions and drop any that fail 'does it fit the strategy' or 'could this run for months as a series'.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: The most reliable idea is often to show the product with utter simplicity and make it the hero, because there are no dull products, only dull writers.
do: Put the product in frame and in use within the first seconds of the reel instead of leading with a clever concept that hides it.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: For near-identical products, it is enough to convince people yours is positively good by saying what is good about it more clearly and honestly, without claiming it beats the competition.
do: Write the proof section as plain, honest statements of what the product does well, not as a comparison against rivals.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: A good ad should be repeated until measurement shows it has worn out, because each new audience is seeing it for the first time.
do: Keep a winning reel running and make small variations on its hook and cut instead of retiring it early.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: Gallup-style readership research found that pictures with story appeal, and finished-result photos over raw ingredients, consistently draw more attention.
do: Open on an image with a built-in question or story (the eyepatch idea) and show the finished result rather than the raw product or process.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: Direct-response advertisers, who know exactly what each ad sells, consistently use longer commercials, later airtimes and long copy, contradicting what general advertisers do.
do: Do not assume shorter is better: test a 45 to 60 second version with full explanation and offer against the 15 second cut and let sales decide.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: The measure of a good ad is how much it sells, not how much it pleases, and plain down-to-earth ads often outsell fancy award-winning ones.
do: Judge every reel by sales and cost per purchase, and favour the blunt version with a clear offer over the stylish one.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 2: How to produce advertising that sells
says: Sex or shock in an ad works only when relevant to the product; an irrelevant nude sold nothing for a cooking stove.
do: Cut any attention-grabbing hook, image or trend that is not tied to what the product does.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Most people read only the headline, so it must carry the product's benefit or news, because the body copy will not be read.
do: Put the single biggest benefit or the news in the first line and first frame of the reel, and never save it for later.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: News, helpful information, the brand name and a word that flags the target buyer all lift how many people notice and remember a headline.
do: Open with a line that names who it is for (for example 'if you have dry skin') and say the brand name early.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Specific facts beat vague claims, clever or blind headlines lose readers, and a headline must say plainly what the product does.
do: Replace vague hook lines with one hard number or fact, and skip puns and teaser hooks that hide what the product is.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Helpful information and photographs that make the viewer ask 'what goes on here?' draw more attention than plain product copy.
do: Open on an odd or unexplained visual that makes the viewer wonder, then pay it off with the explanation inside the reel.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Before-and-after pictures fascinate readers and every before-and-after campaign Gallup studied raised sales, and photographs beat drawings and simple single-person pictures beat crowds.
do: Build the reel around a before and after of the product's result, with one person in frame and not a group.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Don't assume your own interests interest buyers, and viewers identify most with people like themselves.
do: Cast the person on screen to match the buyer, and check the subject against what the audience cares about, not what the team finds interesting.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Colour pays for itself, and food ads work better showing the finished dish than the ingredients.
do: Show the finished result in use, not the raw components or the pack alone.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Write to one person alone, as a letter from one human to another, in short sentences and plain words.
do: Script every voice-over and caption in second person singular with short sentences, and cut any word the average viewer might not know.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Use everyday language, tell what the product does with specifics, use story form, and avoid analogies because people misread them.
do: Write as people talk, tell the sell as a short story, and drop 'just like X, so is our product' comparisons.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Boasts and superlatives convince nobody, while testimonials from fellow customers make claims believable.
do: Replace 'best in the world' lines with a real customer saying it, on camera or as quoted review text.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Celebrities are remembered while the product is forgotten, experts persuade, and special offers and visible prices lift recall and stop people turning the page.
do: Put the price or the offer on screen in the reel and use an expert or real user, not a famous face.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: The more pertinent facts you give, the more you sell, and a long ad only holds people if its first line grabs them rather than stating the obvious.
do: Never open on a bland statement of the obvious; start with a startling concrete line and then stack real product facts behind it.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Ads that look like editorial content get far more readers than ads that look like ads, and captions under pictures get read more than body copy.
do: Make paid reels look like native content from the platform and put the brand name and promise in the on-screen captions.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Posters work best with a striking visual, the promise shown as well as written, the largest type, and no more than three elements.
do: Keep any single frame to three elements at most, with the biggest possible text, and show the promise visually as well as in words.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: All-capital headlines, text laid over pictures, and full stops at the end of headlines all slow reading.
do: Set on-screen text in sentence case, on a clean area of the frame, not over busy footage.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: Familiar typefaces, reasonable line width, a short opening paragraph and regular cross-heads keep people reading.
do: Keep the opening line to eleven words or fewer and use a familiar, readable caption font.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 7: Wanted: a renaissance in print advertising
says: A charity raised twice as much with black type on white as with white type reversed out of black.
do: Test dark-on-light caption styles against light-on-dark and keep text high-contrast and legible at phone size.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: Humour and slice-of-life playlets now change brand preference, but very few writers can actually write funny commercials.
do: Only script a funny reel if the writer or creator is genuinely funny, otherwise use a plain doubter-converted scene.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: Slice-of-life playlets and testimonials where a loyal user defends the product against a doubter are persuasive.
do: Script a short scene where someone pokes at the product and a real user defends it in their own words.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: Unpolished, amateur-sounding users are more credible than polished performers, and unusual characters and live demonstrations raise persuasion.
do: Cast real customers or creators and leave their delivery rough, and build one striking demonstration into the reel.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: Naming competitors makes commercials less believable, while problem-solution and talking-head formats work above average, especially for new products.
do: Use a problem-then-solution structure, or a straight to-camera pitch for a new product, and don't name rivals.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: Recurring characters, a rational reason why, and news all raise performance, and products draw most attention when new.
do: If there is anything new about the product or a new way to use it, make that the lead line of the reel.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: Emotion can sell as well as rational appeals when the product has nothing unique to say, but viewers still need a rational reason to justify the feeling.
do: Lead with the feeling, then give one plain rational reason to buy, and only go emotional if the footage can really deliver it.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: Celebrities and cartoons are remembered or watched without lifting sales, and many viewers recall the commercial but forget or misattribute the brand.
do: Use live action with real people, not celebrities or cartoons, and make the brand name unmistakable.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: Grab attention in the first frame with a visual surprise, say the brand name within ten seconds, end on the package, and use close-ups and moving food.
do: Make frame one the most surprising shot, say the brand in the first ten seconds, finish on the pack, and use tight close-ups.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: Voice-over holds the audience less well than people talking on camera, background music does nothing measurable, and real sound effects help.
do: Put people talking on camera, keep music low or off, and use natural sound like sizzling and pouring.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: On-screen words must exactly match the spoken promise, commercials with many short scenes do worse, and a singular visual burr beats stock happy images.
do: Burn the promise in as on-screen text matching the voice word for word, use fewer longer scenes, and include one unusual repeated visual.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: Show the product in use and its end result, and make the message crystal clear because every commercial tested was misunderstood by at least 19 per cent of viewers.
do: Show the product being used and the result on screen, and state the single point so plainly that no viewer can misread it.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: Expensive production does not make commercials sell more, and radio ads should name the brand and promise a benefit early and often.
do: Shoot simple, with fewer actors and a plain setting, and spend the budget on the idea, not the production.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: The first job is to get people to listen by surprising them or arousing curiosity, then talk like one human to another.
do: Start with a surprise or open question in the first line, then switch to warm, direct talk.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 8: How to make TV commercials that sell
says: A frequently heard commercial wears out, so make several different ones, and a honest, funny tone worked for a beer.
do: Make several variations of each reel so the same viewer does not see one version repeatedly.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: To persuade on a complicated issue, simplify it and put the case in terms of the reader's self-interest without being simplistic.
do: Boil the message down to one simple point framed around what the viewer gets.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Disarming candour about a poor reputation, and giving both sides, improved how a company was seen, as with a long-running retailer campaign.
do: If buyers hold a negative belief about the brand, say it openly in the reel and show what changed.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Research on what tourists most wanted to see led to the ads featuring it, and it worked even when critics wanted a different image.
do: Choose what to feature by what customers say they want, from reviews and comments, not by what the brand likes to show.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Show visitors what they most want to see, and correct a false image by showing the reality.
do: If a false belief holds buyers back, show the product as it really is in the reel.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Answer buyers' known worries with real specific information, such as actual prices, and show what is unique to the place or product.
do: Put the real price and the practical details on screen to answer the main objection, and show what only this product offers.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: People dream of buying, so turn the dream into action with tempting pictures plus specific how-to-do-it information, and ease the main fears such as cost.
do: Pair a desire-building visual with concrete next-step details (price, how it works, delivery) and answer the top fear before the end.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Business ads work with the same tools as consumer ads, and need specific promises with numbers, expert testimonials, demonstrations and news.
do: State the promise with a number, such as percentage, time or money saved, and demonstrate something the viewer can try.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Don't lure interested buyers with irrelevant bait like babies and bosoms, and a headline should promise a benefit, deliver news, recognise a problem or quote a customer.
do: Pick the hook from benefit, news, problem or customer quote, and don't use an unrelated attention-grabber.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Products that need explaining call for long copy, inexpensive direct commercials can work, and humour must support the end promise.
do: Let any joke lead straight to the promise at the close.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Even commodity products can be differentiated, by low cost or reputation, or by latching onto a seemingly minor distinctive feature.
do: When the product looks like every other, make one visible distinct trait, like colour, the hook.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Price and payment terms are among the most important things to test, and a lower price or a smaller starting offer can win more revenue than the full offer.
do: Test a lower-priced or smaller entry offer against the full offer and judge by revenue, not just clicks.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Free offers and low prices lift first response but do not always bring long-term buyers, so keep a winning version as control and keep testing against it.
do: Treat the best-performing reel as the control and test one change at a time, watching repeat buyers as well as first orders.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: In direct response the headline matters most, one headline produced five times the orders of another, and long copy sells more when the price is high.
do: Make several different hook lines for each reel and test them, since the hook alone can multiply results.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Readers put off responding and never return, so give a reason to act now such as limited supply, and make the response piece a mini-ad.
do: End with a clear reason to act now, such as limited stock or a price deadline, and repeat the brand, promise and product at the call to action.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Watch the media and ads your competitors keep running, since those are the ones that pay off, and test space units.
do: Study the ads competitors have kept running for a long time in the ad library, and borrow their hooks and structures.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Direct-response commercials that set up a problem, demonstrate the solution, give a guarantee, state the price and ask for the order urgently work, and repeat exposure wears out response.
do: Script direct-response reels as problem, demonstration, guarantee, price, then an explicit urgent ask with the how-to-order shown clearly.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: A blunt headline quoting a real teenager and a surprising specific statistic drew record readership.
do: Open with a real person's blunt line or one surprising number as the first thing seen or heard.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: A hopeful theme with real people who had been cured tripled check-ups, and a conservation ad pulled thousands of sign-ups.
do: Show real people who got the result and keep the tone hopeful.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: P&G ads promise one important benefit, include a moment of confirmation, demonstrate in most cases, say the brand early, and end by repeating the promise.
do: Structure each reel as one benefit promised up front, a visible moment proving it, the brand named early, and the promise repeated in the close.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: P&G uses unknown actors, shows what the product does without always explaining why, avoids naming rivals, and keeps a working strategy while testing new executions of it.
do: Keep a proven strategy and test new executions of it, using unknown real-looking people and showing the benefit in familiar settings.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Research can find the benefit that persuades and the words buyers use, and advertising with no promise to the consumer does not sell.
do: Before writing, state the one benefit the viewer gets in a single line and make sure the hook and the first seconds deliver it, using the customers' own words.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Headlines that promise a benefit are read by four times as many people, and the promise should be both persuasive and unique, tested by running two versions against each other.
do: For each product, cut two hooks that each lead with a different benefit, run them as a split test, and prefer the benefit competitors are not already claiming.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Test whether an ad changes brand preference rather than whether it is remembered, because celebrity and gimmick ads score high on recall but low on persuasion.
do: Judge a cut by clicks, add-to-carts and purchases, not by views or how memorable it felt, and do not lean on a celebrity or a stunt to get attention.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: A shock gimmick inflates recall, advertising wears out, and switching the angle from demonstration to testimonial revived Shell's results, while captions get read more than articles.
do: When a winning reel's results plateau, remake it with a different angle such as a customer testimonial in place of a demo, and keep on-screen captions prominent.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: People judge quality by price and by packaging, so cheaper does not always sell better, as the higher-priced cheese showed.
do: Do not make the lowest price the whole ad; show the quality cues that justify the price before any discount.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 16: What little I know about marketing
says: New products fail mostly because they offer no perceptible point of difference, and it helps to tie that difference to something familiar.
do: In the first seconds, name the one clear difference and anchor it to a category the viewer already knows.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 16: What little I know about marketing
says: Price-off promotions give only a temporary lift and people return to their usual brands, while price is mostly guesswork and higher prices raise perceived value.
do: Do not let a discount carry the whole video; lead with the product's value and keep the deal as a brief close.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 16: What little I know about marketing
says: A small share of heavy users buys most of a category, and they are motivated differently from occasional users.
do: Write the script to the heavy repeat buyer's reasons for buying and not to the casual browser.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
chapter: 16: What little I know about marketing
says: Advertising mostly reinforces existing users and makes them buy more often, and people mostly ignore ads for brands they do not use.
do: Make cold-audience cuts earn attention from the first frame, and make separate reminder cuts for people who have already bought.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Ads showing real people who had been cured tripled check-ups at the Indian Cancer Society's clinics within two months.
do: Put a real customer with a real result on screen, speaking to camera, in proof sections.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Lasker found by asking a few wives why they did not buy Kotex that embarrassment was the barrier, and plain-wrapped packages removed it.
do: Ask a handful of real customers what stops them buying and answer that exact barrier in the script.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Rubicam's agency used readership research to get its ads read first, because the way to sell is to get read.
do: Spend the most effort on the first two seconds of every cut, since nothing else sells if it is not watched.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Burnett held that every product has an inherent drama that must be dug out and used, after steeping yourself in the subject.
do: Before scripting, list what is dramatic or surprising about the product itself and build the reel around that.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Burnett rejected difference for its own sake and collected earthy, honest everyday phrases to use later.
do: Keep a swipe file of real customer phrases and local expressions and use them in hooks and voiceover.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Hopkins was wrong that only new customers matter, because users of a product read its ads more than non-users do.
do: Make cuts aimed at existing buyers too, such as reorder, new-use and refill angles.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Hopkins held that questions are answered by test campaigns and not by debate, that selling beats applause, and that a headline change can multiply results.
do: Settle creative arguments by running both versions, and cut for sales rather than for how clever the reel looks.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Bernbach insisted that even clever, original advertising should make the product the hero.
do: Check each finished cut and make sure the product is on screen, doing something, in the key moments.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Advertising can sell a bad product only once, and car ads full of slogans lack facts, whereas Rolls-Royce sold on facts with no adjectives.
do: Replace adjectives in the script with specific facts, figures and demonstrations.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Factual advertising always sells better than empty advertising, as Ogilvy learned selling stoves door to door by giving customers the facts.
do: Write the body of the script as concrete facts and specifics the viewer needs to buy, and do not substitute mood or slogans for them.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: The Rolls-Royce ad sells with a string of specific, checkable details, led by the electric clock being the loudest noise.
do: Pick the most striking true detail about the product and lead with it, then back it with further specifics.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: Reader's Digest titles pique curiosity and promise to satisfy it, and its cover lists the contents as a tempting menu.
do: Write hooks that open a curiosity gap and promise the answer inside the video, in the style 'What truckers say about your driving'.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: More than half the battle is writing headlines that grab attention and force people to read on, learned from studying the Digest.
do: Draft many hook lines for each script and spend the most time choosing the first line.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: The Dove ad sells through a woman's gushing phone call about her bath, then closes with a plain note giving the product facts and a money-back guarantee.
do: Write a 30-second reel as one person talking to a friend about the first use of the product, full of sensory words and small concrete details, then end with a plain voiceover or text card giving the real facts and the refund guarantee.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: The Volkswagen ad opens on a tiny flaw that got a car rejected, and uses exact counts of inspectors and checkpoints to prove quality, ending on a punchy line.
do: Open a reel on a small rejected defect, then show the actual inspection or checking process with exact numbers on screen, and end on a short punchline like 'We pluck the lemons; you get the plums.'

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: The Viyella ad pairs a playful opening with a replace-if-it-shrinks promise and a real customer quote about eleven years of wear, while the Volkswagen TV script runs a will-reading gag to land 'it pays to own'.
do: Pair a risk-reversal line (replace or refund) with one real customer quote giving a specific time and result, and put it on screen as text over the product.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: The British travel ad paints a vivid scene to make the reader feel it, then closes with a concrete low price and a call to action.
do: Open a reel on one sensory moment shot close up, then end with the exact price and one clear next step on screen.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: The Olympic coin ad makes scarcity credible by giving exact mintage numbers against earlier issues and adding a certificate of authenticity.
do: When you claim limited stock, show the actual numbers against a past run and mention a certificate or guarantee, rather than just saying 'limited'.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: The Sierra Club ad uses an absurd headline and then a numbered list of concrete threats to make a cause feel urgent.
do: Open with an absurd, provocative line that exposes the problem, then list the specific issues as short numbered on-screen beats.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: The Sierra Club ad ends by telling readers exactly what to do (write to named officials and send money) and why it is urgent now.
do: Close with one specific ask that names who to act on, plus a reason why now.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: The Shell ad opens with a challenge question, answers it with a named insider's account of exact steps taken, and ends with a one-line brand claim.
do: Open with a question the viewer already doubts, then answer with a named person on camera saying specifically what was done, and close on a short brand line.

title: Ogilvy on Advertising
author: David Ogilvy
says: The Steinway ad proves quality by walking through how the piano is built, with exact measurements and reasons each choice matters.
do: Cut a close-up product-making sequence with spoken or on-screen specifics (the measurement, the reason it matters), in the order a visitor would 'examine' it.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Cutting to temp music muddies your direct experience of the footage's own rhythm and imposes another piece's rhythm on your edit.
do: Build the first rough cut of a reel on picture and voiceover alone, then lay the music track in afterwards and adjust cuts to it.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Music is stronger than picture, so a temp track makes a weak flow of images seem to work and hides the faults in the cut.
do: Judge every cut with the sound off or on voiceover only before adding music, then check again with music; if a cut only works because of the track, fix the cut.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Editors find rhythm cues in the movement already inside the raw footage: its pulse, effort, speed and shape.
do: Before cutting, watch the raw clip once and note where the movement pulses, such as a gesture, a pour or a turn, and cut on those beats.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Viewers physically respond to movement speed and direction even if they have never done it, and mirror neurons make us feel intentional movement as if doing it ourselves.
do: Pick shots where the person or hand is visibly doing something with intent, such as reaching, applying or opening, because viewers feel that movement.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Joining two shots that each have their own rhythm produces a third rhythm that is not simply the sum of the two.
do: Judge a cut by how the two shots feel together, and swap the second shot for another take if the joined rhythm feels off.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Viewers read people's intentions from posture, speed and attack of movement without hearing dialogue.
do: When choosing takes for a testimonial or talking-head, mute the audio and keep the take whose body language already reads as the intended feeling.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The editor tunes to the performer's rhythm, such as where they blink, and cuts so the film extends those rhythms; a cut that fails to sync with them feels wrong.
do: On talking-head or creator footage, cut on the speaker's blinks and breath pauses rather than on the dead air between words, and re-check by playing the cut against your own breathing.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The editor must breathe and blink with the performer first, using her own body to stand in for the viewer's, and breath rhythms carry each person's state of mind.
do: Read your script lines aloud on one breath and cut the video to match where the speaker would naturally breathe.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Editors feel their way through a performance with their bodies, and if a sigh or pause feels too short in the body, the cut is adjusted.
do: Play the cut while physically tapping or breathing along, and lengthen any beat that feels clipped in your body.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: When stuck, ask what real-world rhythm the edit is being compared to, since 'doesn't feel right' always implies a comparison.
do: When a cut feels wrong, name the rhythm you want, such as a heartbeat, a footstep or a sales patter, and recut to match it.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: When a shot has several competing rhythms, the editor picks one line of movement as the initiating rhythm and subordinates the others to it.
do: In each shot pick one lead rhythm, such as the voiceover cadence or the main on-screen action, and time every other element to it.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Shots with very different time pressure cannot join cleanly, and movement inside the frame drives the cut from frame to frame.
do: Don't cut a slow, held shot directly against a busy fast one without a bridging shot; match movement intensity across the cut.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Meaning lives in emphasis points; speech with no accents is unintelligible, and the editor creates patterns of emphasis by choosing shots and shot lengths.
do: Mark the key word or gesture in each line and make sure a cut or visual change lands on it, not on filler.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Editors choose takes and cutting points to sustain, change or coordinate pulses, and cuts can shift where the accent falls.
do: Choose between takes by where the accent falls, and trim so the strongest word or movement lands at the end of the cut.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: When working from fragments, the editor builds phrases by designing rises and falls of emphasis, direction, speed and size.
do: Cut UGC fragments into short phrases with a rise and a landing, rather than a flat run of equal-length clips.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Phrasing a simple action across takes, such as quick entry, hesitation, then a deliberate walk, carries emotional meaning that viewers feel directly without being told.
do: Build a product moment, such as unbox, pause, reveal, from separate clips and vary speed on purpose: quick, then a held beat, then deliberate, so the feeling is carried by movement instead of caption text.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Story context tells viewers what a feeling is about, but the hesitation and the deliberate pace of the movement create the feeling itself, so viewers feel it and move on.
do: Use pacing of the action, such as a hesitation beat, to create anticipation rather than explaining it with text overlays.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: A smooth style relies on symmetry and even pulse, so breaking that evenness becomes a dramatic moment, and the editor can ask when to switch from measured to manic.
do: Hold an even cutting pattern through the body of a reel and break it once, at the offer or reveal, so the break reads as emphasis.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Choosing between tight individual frames and looser group frames, and between scattered and unified movement, shapes the emotional flow.
do: Use a tight single-subject frame for a personal claim, and a wider busy frame for social proof or crowds.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Editors can ask where the rests, high points and breaths are, and whether shot sizes progress smoothly or jump hard, because jarring size jumps create a destabilising rhythm.
do: Map a reel's rests and high points, and use a hard wide-to-extreme-close jump only deliberately, at the point you want a jolt.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The same scene changes feeling and meaning when only its speed or duration is altered, only its space and shot size, or only its energy.
do: When a cut feels flat, change only one variable at a time: pick the faster take, move to a closer shot, or trim where you enter the action, and compare.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 3: Timing, Pacing, and Trajectory Phrasing
says: The exact frame you cut on can change meaning, since cutting one frame earlier or later changes whether a smile is seen and so what the reaction means.
do: Check each cut on a reaction or gesture frame by frame, and cut just before the expression lands when you want the next shot to read as the cause or response.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 3: Timing, Pacing, and Trajectory Phrasing
says: A shot's felt length depends on the lengths of the shots around it and on how much happens inside it, not on its clock time, and placement controls when a punch line or reveal lands.
do: Set shot lengths relative to neighbours: make the hero or offer shot clearly longer than the quick shots before it, and place the reveal late enough that it lands as the payoff.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 3: Timing, Pacing, and Trajectory Phrasing
says: Shot order controls the plot's movement and the feel of a character; repeating a pattern of shots builds emphasis, and a break in the pattern marks resolution.
do: Alternate two setups, such as problem and reaction, then cut to a new shot type when the issue is resolved to signal the turn to the product.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 3: Timing, Pacing, and Trajectory Phrasing
says: Cutting often around a conversation makes it seem edgier, while leaving full arcs of movement intact makes it feel slower, and every cut introduces a new change.
do: For an urgent or edgy section cut tight on gesture; for a calm product moment let the full movement play out before cutting.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 3: Timing, Pacing, and Trajectory Phrasing
says: Cutting more often can make a sequence feel slower, because showing each full action in its own shot removes the uncertainty that makes things feel fast.
do: To make a reel feel faster, don't just add cuts; pack several actions into one shot and show only the peak of each action, and avoid giving every gesture its own full-length shot.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 3: Timing, Pacing, and Trajectory Phrasing
says: A fast pace can come from fast cutting, fast events, or fast movement and emotion within the shots, and any one of the three can be used alone.
do: If footage is thin on cuts, get pace from rapid-fire voiceover, quick changes of claim or on-screen movement instead of cutting every second.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 3: Timing, Pacing, and Trajectory Phrasing
says: The same movement reads as aggressive, playful or meaningless depending on the energy behind it, so energy carries the meaning.
do: When choosing between takes of the same action (a pour, a reveal, a smile), pick by the energy in the performance, not just the framing.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 3: Timing, Pacing, and Trajectory Phrasing
says: Cuts can link movement smoothly (matching screen direction) or collide it for a small shock.
do: Match screen direction for smooth product-demo flow; deliberately cut against it where a reel needs a jolt, such as the hook-to-problem switch.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 3: Timing, Pacing, and Trajectory Phrasing
says: Even when cuts match, the rhythm depends on which energy qualities you pair, such as a hesitant move against a confident one.
do: When cutting a testimonial or UGC exchange, choose takes so the energy contrast serves the story (hesitant before, confident after the product).

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 3: Timing, Pacing, and Trajectory Phrasing
says: Two shots of equal length create different accents because shot size and the energy inside the shot set the stress.
do: Place your hardest accent (price, offer, product reveal) on a tight, high-energy shot and let the quiet shots sit in wide, low-energy releases.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Tension comes from an unanswered question, and timing, energy and the release of information control how it builds and releases.
do: Open the reel on a question the viewer wants answered, delay the answer through the middle, and time the release to land on the offer.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Rhythm modulates the game of revealing and withholding information, and an unanswered question can only be held so long before interest is lost.
do: Set a limit on how long the hook question stays open; give a partial answer within a few seconds, then raise the next question.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Cutting to small sharp actions like a drink or keystrokes creates a rhythmic volley that lifts energy even when nothing dramatic happens.
do: Cut on small sharp gestures (tap, click, snap of a lid) to keep energy up through a flat stretch.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Time pressure creates tension reliably, and a calm shot dropped between others works as a rest.
do: Add a visible clock to urgency offers (sale ends, stock left) and use a calm reaction or product shot as a breath between intense beats.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Repeated, steadily accelerating rhythmic sounds and movement raise the viewer's heart rate even when they know where it leads.
do: Build repeated beats (cuts, text hits, sound) that speed up toward the offer.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Three quick cuts and a single word can cap a tension build while keeping the bigger question open.
do: End a build with a short burst of three fast cuts and a single command word, and leave the bigger question open for the call to action.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 5: Physical, Emotional, and Event Rhythms
says: Event rhythm is the rate and strength of change in the story, meaning new information or a shift in direction.
do: Check a script beat by beat: each few seconds should deliver one new piece of information or one change of direction.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
chapter: Chapter 5: Physical, Emotional, and Event Rhythms
says: Physical, emotional and event rhythm build on each other, and naming them helps locate where an edit is failing.
do: When a cut feels wrong, check which layer is off: the movement, the emotion or the information flow.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Start a movement in one shot and finish it in the next, so the editor keeps only the most dynamic part of each shot.
do: Start a product action (pour, throw, open) in one angle and complete it in the next, trimming the dull middle.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Ask what story a movement tells and where we are in it, and cut to emphasise the right energy for that story.
do: Before cutting action footage, name the physical story (who is winning, where it turns) and pick shots whose energy matches each stage.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The cut itself is part of the action, and rapid hit-hit-hit cuts can build the choreography of a moment.
do: Cut on the action beat so each cut is itself the hit; make a rapid sequence of short moves read as one phrase.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Editors test cuts by sensing or humming their phrasing to find a false note.
do: Play the cut and tap or hum along; any beat that feels off against your body is a trim point.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: A long, still shot builds a desperate wish for change so that the movement that follows is valued more.
do: Hold one deliberately still or slow beat before the product payoff so the speed-up feels earned.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Stay close to feel small movements like breath, because wide shots read as bland, and fewer repeats were needed once the cause and effect worked.
do: Stay in close-up for details that need feeling (texture, steam, tapping) and cut the repeated shots once the point lands.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Cutting only peaks of energy, in short stabs matched on screen direction, builds intensity beyond the real-time movement.
do: For high-energy sections, cut only the peak of each move and keep screen direction consistent.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Temp music can impose its rhythm on images, so editors strip it out periodically to check the visual flow stands alone.
do: Mute the music track and check the cut still works; then lay sound effects for the punctuation points.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Temp sound effects matter more than temp music in physical scenes because much of the emphasis is carried by sound.
do: Keep a bank of hits, whooshes and thuds and place them on the accent cuts.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Each cut throws the energy of one shot to the next, so the second shot reads as a response to the first.
do: Cut from a person's action or expression to a reaction or product shot so one seems to cause the other.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Viewers follow the invisible energy, so the editor should cut with timing that keeps the eye following it.
do: Cut where the viewer's eye is already heading, such as a glance or a pointing hand, to guide them to the next shot.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Every movement has preparation, action and recovery, and the editor chooses which phase the next shot needs.
do: Decide whether a gesture needs only its wind-up or the full arc, and cut at that phase.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Actors' underlying intentions can be read in voice and body, and cuts at the optimal point make mismatches go unnoticed.
do: Cut at the moment of the peak intention (pleading, boasting) rather than the line end; viewers forgive small continuity slips.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Small movements such as blinks, breath, head tilt and eyebrows throw emotion, especially in close-up.
do: For testimonials, cut on small face movements such as a raised eyebrow or a smile to carry the reaction.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The editor chooses both how the emotion is thrown and how it is received, choosing reactions to fit.
do: Choose reaction shots deliberately: pick the take where the receiver reacts the way the story needs.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: A beat is when a person changes tactic, and the editor builds the exchange as a cause-and-effect chain of these changes.
do: In a two-person or skit script, change the character's tactic (ask, then demand) at each beat and cut at those changes.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Beats show up as changes in eyes, breath and head, which are good cutting points.
do: Mark breaths, looks away and blinks in a raw clip and use them as the cut points.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: A wide two-shot after shot and reverse shot works as punctuation, signalling that the scene's objective has been achieved or thwarted.
do: Close a back-and-forth section by cutting wide to show both people, so the viewer reads the question as answered.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Holding a charged moment works best with fast, light cuts between concentrating faces rather than long static holds.
do: In an emotional beat, alternate quick shots of faces with tight timing instead of sitting on one shot.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Cutting away from a fake smile as it begins and back as it fades makes the smile a throw and catch of emotion.
do: Cut away as a speaker puts on a bright face, then return as it drops to show the truth.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Event rhythm balances information so there is enough to engage but not so much that it confuses, and losing curiosity loses momentum.
do: Give each beat of a script one new point and one open question, and cut anything that adds a second idea.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Rhythms must be designed for the target audience, because different markets share different paces, energies and attention spans.
do: Set pace and cut density per brand audience, and test the rhythm against that audience's usual feed.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Different audiences and genres expect different energy and pace, so the rhythm of a piece should be shaped to what its audience wants to feel.
do: Set the cut pace per brand and audience before editing: urgent sale reels cut fast and relentless, a slow luxury fragrance reel gets longer holds.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Tension comes from open questions with something at stake, and cutting out the answer scene to jump to the aftermath makes the viewer fill in the gap and feel more energised.
do: Pose a question in the first seconds, then skip the explaining beat and cut straight to the character already acting on the answer.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Moving images often carry what a script spends pages explaining, so one well-chosen shot can replace a long set-up.
do: Replace spoken or on-screen explanation with one telling shot (the unboxing, the pour, the door slam) and delete the line that described it.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Once an emotional or informational beat has landed, repeating it dulls impact and kills the viewer's forward momentum.
do: Watch each cut for repeats of the same beat (second reaction, second claim, second product shot) and delete the weaker one.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Editors should watch their own attention and pinpoint the exact moments they tune out, then ask what information is being given and whether it has already been absorbed.
do: Watch a draft reel once cold with no editing tools and note the second where your attention slips; cut or tighten that spot.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Beautiful polished material can seduce an editor into keeping shots that do not serve the structure, so each shot must justify its place by what it tells us.
do: Check every gorgeous shot: if it adds no new information or feeling in the sequence, cut it however good it looks.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Good storytellers set the film's rhythm and its dramatic questions in the opening, so the first moments tell the audience what kind of ride this is.
do: Make the first two seconds of a reel already move at the pace and energy of the whole piece.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Montage of disconnected images is a staple of ads because viewers form the message themselves through associations, shaped by rhythm.
do: Build a montage opening of unrelated lifestyle images that together imply the problem or desire, without saying it, and time it to a beat.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Cutting a single action into several shots is worth doing because each shot offers its own timing, size and movement for finer control of rhythm.
do: Shoot one action (spray, apply, wear) in several sizes and angles so the edit can speed it up or stretch it.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Cutting out stretches of time between events keeps tension, removes irrelevancies and makes the story move faster.
do: Cut on the action and drop the walking, opening and waiting; show only the beats that carry the story.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Cutting between differences in light, size, direction or movement makes viewers work a little harder, which makes the piece feel more energetic.
do: On energetic reels, cut dark to light, wide to tight and left-moving to right-moving rather than matching them.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Collision cutting is the standard for upbeat ads and music videos, because rhythm is only perceived through difference.
do: When a reel feels flat, vary shot size, direction, brightness and speed from cut to cut so each cut shows a clear contrast.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: In smooth linkage, any shot that sticks out in shape, size or movement breaks the viewer's immersion.
do: For testimonial or story reels where trust matters, keep neighbouring shots similar so nothing jolts the viewer out.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Smooth cutting means similar lighting, stepwise shot-size changes and matched movement direction, with match-on-action as its cornerstone.
do: For a smooth reel, step wide to mid to close, keep movement in one direction, and cut on the action.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Cutting away before a viewer has taken in a shot or finished a movement creates collision and tension about what was missed.
do: For an urgent hook, cut each opening shot a beat before the movement peaks so the viewer is pulled forward.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The Psycho shower scene is one action cut into many shots that collide in direction, shape and sound to control rhythm and effect precisely.
do: For a high-energy product moment, cover it with many tight angles that contrast in direction and texture, backed by sharp sound hits.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Violence in Psycho is felt through the collisions between shots rather than seen, so implication can replace explicit images.
do: Imply the result through cut rhythm and sound instead of showing the explicit thing, for example the effect of a product rather than the process.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Breaker Morant repeats a small set of shot sizes to build a steady pattern and breaks the pattern with new angles when a revelation lands.
do: Hold a steady cutting pattern through the setup, then change it abruptly at the offer or reveal so the break signals the moment.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The courtroom scene holds still, close shots just before a damning answer, stretching time with minimum collision, and cuts quickly on a victory to underline the change.
do: Hold a tight still shot for a beat before delivering the key claim or price, then cut short on the payoff.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Requiem for a Dream uses fast, percussive montage that feels fun at first, then lets the same device get longer and messier as the story turns.
do: If using a repeated montage motif, keep its rhythm identical each time so viewers learn it, and vary it only when the message changes.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Jump cuts have lost their power to disrupt and are now an accepted editing device in mainstream work.
do: Use jump cuts freely to remove dead air in talking-head and UGC clips; viewers read them as normal, not as a mistake.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Parallel action shows the story by letting the viewer see two places at once and draw their own conclusions, instead of being told.
do: Cut between two contrasting situations (problem versus product in use) and let the viewer reach the conclusion unprompted.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Audiences often know the outcome of a parallel sequence but still enjoy the tension, so the editor's skill is in controlling when the two strands converge.
do: Tease the payoff by cutting between the struggle and the solution and delay their meeting by a beat or two.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Strangers on a Train accelerates cuts and music between two pairs of feet to build an expectation of collision, then subverts it.
do: Build expectation with accelerating cuts between two things moving toward each other, then twist the payoff.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Cutting lets viewers tell themselves the story by connecting two images, giving them tension and a surprise.
do: Withhold the connecting shot so the viewer makes the link.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: In a parallel sequence one strand can be action and the other what is at stake, and spending the time on the stakes is what produces feeling.
do: In a problem-and-fix reel, spend more screen time on what is at stake for the person than on the action itself.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: When cutting parallel action, the editor should decide where the action is, where the emotion is, and the balance between them.
do: Mark each cut sequence as action or emotion, and adjust the time given to each to get the reaction you want.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The Godfather baptism pairs matching gestures across the two strands to make a metaphor the viewer can draw.
do: Cut between two matching gestures (applying the product, applying a feeling) to suggest a link without stating it.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Dialogue and music from one strand run over the pictures of the other so the sound reinterprets the images and the timing of cuts on the performance shows what a character knows.
do: Let a voice-over line run over a contrasting visual so the mismatch carries the meaning.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Shifting a cut by just 1½ seconds changes what the viewer believes a character is thinking, so cut timing on a face decides meaning.
do: On reaction and face shots, trim or extend the cut by a few frames and re-watch; the choice changes what the viewer thinks is going on.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Parallel action works through metaphoric juxtaposition, overlapping sound, and cut timing that throws energy and shapes empathy.
do: When intercutting, choose shot pairs that compare or contrast on purpose, and carry audio across the cut.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Sound carried across the cut moves emotion from one side to the other, and the release beats matter as much as the builds of tension.
do: Put a quiet release beat after each build in a reel instead of keeping the tension constant, and use audio to bridge cuts.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Parallel action puts the viewer wherever the action is, so an editor should always ask 'Where is the action?' because that is where the audience wants to be.
do: When cutting between two things (product vs problem, talent vs demo), at every cut ask where the action or emotion is and cut to that side.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Slow motion heightens emotion because it adds emphasis through longer duration and through a greater sense of bodily effort.
do: Put slow motion on the single moment that carries the feeling (pour, reveal, first use of the product) and keep everything around it at normal speed.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Chariots of Fire plays the climactic race fast in normal time first, then replays it in slow motion so the viewer can feel the effort.
do: Show the key result at real speed first, then replay it in slow motion so the viewer can feel it, such as a before/after or a product action.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Emotion is felt while a change is happening and fades once it is reached, so slow motion prolongs the journey and lets the viewer feel it longer.
do: Slow down the moment of transformation or arrival (the unboxing, the pour, the fit) and cut away soon after it lands, because the feeling fades once the result is known.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The Navigator slows a drifting glove instead of the falling boy, because showing the thing itself would be too much and a stand-in object carries the feeling.
do: For an emotional beat, slow down a detail or object (hand, fabric, droplet) rather than the whole obvious action.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Thelma and Louise uses slow motion, a freeze frame, a fade and upbeat music at the end to sustain a happy feeling rather than let the energy end.
do: End a reel on a slow-motion or freeze-frame of the happy moment with upbeat music so the viewer leaves on the feeling.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Fast motion tends to make moments comic and lowers emotional weight, because bodies seem to feel less.
do: Use sped-up footage for dull steps (setup, packing, waiting) and for light, funny beats, never for the emotional payoff.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Romeo and Juliet speeds up the mother's actions against the normal-speed daughter to show she is silly and feels nothing.
do: To show a rushed, careless or overwhelmed person (the 'before' state), speed up their footage against normal-speed footage of the calm hero.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Two for the Road runs a whole tourist visit in fast motion under two minutes to show experiences that carry no meaning, and it plays as funny.
do: Compress a list of generic, meaningless steps into a fast-motion run to make them funny or empty, then contrast with a real-speed moment of the product.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Mixing slow and fast speeds can signal confusion or superhuman control, and speed ramping does both in one shot.
do: Ramp from slow to fast (or fast to slow) on a single action shot to give a punchy transition, using it sparingly.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Any shot and reverse shot is parallel action, and for every two-sided cut the editor must decide which side gets emphasis and where the action and emotion are.
do: When cutting between speaker and listener or problem and product, decide which side carries the emotion at each cut and hold on it.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Drama comes from characters pursuing goals against obstacles, and the conflict's substance (the underlying desire) is what the editor shapes, not the surface subject.
do: In a script or cut, define what the person really wants and what blocks them, and cut for that desire rather than the literal words.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: A scene needs a turn where expectations are thwarted and redirected, and turning the scene is the heart of the editor's craft.
do: Give every reel one clear turn (expectation then reversal, problem then fix) and cut on that moment.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The editor can create or move a scene's turn through shot patterns and choice of moment, so the scene can be rewritten in the edit.
do: If the turn is weak in the footage, choose a different shot or moment to land it instead of relying on the script's placement.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: At the turn of the scene the shot pattern shifts from wide, sharp two-shots to tight close-ups with soft backgrounds.
do: When the emotional realization lands, switch from wide to a tight close-up with soft background.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Changing the pattern of shots is the editor's tool for marking emotional change, and what matters is that the pattern changes, not how.
do: Hold one shot pattern through the setup (e.g. steady wides or even cuts), then break it exactly on the turn with a close-up, a hold or a burst of cuts.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: A change in shot pattern is a visual cue to the subtext, so it can punctuate or create meaning that the dialog does not state.
do: Use a change in cutting pattern to signal what the speaker isn't saying, such as a close-up on a reaction while the voiceover stays smooth.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: A five-step scene check: define the conflict, note the opening value, break into beats, compare closing with opening value, and locate the turning point.
do: Before cutting or writing a reel, note the starting mood, the ending mood, and the one beat where it flips, then check that the cut hits that beat.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The editor features the dominant character in frame to make the forces against the protagonist feel larger and keep sympathy with her.
do: Choose the shot angle that makes the obstacle look big and keeps the viewer with the hero, such as the cluttered 'problem' large in frame and the hero small.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The first cut after a long single take lands exactly on the moment the protagonist's hope dies, drawing attention to her reaction.
do: Hold a long shot, then make the first cut on the reaction moment where the emotion changes.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: After the turn, cutting speeds up for the confrontation, then returns to the original held shot to signal no change in the balance of power.
do: Return to the opening shot or framing at the end when you want to say nothing changed, and use quicker cuts only during the struggle.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Kiss or Kill uses constant jump cuts in a scene where nothing changes to express that change is constant, meaning cut speed can carry theme, not only action.
do: Pick a cutting rhythm that matches the brand's feel (jumpy and unsettled vs smooth) and keep it consistent across the reel.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: In any two-sided scene, decide who is action and who is emotion, and the editor's question is which side we are on, when and for how long.
do: In each two-sided sequence, label which side drives the action and which holds the feeling, and give time to the side the viewer cares about.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Chase cutting rests on four elements from Dancyger: identification, excitation, conflict and intensification, and the viewer must care.
do: For high-energy reels, check you have a character the viewer cares about, movement, a back-and-forth tension, and varying shot lengths.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Viewers must care about the character, kept close with close-ups and point-of-view shots, and excitation comes from movement and quickening pace.
do: Open and keep returning to close-ups and POV shots of the person so the viewer stays aligned with them, and pile on movement to raise energy.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Cutting before the viewer fully grasps a shot creates edgy excitation, but too much uncertainty turns into irritation and lost interest.
do: Use short, hard-to-read shots to build energy, but pair them with shots held long enough to read so viewers don't lose the thread.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Viewers grasp much more the second time they see an image, so repeating a shot briefly lets the editor cut quickly and still build suspense and a reveal.
do: Flash a product or key shot briefly early, then return to it later so the viewer reads it fully and gets the reveal.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Intensification comes from varying shot length and breaking an established pattern, such as a long hold into a flurry of short shots, not from short shots alone.
do: Set an even cut pattern then break it, or hold one shot long before a burst of short cuts, instead of cutting fast throughout.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The four chase ingredients should be mixed in different proportions depending on the story being told, like a recipe.
do: Decide before editing which element leads (character, movement, tension, or rhythm change) and weight the cut toward it.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The French Connection chase keeps tension through intercutting both sides, dynamic movement, and sound design instead of music.
do: Try letting natural sound effects carry the rhythm of a high-energy cut instead of a music bed.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Bystanders in danger deepen identification, and after furious cutting the climax is held long and lyrical.
do: After fast cutting, end on one long held shot of the result to let the payoff land.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: The chase works through identification, with about one in four shots a close-up of the vulnerable boy and fifty more his point of view.
do: Put the person with the most at stake in about a quarter of shots as close-ups, with more as their POV.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Even cutting around one second with little intensification or excitation makes a sequence feel mechanical.
do: Avoid a uniform cut length across a whole reel; vary the rhythm so it rises and falls.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Rhythm exists to create cycles of tension and release that sync the viewer's body to the film.
do: Build each reel as waves of tension and release rather than a flat run of cuts.

title: Cutting Rhythms
author: Karen Pearlman
says: Event rhythm depends on knowing the audience's rates of assimilating information and expectations of change.
do: Set cut pace and information density to how fast the target shopper reads on the feed, and check by watching with fresh eyes.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: People's wants do not change, only their direction does, so copy cannot create want but can channel existing wants onto a product.
do: Do not try to make viewers want something new in a script. Find a want they already have and point it at the product.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Advertising that fights a mass desire fails, as the Chrysler, Ford safety and Edsel campaigns showed, so you must ride the demand already there.
do: Before briefing a script, check the desire is already rising in the market and build the hook on it, not against it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: What Is This Mass Desire—and How Is It Created?
says: Mass desire is a private want shared by enough people to be profitable, and advertising that taps it earns many times what it spends.
do: Write each script to one want that many South African shoppers already share, not to a niche need you have to explain first.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: What Is This Mass Desire—and How Is It Created?
says: When advertising has to create the desire it becomes education and returns at best a dollar of sales per dollar spent.
do: Do not spend a reel teaching the category. Open on the want and use the rest to show the product satisfying it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: In permanent-desire markets like looks and health, the job is to distinguish your product with a fresh appeal and stronger believability.
do: For beauty or health brands, find one angle or reason to believe that rivals have not used, and lead with it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Channel Mass Desire Onto Your Particular Product
says: Pick the one mass desire strongest in urgency, staying power and number of people, because that choice sits in the headline and everything else depends on it.
do: For every brief, score the candidate desires on urgency, repeat need and audience size, and choose one before writing a word.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Channel Mass Desire Onto Your Particular Product
says: The opening must start at the prospect's current awareness: with the product if they know it, the desire if they do not, the problem if they only feel a general problem.
do: Label each reel by what the viewer already knows and open there: product name, the desire, or the named problem.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: The Analysis of Your Product: What It Is—and What It Does
says: People buy what a product does, not the materials it is made of, and physical facts only serve to support the promised performance.
do: Show the product doing the job in the first seconds. Save fabric, weight or build details for proof lines later.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: The Analysis of Your Product: What It Is—and What It Does
says: Physical product facts earn their place by justifying the price, documenting quality, promising lasting performance, sharpening the mental picture, and giving a fresh reason to believe.
do: Turn each product spec into a proof beat that backs the main promise, such as a durability test or a close-up of the mechanism.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: The Analysis of Your Product: What It Is—and What It Does
says: List everything the product does, group each by the desire it serves, and feature the one performance with the most selling power now.
do: Before scripting, list the product's benefits in a column, tie each to a desire, and cut one script per top benefit rather than mixing them.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: The Analysis of Your Product: What It Is—and What It Does
says: An ad can carry only one thought through a reader's indifference, so choose the single dominant performance from the many a product offers.
do: Give each reel one benefit in the hook and make later benefits support it, never compete with it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: The headline does not have to sell; its only job is to make the prospect read the next sentence, and each sentence has the same job.
do: Judge a hook only by whether it earns the next line, and make every line in the reel earn the one after it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: What Your Prospect’s State of AwarenessDemands From Your Headline
says: The more aware the market, the easier the sell and the less you must say, and the stages run from the most aware down to the least.
do: Set reel length and effort by awareness: short and direct for aware viewers, longer and more built for unaware ones.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: For the most aware buyer who already wants the product, you need only the product name and a bargain, because price or a gift is the news.
do: For retargeting and returning customers, cut a short reel: product, the offer or price, delivery detail, then the buy prompt.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: 2. The Customer Knows of the ProductBut Doesn’t Yet Want It
