says: When the product is known but not yet wanted, show its name and then use the headline to reinforce, sharpen, extend, prove or announce a new mechanism or change of image.
do: For known brands, pick one of the seven tasks per reel, such as new proof or a new mechanism, and show the brand clearly.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Strong known-product headlines make the benefit concrete through a sensory picture, a vivid demonstration, a new use, or specific proof such as a count.
do: Pick one vivid demonstration or a hard number as the proof moment, for example a stress test shown on camera.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: When people want the result but do not know your product exists, name the desire, prove it can be done, then show your product holds the mechanism.
do: Structure product-unaware reels in three beats: name the want, show it can be achieved, then reveal the product as the way.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Good headlines give a name and sharp focus to a vague desire, sometimes plainly and sometimes with proof, mystery or wonderment.
do: Write several hooks that name the want, from plain to curious to astonished, and test them.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: 4. How to Introduce Products That Solve Needs
says: When the prospect knows the need but not the link to your product, name the need, dramatize it until the cost is felt, then present the product as the inevitable solution.
do: Script problem-aware reels as problem on screen, a moment that makes it hurt, then the product as the fix.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: 5. How to Open Up a Completely Unaware Market
says: A psychological wall separates each awareness stage, so a headline that works at one stage fails at another and fails again when the market moves on.
do: Do not reuse a winning hook for a colder audience. Rewrite it for their stage.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: 5. How to Open Up a Completely Unaware Market
says: For an unaware or resistant market, price and the product name mean nothing, so drop them from the opening.
do: In cold prospecting reels, keep price and logo out of the first seconds.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: 5. How to Open Up a Completely Unaware Market
says: With a totally unaware market you cannot mention price, product, function or desire, so the opening must call the market together by echoing what they feel.
do: For the coldest audience, open with a line or scene that says who they are and what they feel, with no pitch at all.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: 5. How to Open Up a Completely Unaware Market
says: An identification opening tells people what they are and exists only to pull them into the next paragraph, building step by step to the product.
do: Plan the reel as a chain: identify the viewer, grow awareness of the problem, show a solution exists, then land on the product.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: To Project a Hidden Desire WhichCannot Be Put Bluntly Into Words
says: When a desire cannot be said aloud, such as virility, show it through imagery, and a resentment can open a wider market than the direct promise.
do: For a desire viewers would not admit, let the visuals carry it and leave the words out; otherwise open on a shared annoyance.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: WHY HAVEN’T TV OWNERS BEEN TOLD THESE FACTS
says: The TV repair ad opens on the reader's own frustration and promises relief in plain, specific terms before introducing the book.
do: Start with the viewer's specific annoyance, such as a number or repeated event they know, and promise relief in their terms.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: THEY LAUGHED WHEN I SAT DOWN AT THE PIANO. BUT WHEN I STARTED TO PLAY!—
says: The piano ad tells a first-person story with a sceptical audience, a surprise and a triumph before it explains the method.
do: Try a creator-led reel with doubters, the reveal, and the reaction before explaining how.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: The identification opening is the hardest to get right, and it must be the prospect's own problem and mind and be able to turn away people who are not prospects.
do: Test cold hooks by asking whether the target viewer would say that is exactly me, and accept that it should lose the wrong viewers.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: A Final Word on Style in Advertising Copy
says: Advertising styles such as verse or first-person stories go stale and stop being believed, but the strategy beneath them stays valid.
do: Do not copy a trending format that viewers are tired of. Keep the underlying strategy and reshape it in a fresh format.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: If You Are First in Your Market
says: If you are first in a market, prospects have no earlier information and will believe more, and novelty can come from a new product, a new audience, a new medium or a newly noticed use.
do: Ask whether a new audience or an overlooked use of the product is a first, and build the reel on that.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: If You Are First in Your Market
says: When first, be simple and direct: name the need or claim, dramatize it, then bring in the product and prove it.
do: For a genuinely new product, state the claim plainly in the hook with no wordplay, then dramatize it and prove it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: When you are second and the direct claim still works, copy it and enlarge it, but enlarged claims eventually lose believability.
do: Make the claim bigger and more specific than the rival's, but stop before it sounds untrue.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Once all claims have been heard and doubted, the market still wants the result but no longer believes simple promises.
do: In crowded categories, assume the viewer has heard your claim and doubts it, so do not just repeat it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: For a market that has heard every claim, lead with a new mechanism, how it works, and let the claim shrink into shorthand.
do: In crowded categories, make the hook the how, a new ingredient, process or device, with the claim as a short follow-up.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: In third-stage ads the mechanism takes the headline and the full claim is restated right after, once the prospect sees a fresh chance.
do: Order the reel as mechanism first, then the full claim and everything the viewer gets.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Rivals quickly copy a new mechanism, so the fourth stage elaborates the mechanism until it too strains belief, at which point only a new believable mechanism or identification will work.
do: If a competitor has the same mechanism, make yours easier, faster or fuller, and have a next mechanism ready.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: When the market no longer believes any advertising, the answer is identification with the prospect rather than promise or mechanism.
do: For exhausted categories, make a reel about the viewer's life and feeling first, with the product kept quiet.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Let’s Look at an Industry That Went Through All Five Stages of Sophistication
says: A taboo market was opened by a romantic scene and four words of dialogue, not by a claim or a picture of the act.
do: For a sensitive desire, stage a small scene with one line of dialogue that implies the desire.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Verbalization strengthens a claim, freshens it, or pulls the prospect into the body, and the barest statement is best when you are first.
do: When a hook feels flat, ask whether it needs to be stronger, fresher or more curious, and rework it for that.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: A claim gains force when it is measured in size or speed, compared, made metaphorical, made sensory, demonstrated, dramatized or tied to admired people.
do: Put a number, a speed, a comparison or a demonstration in the hook and show it on screen.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: More ways to sharpen a claim include a question, an information promise, an authority, before and after, newness, exclusivity, a challenge, a quoted testimonial and a parallel symbol.
do: Write three hook variants using different devices from this list, such as a before-and-after, a challenge or a customer quote.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Hooks can also connect mechanism to claim, name the problem, warn of pitfalls, show ease through a shared limitation, state the difference, or show an old limitation overcome.
do: Use a surprising demonstration where an old limitation is visibly gone, or a name for the problem the viewer has felt.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Further hooks address people who cannot buy, speak to the prospect directly, show how hard the product was to make, accuse it of being too good, or challenge a limiting belief.
do: Try a hook that talks directly to one viewer type or that challenges a belief they hold about themselves.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Swapping your product into a winning headline makes an echo ad that ignores the unique product, market and timing, and formulas help only with wording.
do: Do not clone a competitor's winning hook with our brand swapped in. Use competitor ads to find the angle, then rewrite.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: On Motivation Research and ItsRelation to the Copy Writer
says: Motivation research reveals hidden desires, taboos and market splits, but a finding is only a direction and still needs a creative idea.
do: Mine reviews, comments and DMs for hidden wants and taboos, then turn each into a script idea rather than copying the wording.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: On Motivation Research and ItsRelation to the Copy Writer
says: Over a long campaign the writer holds a conversation with the market, and the failures and limits in response raise the research questions that produce new themes.
do: After each batch, read where ads underperformed and the comments and returns, ask why, and brief the next round on those questions.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: On Expressing the Personality of a Product in Your Headline
says: A product has a personality made of many traits, but one dominant trait should lead every headline and the others should support it.
do: Name the one trait that defines the brand and have every reel in the series lean on it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: On the Only Type of Prevention Headline That Will Sell
says: Prevention messages work when the future harm falls on someone the viewer loves, because people will not picture disaster happening to themselves.
do: For prevention products, show the problem hitting a child, partner or parent in the scene, not the buyer.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: On the Selection of Splinter Markets to Avoid Competition
says: A small advertiser can avoid big rivals by targeting one segment with its own reason for wanting the product and building the whole campaign around it.
do: For small brands, pick one segment, such as health reasons rather than looks, and tailor hook, mechanism and proof to it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Five to ten words carry about 90% of an ad's value, so most of the effort belongs in finding the unique element of this product and market.
do: Spend most of the writing time on the first line and the one angle, and write many options before touching the rest.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Existing desires cannot be created or fought, only expanded, sharpened and channelled, so the first job is to make the viewer picture every moment of the wish coming true.
do: Start the script from a want the viewer already has, then spend most of the runtime showing the fulfilment in concrete moments (using it, friends reacting) before the offer.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: People also buy a product to play a role and project a personality, and this doubles the pull of the plain physical desire.
do: Show the kind of person who already uses the product (their look, setting, status) in the reel so the viewer sees who they join by buying.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Beliefs are a filter the product information must pass; advertising can't argue them away, it must build conviction along the prospect's own logic.
do: Write the proof beats in the viewer's own kind of logic and vocabulary, not the brand's, and never open by contradicting something they firmly believe.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Vague, hazy desires gain power when filled out with concrete images of every way they can be satisfied.
do: List five specific scenes of the life after purchase and show at least three of them in the reel instead of one abstract benefit line.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Short formats must compress the desire into a few key words and repeat it across a series with fresh embellishments, because the viewer leaves with only one dominant image.
do: Pick the single image the viewer should carry away, state it in a few words, and make every new reel in the series restate it with a different scene.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: You cannot repeat the same promise but you can reinforce it with a fresh viewpoint each time, and stale phrasing bores a market that has seen it before.
do: When a reel repeats its promise, change the setting, person or angle each time; cut any beat that says the same thing in the same way.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: MORE ROSES THAN YOU EVER SAW ON ANY ROSE BUSH…
says: The rose ad piles up exact numbers and vivid pictures of abundance to make the benefit feel enormous.
do: Use a countable, specific figure on screen (such as 50 a day) and picture what that quantity looks like in a real room.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: MORE ROSES THAN YOU EVER SAW ON ANY ROSE BUSH…
says: Describe the moment of first use through the reactions of the people around the buyer, such as gasps and kids' faces.
do: Open or climax on the reaction shot: the unboxing or switch-on moment with the family or friends reacting in real time.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Show how the product works in action, step by step, not only what it looks like and what it promises.
do: Build a demo beat where the product is used from start to result in sequence, with the ability or result getting bigger as it goes.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Put the viewer inside the story by describing what happens to them the first day they own the product.
do: Script a second-person first-day scene ("next weekend you...") and cut it as a point-of-view sequence ending on the surprised reaction.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Show Him How to Test Your Claims
says: Turn the demonstration into a test the viewer pictures doing themselves, so they prove the benefit immediately and specifically.
do: Give the viewer a quick do-it-now check they can imagine (a before and after measure or a ten-second trial) and show it being done on screen.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Stretch Out Your Benefits in Time
says: Extend the benefit across time, showing a staged flow of results over weeks and months.
do: Structure a reel as day 1, week 2, month 1 beats with a visibly bigger result at each stage and a payoff scene at the end.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Bringing in other people, whether celebrities or ordinary users, lets the viewer see the product through fresh eyes and strengthens the picture.
do: Cut in short reactions from several different kinds of users, each describing a different result, rather than one testimonial.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: The astonishment of experts is especially persuasive because surprise, competition and discovery combine.
do: Stage a head-to-head test against the leading alternatives and film an expert's or professional's surprised reaction to the result.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Set old way against new way in parallel, repeated sentences so the advantage stands out.
do: Write a repeated structure ("while others paid X, you got Y") and cut it as a rhythmic three-item split-screen.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Paint the problem in full black first, then the solution in parallel, to get both repulsion from the old and attraction to the new.
do: Open on the ugly problem close-up (the filth, the damage) and then reveal the clean result in the same framing.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Show How Easy It Is to Get These Benefits
says: Every touchpoint such as ease of use, price and unwrapping gives a fresh angle to restate the benefits, e.g. big result for 30 seconds of work.
do: Pair a tiny visible effort with a list of big results, repeating the same effort line before each result.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Metaphor and personification can present facts more dramatically than literal description.
do: Personify the product's function (a voice at your elbow, a guard) in one short visual metaphor.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Keep adding fresh angles only while they renew interest; cut them once they merely repeat, and finish with a condensed catalog of benefits.
do: Re-watch the rough cut after a break and delete any beat that repeats; end with a one-line-per-benefit recap.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: After developing one dominant desire at full intensity, close by shotgunning every use and benefit in a fast catalog to hedge.
do: End the reel with a quick-cut run of uses or benefits, one beat each, no elaboration.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: A desire catalog summarises the product as freedom from each old hassle and then a list of new rewards.
do: Close with a rapid "frees you from X, Y, Z" run of old pains, then the payoff.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Make the guarantee the climax, restating each key performance as a specific promise backed by money back.
do: Voice the guarantee as a numbered list of the actual benefits promised, not a generic "money-back" line.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Apply These Principles ofIntensification to the Campaign
says: In a series, the central idea can't stay as the headline, so you must restate it through variations so different the audience keeps engaging yet so fresh the idea feels new.
do: Set one central campaign idea per brand and brief every reel as a different disguise of it, with a new hook each time.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Apply These Principles ofIntensification to the Campaign
says: Colgate varied only a startling opening demonstration and kept the selling message identical, so a quick emotional jolt welded onto a fixed message.
do: Keep the body and close of a reel fixed and test many different startling first-ten-second openers on it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Apply These Principles ofIntensification to the Campaign
says: Toni and Clairol repeated one verbal line while changing the main picture each time, which kept the line fresh.
do: Hold the on-screen line or spoken hook constant and change the lead visual or person across variants.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Apply These Principles ofIntensification to the Campaign
says: Volkswagen shows the product alone against a bare background and varies the facts, so each short ad is enough and the series builds one theme.
do: Shoot the product in clean close-up with no distractions and make each reel about one new fact.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Apply These Principles ofIntensification to the Campaign
says: The VW headlines pull people into the body by contradicting the picture or an accepted idea, and they leave the product out of the headline.
do: Pair an opening line with an image that appears to disagree with it so the viewer must keep watching to resolve it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Every product should give two reasons to buy: the physical need it meets and a role it lets the buyer play to the outside world.
do: For each script name the functional benefit and the role the buyer gets, and show both on screen.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Buyers now purchase roles such as modern, slim or adventurous, so each role gives another mass desire to attach to the product.
do: List the roles the product could signal and choose one to anchor the script around.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: A product can help someone master a character role, speed it up, or symbolise it so friends notice.
do: Show the product on display or being noticed by others, not only being used.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Many purchases make sense only through the role they give, and character roles live in the subconscious and are never put into words.
do: Imply the role through the person and setting in frame rather than naming it in a line.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: People accept a flattering character role implied by a wordless image more readily than a performance claim, because nothing has to be defended.
do: Carry the identity pitch through casting, setting and props with no spoken claim, and keep spoken lines for performance.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Achievement roles are invisible titles that people must display through the products they own.
do: Show the product as a visible marker of arriving at a milestone (new home, new job, new baby).

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Put These Longings for Identificationto Work for Your Product
says: When competing products perform the same and price is no longer a factor, the role your product offers decides the sale.
do: For commodity-like products, lead with the role and identity difference, not the specs.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Put These Longings for Identificationto Work for Your Product
says: Existing product perceptions are walls you cannot break; build on them instead, and only prestige products already carry identity appeal.
do: Check what viewers already think of the product category and build the identity from that starting point.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Put These Longings for Identificationto Work for Your Product
says: Most products lack built-in prestige and need it built on a bridge from their existing image toward widely wanted roles like success or being modern.
do: Pick one widely wanted role and link it to the product through its real existing trait.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: The Primary Image of Your Product
says: Every product already has a primary image in the buyer's mind, and that image is the raw material for building richer images.
do: Write down the product's primary image in one phrase and make it the base of the concept.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: The Primary Image of Your Product
says: Marlboro intensified virility three ways: virile men, virile situations, a primitive symbol, and that is only the beginning of building prestige.
do: Show the core trait through three different visual cues in a single reel (person, situation, symbol).

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: The Primary Image of Your Product
says: Replacing an unfavourable or dull product image with a better one fails; instead keep it, lower its intensity, and use it as a bridge.
do: When a product has a negative or dull image, acknowledge it briefly and move quickly to a bigger appeal rather than denying it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Build New Images Into Your Product
says: Chesterfield kept the accepted image (the man) but darkened and subordinated him so the eye lands on the woman and a larger romantic scene.
do: Keep the accepted figure in frame but dim and de-emphasise it, directing the eye to the new emotional focus with lighting and posture.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Build New Images Into Your Product
says: New favourable images can be added only if they grow out of the primary image and stay logically consistent with it, signalled by props and settings.
do: Add status, adventure or romance cues via wardrobe, props and location that fit the product's own base image.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Build New Images Into Your Product
says: Multi-role symbols widen the market and deepen attraction, so a neutral product needs an inventory of its primary images before adding appeals.
do: Choose props that signal several roles at once, such as success plus taste plus accomplishment.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Build New Images Into Your Product
says: Glamour spelled out in words sounds corny, but the same images shown visually enter the mind unnoticed and are accepted.
do: Carry status and mood through set, car, clothing and tools in the shot, and don't state them in the voiceover.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Build New Images Into Your Product
says: Small details (roll bar, chronometer, casual clothes), composition and lighting build a mood of precision and excitement that invites the viewer in.
do: Choose three telling details per shot to signal character and let framing and light carry the mood.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: On the Limits to the Images Your Prospects Will Identify With
says: Identification images fail when the market can't picture itself in them, and the fix is a bridge image from what they already believe.
do: Test whether the on-screen person looks like the real buyer or their next step up, and add a relatable bridge shot if not.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: On the Limits to the Images Your Prospects Will Identify With
says: Don't ask the viewer to leap across a believability gap; build a bridge from an image they already accept and they will follow you almost anywhere.
do: Open each reel on a scene the viewer instantly recognises as their own life, then step up to the aspirational image.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: On Saleable Identifications Springing From the Physical Product Itself
says: Micrin borrowed the glass shape of a doctor's office container to signal effectiveness instantly, since packaging can carry the product's background.
do: Borrow the visual cues of the product's real background (lab, clinic, workshop) in packaging and shots.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Belief gives emotional security and was set in childhood, so people won't abandon an established belief unless frightened beyond belief.
do: Don't ask the viewer to give up a long-held belief in 30 seconds; work inside it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Violating an established belief sinks the ad, while one claim fully backed by his belief outsells a pile of half-believed promises; Gradualization means leading from accepted facts to more remote ones.
do: Cut the script down to the one claim the viewer will fully believe and build it from facts they already accept.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Gradualization determines the structure and order of the ad, while proof, reasons and testimonials add belief on top of it.
do: Order beats so each claim is prepared by the one before it, and treat proof as a separate layer.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: A claim's strength comes from its content and from the preparation before it, so sequence can be adjusted to raise belief, and the ad is an architecture of reactions.
do: Storyboard the viewer's reaction at each beat, not just the content, and move claims later until the earlier beats have earned them.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: The most powerful claim is not always the best headline, because if the viewer can't believe it they leave; test a less ambitious opener and bridge to the big claim.
do: Write a believable, softer hook as variant B against the big-claim hook, then bridge to the same claim in the body.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: The TV repair manual's blunt save-money headline failed because buyers didn't believe they could fix their own sets, so two beliefs had to be built first.
do: Name the beliefs that must be true before the offer lands (can I do it, will it save me) and design the early beats to establish them.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: The winning ad opened with a no-promise headline echoing the viewer's suspicion, followed by an easy-yes question, to start a habit of agreement before the first claim.
do: Start a reel with a line the viewer agrees with and a question nearly everyone answers yes to, then make the first promise.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How Belief Was Built Into the Opening
says: Lead-in words like "Then" imply exclusion and add credibility, and listing symptoms the viewer already has produces repeated yes reactions that carry into the promise.
do: Before stating the benefit, list two or three recognisable problems on screen so the viewer nods at each, then deliver the promise.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How Belief Was Built Into the Opening
says: Describe the viewer's symptoms and the savings in specific terms, but hold back how the product works until a string of small yeses has made him ready for it.
do: Open the reel with two or three symptom lines the viewer will nod to. Show the product mechanism only after those, never in the first seconds.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Before the ad makes its second, bigger claim, it first proves the product is dependable by describing the maker's own punishing tests.
do: Put one vivid proof beat, such as a stress test or a number of units tested, before the new or surprising claim in the script.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: What TV Experts Have Learned About Your Set!
says: Repeat the earlier claims almost word for word and then back each with logical proof, so each proof rests on the one before it.
do: Restate the hook promise in the middle of the script with its proof attached, using the same words the viewer first heard.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: A new and harder claim is slipped in as if it were one more in a series the reader has already accepted, using tie-in words and parallel wording.
do: Start the new claim line with the same sentence pattern and tie-in words (And, most important) as the accepted lines before it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: A Restatement of Our Basic Theory
says: Belief comes from how a claim is prepared, and one fully believed promise outsells piling on more promises, which only adds resistance.
do: Cut the reel down to one promise and spend the saved seconds making that single promise believable, instead of adding more benefits.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: A question that the target viewer answers yes to makes him identify with the ad right away and puts him in the yes group.
do: Open with a yes-question aimed at one specific viewer, such as Do you...?, and make sure only the right buyer would say yes.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Listing the reader's exact symptoms and problems shows you have been there, but it only works if the details are accurate, so research first.
do: Open a script with three or four specific, true complaints in the customer's own words, taken from reviews and comments, before pitching.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: You can open by bluntly telling the reader that what he believes is false, backed by strong authority, to loosen old beliefs before introducing your claims.
do: Try a myth-busting hook that says Forget what you have heard about X, then follow at once with the new positive claim.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Logic words like because, therefore and here's why carry conviction by themselves, so weave them in wherever a claim follows from the one before.
do: Put a Here's why or That's because bridge line between each claim in the voiceover so the script sounds like reasoning.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: A short chain of logic, where each step leads to the next and size equals power, makes the reader feel the product must work.
do: Write the mechanism as a three-step chain (A causes B, B causes C, so the product does C) and show each step on screen in order.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Remove Objections to Your Product
says: Products with drawbacks (too complicated, too narrow, too expensive) need redefining so the roadblock is gone before the viewer notices it.
do: List the product's biggest objection and write one line that redefines it before the viewer raises it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Remove Objections to Your Product
says: Lifebuoy turned its bad medicinal smell into proof of power, a flip that makes the liability an asset.
do: Find the product's most obvious flaw (smell, size, price, slow results) and test an ad that presents it as proof of strength.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: The TV ad that failed led with the hard task (do your own repairs), while the winner talked about breakdowns and costs and brought in the product only later, in a smooth turn.
do: Open on the viewer's problem or cost, not on the effort the product asks of him, and bring in the product with a smooth turn line.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: The ad avoids the scary word repair until the reader has been walked into seeing repairs as small outside adjustments.
do: Check the hook for any word that signals effort or difficulty and swap it for a softer one until the viewer is ready.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Five Minutes a Week for Perfect Reception.
says: Comparing the TV to the body and renaming repairs as warning signals and adjustments removes the mystery and the fear of doing it himself.
do: Use a familiar everyday comparison to explain how the product works, and rename the hard-sounding step with an easy word.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Five Minutes a Week for Perfect Reception.
says: A new easy-to-use product is not believed just because you shout easy, so you have to redefine the field and then show the ease in a mechanism.
do: If the pitch is that it is easy, show the steps being done on screen and never rely on the word easy alone.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Five Minutes a Week for Perfect Reception.
says: The Cody ad made English feel easy by shrinking the task to a few countable facts: 69 words, 12 rules, 25 errors, 15 minutes a day.
do: Break the job into a few small named numbers (3 steps, 2 minutes, 1 tap) and put them on screen as a count.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: A product with too narrow an appeal can be escalated by redefining the larger role it plays in the buyer's life.
do: Pitch the product as a way to a bigger outcome the viewer wants, such as winning people over, and not just as the thing itself.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: To make a price feel lower, do not defend it but switch the comparison to a more expensive standard.
do: Give the price after naming a higher reference figure (a salon visit, the handmade price, a full set), and never against a cheaper rival.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: The spark plug ad stacks ten bargain cues in two paragraphs: handmade, a high price named twice, a magic word low, payback, a condition and a favour tone.
do: State the high comparison price twice before the real price, then give the real price as a favour you are allowing.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Verbally Prove That YourProduct Does What You Claim
says: The viewer silently asks for three things as he watches: tell me more, who says so, and how does it work, and the copy must answer each.
do: Mark the points in the script where a viewer would think Oh yeah? or How?, and answer them in the next beat.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: How to Verbally Prove That YourProduct Does What You Claim
says: You must play both writer and viewer, anticipate the exact point he wants proof or a mechanism, and switch direction right then.
do: Read the script as the viewer and mark each place he loses interest or wants proof, then put the matching proof or mechanism beat exactly there.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: How much mechanism a piece of copy needs depends on whether the prospect already knows and accepts how this kind of product works.
do: Before writing, decide if the viewer already knows how the product works; if he does, name the mechanism, and if not, explain it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: When people already understand the mechanism, you only need to name it in bold and compete on price or features.
do: For a familiar product type, show the mechanism names as bold on-screen labels, skip explaining them, and spend the time on price and offer.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: When the mechanism is not understood or everyone shares it, you describe it in a promise then reason-why structure.
do: Run the first few seconds on the promise and then switch to a because line showing the reason it works.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Mechanism copy must be loaded with promise and emotion, not turned into dull scientific explanation, and in a sophisticated market it needs to go much deeper.
do: Write the how-it-works beat so every line also sells the benefit, and make the mechanism more specific the more crowded the market is.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: In a sophisticated market, a strong new mechanism can become the headline itself, offering a new way when everything else has failed.
do: When viewers have heard every promise, lead the hook with the mechanism or ingredient that is the new way.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: A price cut or deal is not believed without a reason behind it, and without one you get only a fraction of its sales power.
do: Give a true reason in the script for the sale or discount (overstock, season end, batch size) before stating the price.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Collier told the story of the weather and the overstocked mill for six paragraphs before the bargain, which made the bargain believable.
do: Tell the short story behind a deal first, such as the cause and what it led to, and only then give the discount.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Attack a competitor's weakness only if you show at once that your product fixes it, or the attack just looks biased.
do: In any comparison reel, pair every rival flaw you name with your product removing it in the next beat.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Let’s See How He Does It
says: The sequence works through repeated one-for-one bad then good contrast, with parallel wording and a weak word against a strong one, each with a cause.
do: Cut a comparison as alternating bad and good beats, using the same sentence frame and matching visuals, one performance point at a time.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: When points cannot be compared one by one, tell the viewer's familiar experience with current products as a time sequence, ending in failure, before introducing yours.
do: Script the viewer's past sequence of trying and failing (tried this, then this, then it came back) before the product appears as the answer.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: The contrast can be cut to a single line, and success is measured by whether the reader questions a habit or shifts a loyalty, not by length.
do: Try a one-line contrast hook that implies the weakness of the usual alternative and the benefit of yours.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Let’s Look at a Few Examples
says: Making the ad match the look and format of the medium it runs in lets the reader slip in without switching to ad mode, and one such change lifted results hugely.
do: Cut each reel to look native to its placement, with the same caption style, framing and pacing as the organic content of that feed.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Let’s Look at a Few Examples
says: Plain and even ugly details copied from the real publication, such as its headline type, sub heads and line drawing, are what carry belief, while polished layout loses it.
do: Use the platform's own plain look (default caption font, phone footage, no polished graphics) so nothing signals Ad.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: SKIN SPECIALIST DEMONSTRATES HOW TO RINSE AWAY YOUR BLACKHEADS
says: Open in the trusted format of a news report or similar and copy the tone, feel and style of channels people believe so the ad blends in with no jarring change.
do: Try a news-report or documentary-style open: a reporter-like line, hand-held footage and an insider tone before the pitch.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Understatement, with few adjectives and short falling sentences, makes an ad feel sincere and escapes the hard-sell stereotype.
do: Write the voiceover in short flat sentences with few adjectives, make the point quietly and stop, and cut with no hype music or big moves.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Deadly Sincerity, pointing out the flaws in your offer before the benefits, makes the benefits believed much more deeply.
do: Add one honest downside line early in the script, such as who it is not for, before the benefits.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Verification—How to Offer Authorities and Proof
says: Proof should be short, dramatic and specific and still sell, and where it is placed matters as much as what it is.
do: Cut each proof beat to one specific, dramatic line (a number, a name, a result) that also makes the viewer want the product.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Verification—How to Offer Authorities and Proof
says: Proof works best when the reader unconsciously demands it and is ready to accept it as necessary and logical.
do: Hold the proof back until the viewer has the doubt, then bring it in right after the claim that triggers it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Verification—How to Offer Authorities and Proof
says: Proof placed right after a run of believability copy, such as the Air Force reference after the comparison, adds far more than the same proof scattered elsewhere.
do: Put the strongest authority or proof line immediately after the comparison or mechanism sequence, not in a separate block.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Verification—How to Offer Authorities and Proof
says: Documentation is dull by itself, so stage it as the hero of a drama at the point where the reader is hungry for a solution.
do: Introduce the stat, test result or review as the answer to a problem the script has just made urgent, with a build-up and a reveal.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Reinforcement—How to Make TwoClaims Do the Work of Four
says: Two emotional ideas joined the right way have far more impact than either alone, like Avis saying we're second and so we try harder.
do: Pair a weakness or admission with its consequence in two linked lines, such as We're small, so we do X, as hook or tagline.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Reinforcement—How to Make TwoClaims Do the Work of Four
says: A frank admission of the product's flaws placed directly before the positive claim makes that claim more believable and powerful.
do: Put a short honest flaw line immediately before the big benefit line, with no gap between them.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Interweaving—How to Blend Emotion, Image and Logic Into the Same Sentence
says: Every sentence should carry promise, image, logic and emotion together, not facts alone.
do: Check each voiceover line for a benefit, a picture and a reason, and rewrite lines that carry only a fact.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Sensitivity—How to Give Your Reader What He Demands Step In Step Throughout the Copy
says: The ad's architecture depends on spotting where the reader wants something different and shifting copy type there, from promise to mechanism to proof and back, before he gets bored.
do: Map the script into blocks (promise, mechanism, proof, promise) and cut to the next block just before the viewer would tire of the current one.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: For a skeptical audience that has been let down before, agree with the skepticism and then hand a long stretch of the ad to an authority.
do: For a sceptical category, say out loud that others have disappointed, then give the expert or founder a long, calm segment.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: Each product needs its own structure, and a dead feeling while writing signals the point where the copy has lost the reader.
do: When a script goes flat at a certain beat, change the block type there (promise to proof, or proof to promise) and don't just reword it.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
says: The same content in a new structure makes a new ad, so if stuck, restart from the opposite direction, even starting with what was buried in the body.
do: If a reel underperforms, rebuild it with the same facts in a different order, such as starting from the proof or the buried line.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Momentum—How to Draw Your ReaderDeeper and Deeper Into Your Copy
says: Momentum phrases and unfinished statements keep the reader going into the next sentence.
do: Put short bridge lines like Here's how, Just wait or And that's only the start at the join between beats.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Momentum—How to Draw Your ReaderDeeper and Deeper Into Your Copy
says: To keep readers going, raise a specific interest, leave a question about it, and promise the answer later in the copy.
do: At each cut, state an interesting result, hold back how it happened, and pay it off in the next beat.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Momentum—How to Draw Your ReaderDeeper and Deeper Into Your Copy
says: Teaser lines like Caught! 120 Fish in One Hour! both pull the reader on and sell at the same time, so no word is wasted.
do: Write curiosity hooks that name a vivid result and leave out the method, so the line pulls and sells together.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Mood—How to Pack Your Copy With Drama, Excitement, Sincerity or Any Other Emotion You Wish
says: Word choice and rhythm set a piece of copy's mood, with some words sharpening the image and others quietly telling the reader what to feel about it.
do: In a script, split your adjectives into two kinds: image words that make the product visible and emotion words that tell the viewer how to feel. Check that each line has both, and keep the emotion words subtle.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Mood—How to Pack Your Copy With Drama, Excitement, Sincerity or Any Other Emotion You Wish
says: Emotion words must stay unnoticed by your audience, since sophisticated readers who spot them find the copy corny, so tone must match the audience's sophistication and be read aloud for rhythm.
do: Read every voiceover and caption line aloud before cutting. Cut any emotion word that draws attention to itself, and rewrite tone when the same ad moves to a more sophisticated audience or placement.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Mood—How to Pack Your Copy With Drama, Excitement, Sincerity or Any Other Emotion You Wish
says: Power words and plain man-to-man phrasing combine with short, choppy claim-after-claim sentences to propel the reader and overwhelm them, while a sincere tone like Volkswagen's comes from dropping adjectives and adding self-kidding whimsy.
do: For a fast claim-stack reel, write short verb-led lines and cut each claim hard on the beat. For a trust-led reel, strip the adjectives, speak plainly and add a self-deprecating line.

title: Breakthrough Advertising
author: Eugene Schwartz
chapter: Mood—How to Pack Your Copy With Drama, Excitement, Sincerity or Any Other Emotion You Wish
says: Long, clumsy, unscannable sentences and straight-from-the-shoulder phrasing make copy feel honest, and mood-building works because the reader doesn't notice it.
do: For proof or founder-style reels, keep a slightly rough, unpolished spoken delivery and don't smooth every line into a slick rhythm, so it doesn't sound like a copywriter wrote it.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: The book's priorities are salience, distinctiveness, getting noticed and an emotional response, and marketers should find and consistently use their distinctive brand assets such as colours, logo, tone and fonts.
do: Put the brand's own colour, logo, font and tone in the first seconds and keep them in every cut, so the ad could only be this brand.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Advertising mostly refreshes memories people already hold rather than persuading them, so it should consistently use the brand's distinctive assets.
do: Build each reel from the brand's known cues (colour, pack, sound, tone) so viewers recognise it at once, and do not reinvent the look each time.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: In an Australian study only about 40% of viewers noticed a TV ad and only about 40% of those linked it to the right brand, so roughly 84% of exposures were wasted.
do: Check every cut on two tests: would a viewer notice it in the first second, and would they know whose it is. Show the brand early and more than once.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Common marketing mistakes include ads that are barely branded beyond a flash of the brand name and ads that fail to build or refresh memory of the brand.
do: Do not leave the brand to a closing logo flash. Weave the name, pack and distinctive look through the whole reel.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Advertising is best at reinforcing what people already believe and weak at building non-obvious new associations, such as unexpected uses for a product.
do: Pitch the product in the role people already expect it to play. If an unusual use is the point, show it in the product's own familiar setting rather than trying to teach a new habit in 30 seconds.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Campaigns that aim to increase penetration, meaning more buyers, produce larger sales effects than those aiming at loyalty.
do: Write the reel for someone who has never bought from the brand, not as a thank-you to existing fans.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: In IPA effectiveness awards, campaigns aimed at new customers won far more often than those aimed at loyalty, and were about three times as effective.
do: For paid social, make the main cut an introduction to a stranger: assume no prior knowledge and no loyalty.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Buying rates are heavily skewed: the average buyer is not typical, and most buyers of even a giant brand buy only once or twice a year.
do: Write for the occasional buyer who barely thinks about the brand, not for the fan. Open with the brand and what it is, without assuming familiarity.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Marketers forget how rarely their buyers buy, and the typical buyer of a brand buys barely more than once a year.
do: Do not use hooks that depend on the viewer knowing the brand or having bought before. Re-introduce the brand quickly in every video.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Most buyers are very infrequent, so a brand must reach them all because there are so many and they could easily forget about it.
do: Keep a steady flow of branded content so occasional buyers keep seeing the brand, rather than running one big push and going quiet.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: The heaviest 20% of buyers typically deliver about half of sales, so light buyers collectively matter as much, and buyer weight changes unpredictably from year to year.
do: Do not write only to your 'best customers'. Aim the main reel at cold, light and non-buyers, who account for about half of sales.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: When a brand grows, every buyer group buys more, especially light buyers, so marketing needs the widest possible reach.
do: Choose broad, simple creative that works on any viewer over narrow persona-specific cuts.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Price promotions and loyalty programs skew to existing heavy buyers, deliver little extra volume, and sales fall back to normal once a promotion ends.
do: Do not make discounts the whole point of a reel. Lead with the brand and the product, and use any offer as a short add-on.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Marketing aimed at light buyers and non-buyers has the best chance, because it gets wide reach and still hits heavy buyers too.
do: Pick the hook and setting that suit anyone in the category, not just a niche segment.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Competing brands sell to essentially the same kinds of people, so a brand's market is the whole category and its buyers are up for grabs.
do: Write to the general category buyer, and skip a single narrow persona such as 'busy mum, 28-35'.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: A skew in a brand's buyer profile usually reflects history or mistakes, not a real fit, and marketing should usually follow the category norm.
do: If a brand's current buyers skew to one group, still write the reel for the whole category audience.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 6: Who Do You Really Compete With?
says: Marketers should worry less about being different and more about whether the brand is easy to recognise, because ads for an indistinct brand do not work.
do: In the first seconds of each reel, show the brand's recognisable look (pack, colour, logo, product shape) so a viewer can tell whose ad it is even with the sound off.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Smaller brands are bought by heavier category buyers, so a brand grows by recruiting light category buyers and not by targeting super consumers.
do: Write the hook and body for a casual buyer who rarely thinks about the category, with no insider terms or assumed knowledge, instead of speaking to the existing superfan.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Marketers do not need to convince buyers that a product is different before they buy, and rivals like McDonald's, KFC and Pizza Hut actually reduce their differentiation.
do: Do not force a unique-claim angle into every script; lead with the plain category benefit and why this brand's product does it well, and drop the hunt for a USP.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Loyalty rests on mental and physical availability, so a brand must stand out and be easy to identify using distinctive elements like colour, logo, tagline, character, celebrity and style.
do: Pick two or three fixed brand cues (colour, logo, a character or a line, a recurring visual style) and put them in every reel, not just the end card.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Distinctive brand assets make it easier to identify the brand in advertising and at purchase, and make ads more effective when correctly branded.
do: Brand with the distinctive asset early and often in the frame (pack colour, shape, logo placement) so branding does not depend on a logo card at the end.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: A distinctive asset is valuable when many people link it to the brand (fame) and to no other brand (uniqueness), and marketers overestimate how strong theirs are.
do: Before relying on a visual cue, check it: show the muted reel without the logo to a few people and ask whose ad it is.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Distinctive assets must be unique to the brand and widely known, and they are learned only through consistent use over many years.
do: Keep the same brand cues across all reels in a series and over time, and do not drop them for a fresh look on each new concept.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Distinctive assets build only through consistency across campaigns over time, and new campaigns should keep the branding elements the same so people recognise the brand.
do: Give each brand a fixed branding kit (colour, type, logo position, opening or sound cue) and apply it to every new concept, changing only the idea and not the look.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Distinctive assets do not motivate purchase, they tell people where the brand is and which brand they bought, so the aim is unique identifying characteristics and not unique selling propositions.
do: Judge a reel on whether the brand is unmistakable in it, not only on whether it makes a unique claim.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Ads mainly reach occasional buyers and remind them of things they already know, and a small nudge in buying probability can double sales without any new persuasive reason.
do: For awareness reels, remind people of what they already half-know about the brand in a quick, easy-to-notice way, instead of cramming in new arguments, and aim at the occasional buyer.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Successful advertising reaches the many low-probability buyers and nudges mental availability, while a price promotion's whole effect shows within its own week.
do: Judge offer-led reels by the sales in the promotion week, but do not judge brand-building reels by next week's sales.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Forty years of single-source data show some ads are vastly more sales-effective than others, and the best were likeable and visual and not hard-selling, with reach and continuity mattering.
do: Build reels around a likeable visual idea that carries the story without voiceover, and avoid piling on hard-sell claims; run continuously to reach many people.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: An ad must be noticed and processed and also linked to the right brand, and most ads fail one of these, with over 80% of TV ads wasted.
do: Check every reel against both hurdles: does the first second get noticed, and is the brand clear enough that viewers would name it afterwards.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Most ads get screened out, so the main creative job is an idea that earns a small emotional 'I'll pay attention' and keeps the brand at the centre of what viewers process.
do: Open with an emotional beat (laugh, surprise, tension) in the first seconds, and make sure the brand or product is part of that beat, not a tag at the end.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Advertising works mainly by refreshing and building memories that help the brand be noticed and recalled later in a buying moment, not mainly by persuading.
do: Judge each script by what it makes people remember about the brand (what it is, looks like, where to get it, when to use it). Repeat the same cues across reels.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Some ads do persuade, especially informative ones for new products, and persuasion is stronger when it carries an explicit emotional appeal.
do: When stating a product benefit, tie it to a human stake (the Goodyear 'your child's life' move) instead of the bare spec.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Most effective ads don't persuade or claim difference, because sales come largely from people with no prior intention and intentions and attitudes are weakly motivational.
do: Don't force a 'we're better' claim into every reel; a reel that simply keeps the brand fresh and recognisable is doing real sales work.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Chasing persuasive selling messages and intention-based testing leads to campaigns that look different each time and fail to refresh the brand's memory structures.
do: Keep look, voice, and brand cues the same across reels in a batch; don't reinvent the style per ad.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Effective advertising reaches all category buyers without gaps, gets noticed, uses clear brand links with the product shown in use, and only adds a persuasive fact if it doesn't get in the way.
do: Say or show the brand name and show the product in use within every reel, with a distinctive brand asset on screen; add one persuasive fact only if it doesn't crowd these out.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 10: What Price Promotions Really Do
says: Shoppers don't sit in fixed price tiers; most buy across cheap and expensive ranges over time, so 'deal-prone' versus 'premium' audiences are mostly a myth.
do: Don't write a separate 'bargain' script for a supposed discount audience; the same buyers respond to premium framing.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 10: What Price Promotions Really Do
says: Almost everyone who buys on a price promotion has bought the brand before, so discounts mostly don't win new customers.
do: Don't expect a discount-led reel to bring in new buyers; use discounts for existing customers and use brand-building reels for reach.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 10: What Price Promotions Really Do
says: A promotion pulls in infrequent buyers who then go straight back to their low buying rate, because buying on deal is routine and forgotten.
do: Treat a sale reel as a one-off spike and don't promise clients a lasting customer gain from it.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 10: What Price Promotions Really Do
says: One temporary promotion doesn't hurt a brand, but constant discounting lowers its reference price, makes price more salient than other attributes and trains buyers to wait for deals.
do: Avoid making every reel a price or discount reel; keep price messaging occasional so the brand isn't known for deals.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 10: What Price Promotions Really Do
says: Price cuts work much better when they move a brand below a reference price and when the change is explicitly signalled, such as 'was $54 now $30', with promotional support multiplying sales.
do: When a sale is on, show the old price and new price on screen (was/now) in the first seconds of the reel.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 10: What Price Promotions Really Do
says: A big volume increase may add no profit because the margin cut is bigger in proportion; a 10% cut on a 30% margin needs 50% more sales to break even.
do: Before scripting a discount offer, check the margin with the client; prefer shallow offers such as 10% off, or non-price offers such as bundles or gifts.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 10: What Price Promotions Really Do
says: Break-even tables show that deeper discounts need exponentially more extra sales (e.g. 20% off at 30% margin needs 200% more), and promotions can borrow future sales.
do: Keep offered discounts shallow in scripts (around 10%) and avoid deep-cut claims unless the client's margin supports them.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 10: What Price Promotions Really Do
says: Price cuts have strong direct effect but tiny reach, give margin away to people who'd buy anyway, and competitors match them, whereas advertising has broad reach and a lasting effect.
do: Don't rely only on promo-driven reels; keep a steady flow of non-discount reels that build reach.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 10: What Price Promotions Really Do
says: Retailer-wide advertising of a promotion works like ordinary advertising and gets reach, and shallow price cuts with strong communication beat deep cuts.
do: If a promo reel is needed, lead with the brand and the product and keep the discount modest.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: A person sees a few hundred ads a day, each fights for a sliver of attention, and only 16% of viewers noticed the average ad and correctly named its brand.
do: Assume the viewer will not register the brand unless it is made unmissable; get the brand name and look in early and more than once.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Buyers screen out most brands before they evaluate anything, so a brand's sales are largely decided by how many consideration sets it fails to enter.
do: Write for being noticed and thought of first, not for winning an argument; the reel's job is to get the brand into the viewer's few remembered options.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: People filter ads so well they can watch one repeatedly and still get the brand wrong, and evaluation of brand features is less important and less predictable than research assumes.
do: Don't assume one view means the brand registered; repeat the brand name and visual cues within the reel and across reels.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Brands sell more mainly because more buyers remember to consider them, not because people prefer their features or image.
do: Prioritise scripts that put the brand into more buying moments in people's heads over scripts that argue superiority.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Competing brands sell to nearly identical consumer bases, whose buyers hold similar attitudes and are polygamously loyal rather than segmented by demographics or personality.
do: Write for the broad category buyer, not a narrow persona; don't build separate scripts for supposedly different types of buyer of the same product.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: A bigger, fresher network of brand memory links makes a brand more likely to be noticed in varied buying situations, and awareness measures using one cue miss this.
do: Across a batch of reels, link the brand to several different situations and cues (when, where, who with) rather than repeating one.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Mental availability depends on the number, strength and relevance of memory links, and a well-known brand can still sell poorly if it isn't thought of at the buying moment.
do: Build reels around the actual cues buyers meet when buying (occasion, need state, colour, pack) and show them.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Buyers shift between attributes and occasions, and competitors are whatever else answers the same cue, so brands should link to many cues.
do: Write several reels, each tying the product to a different occasion or need (a treat, a gift, a quick fix) instead of one fixed benefit.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Distinctive brand assets like colour, pack shape, fonts and tone let people recognise a brand's ads, and failing to use them makes ads easy to screen out.
do: Put the same colour, logo, pack and tone in every cut, visible within the first seconds.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Because few brands enter the small consideration set, removing a reason not to buy (as McDonald's did with its menu) matters more than being radical.
do: If comments or objections reveal a reason not to buy (price, shipping, trust), answer it directly in the reel instead of adding another benefit.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Product claims such as 'more raisins' matter little; telling existing buyers does nothing and telling non-buyers is mostly a talking point for mental availability.
do: Use a product claim as a hook to get the brand noticed and remembered rather than as the argument; don't spend most of the reel proving it.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Reach all category buyers, especially light and non-buyers who hold most of the sales potential, and avoid narrow descriptions of the target that don't match who really buys.
do: Target and write for a broad audience of category buyers, not just the typical loyal customer; keep cold audiences wide.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Reach is wasted if the brand isn't noticed, since people actively avoid ads and pay little attention, though noticing without full attention still processes something.
do: Design the first second to be noticed by a person scrolling past, and keep the brand identifiable even in a glance.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Emotional, likable ads gain attention and are more likely to be correctly branded, and people notice ads more when they already use the brand.
do: Aim for a small likable emotional reaction (a smile, warmth) that also carries the brand, rather than a cold product pitch.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Repeated exposure makes people favour the familiar without realising, so likable creativity gets ads noticed but is only one way to do so.
do: Plan repetition: show the same product and brand cues across a series of reels so familiarity builds.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Creative ads that don't look like the brand, rarely mention it and show nothing about it build memory of the idea, not the brand, as Miller Lite's 'man law' campaign showed.
do: Check each concept: if viewers would retell it without naming the brand, add the brand name, product and look into the idea itself before filming.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Apple's iPod ads were simple and extremely consistent, always dancing silhouettes with white headphones, and established brands should keep saying the same thing, adding new information on top of the old story.
do: Keep one repeatable visual and verbal format across a client's reels, and put news ('now in blue') inside that familiar format.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Distinctive brand assets let people know which brand an ad belongs to, so memories are refreshed for the right brand, and they work as quick shortcuts without being deeply thought about.
do: Pick two or three assets (colour, character, sound, pack) and use them in every reel, visible in the first seconds, even when the footage is UGC.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: A brand is only recognised if it stays consistent, so good advertising tells the same story again and again in fresh, entertaining ways, using distinctive assets viewers process instantly.
do: Pick one repeatable story shape and one or two brand cues (colour, sound, logo placement, a recurring character or prop) and put them in every reel, changing only the situation and the hook.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Most buyers rarely see a brand's ads and long gaps separate exposures, so even slight inconsistency washes over them and nothing is taken in.
do: Keep the same logo placement, colour treatment, sound sting and end card across every cut so a viewer who sees one reel in a month still recognises it.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
chapter: Chapter 11: Why Loyalty Programs Don’t Work
says: Reasons not to buy, such as an excessive price or constant discounting, hurt sales more than reasons to buy help them.
do: In the offer line, state a fair price plainly and name and answer the one thing that would stop a purchase (delivery, returns, price) instead of leaning on repeated discount codes.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Everyone who buys the category is the target, and great advertising resonates broadly by tapping into shared human traits rather than a narrow audience.
do: Write the hook and story around a universal human moment any category buyer recognises, not a tightly defined persona.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: Reaching light buyers with mass media is cheap and worthwhile, and brands should resist retreating to small niche audiences or customising ads without clear return.
do: Make one broad version of the reel for everyone in the category and only branch into variants where the cost is low and the return clear.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: A new brand with no distinctive assets must build them and can shortcut by borrowing memory structures that already exist in people's heads.
do: For a new brand, reuse familiar cues from the category (recognisable settings, colours, formats) and repeat one invented asset in every video until it sticks.

title: How Brands Grow
author: Byron Sharp
says: The most effective ads are entertaining enough to grab people who are not yet in the market, and their sales effect is spread out over the future rather than showing in one week.
do: Open with an entertaining hook that earns attention from someone not shopping today, and judge the reel on reach and recall, not only same-week sales.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Caples sold a piano course by selling the social success it brings, because the hard work of learning can't be sold.
do: In a script, sell the life the buyer ends up with (admired, confident, popular) and keep the effort or process of the product out of the pitch.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Whatever the medium, first express the product in a plain print direct-response ad, because that exposes the selling points you can reuse in video or other media.
do: Before storyboarding a reel, write the pitch as plain text with no visuals or sound, find the strongest selling point, then build the video around it.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Lateral thinking: forcing three unrelated random words into your product problem produces fresh angles.
do: When a concept is stuck, draw three random words and make yourself write a hook for the product that uses all three.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Spending days learning how a product is made led Sugarman to the one fact, the laser-sealed capsule, that became the headline.
do: Interview the founder or maker and keep asking why nobody did it before; the answer is often the hook.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The laser that made the glowing watch possible became the headline 'Laser Beam Digital Watch', a unique concept that outsold competitors.
do: Find the one unusual how-it's-made fact about the product and make it the hook line.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: You must become an expert on both the product and the customer, ideally by being a typical customer yourself.
do: Before scripting, read reviews, DMs and comments for the brand and write down the customer's exact likes, dislikes and expectations.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: People buy when an event hits close to home, so repeated seed-planting lets the buyer recognise the need when the trigger arrives.
do: Run a sequence of reels that each plant the problem and the solution so the brand is the obvious pick when a trigger moment hits.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: For the burglar alarm he skipped scare statistics, imagined what he himself would need to be convinced (it works, easy to install) and added a credible spokesperson.
do: Name the buyer's top two doubts, spend most of the script answering them, and use a real person's quote as proof.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Scare tactics usually fail; showing what matters about the product let people file the ad and order months later when threatened.
