do: Don't open with fear or statistics; state what the product does well and leave a clear way to order when the need arrives.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: His specific knowledge spotted that the walkie-talkie's frequency sat near a CB channel, so he repositioned an ordinary product as a Pocket CB and sold 250,000.
do: Look for an overlooked feature that connects the product to something already hot in the market and rename the product around it.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Every element of an ad, from headline to layout, exists only to get the first sentence of copy read.
do: Treat every visual and text element in the first two seconds as serving one job: getting the first spoken line heard.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Make the first sentence so short it barely counts as a sentence so the reader slides into the copy like a train gaining momentum.
do: Open every reel with a spoken or on-screen line of two to five words, such as 'It had to happen.', and let the next line carry the thought.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Keep early sentences short, plain and almost incomplete; their only job is to make the reader want the next one, with no benefits yet.
do: Cut the first beat down to simple words and end it unfinished so the viewer needs the second beat.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The opening sentences should only hold attention, because putting the sales pitch first almost always tested worse for him.
do: Don't lead the first seconds with features or the offer; hold attention first and bring the pitch in after the viewer is hooked.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The best place to sell is whatever environment suits the product, and the opening of an ad should create that setting.
do: Choose the setting, sound and tone of the first seconds to match the product (gym for fitness, home for family goods).

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: You control the environment through layout and copy: bargains look busy with big prices, expensive goods look refined and confident.
do: Match the edit to price positioning: big price text and fast, busy cuts for discount brands; slow, clean, restrained frames for premium ones.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Axiom 4: the layout and first paragraphs must create the buying environment most suited to the product.
do: Check the first five seconds of every cut: does the look, sound and voice feel like where the customer would buy this?

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Selling in print follows in-person selling: set the environment, win attention, keep it, then make the buyer trust the seller and tie the product to the buyer's needs.
do: Structure a script in that order: setting, attention grab, a line that keeps it, then credibility and relevance to the viewer's need.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Build harmony by getting the reader to agree with true, obvious statements, since any 'no' or doubt loses them.
do: Write the opening three lines as things the target viewer would nod to, and avoid any line they could disagree with.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The moment the reader thinks 'no' or 'that's not for me' they are lost, so keep every statement believable and relevant.
do: Test each early line by asking whether the target viewer could say 'that's not me'; cut or reword if so.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The Food Crunch ad tied a current shared feeling (the fuel shortage) to the product with a short, true, nod-worthy first sentence.
do: Open by naming a feeling or event your audience is going through right now, in one true short line, and bridge to the product.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Speaking in the target's own language about their frustration (consumers being robbed by inflation) puts them in harmony quickly.
do: Write the opening in the exact words customers use about their problem, lifted from reviews or comments.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Every element must pull the reader to the next like a greased slide, from headline to subheadline to first sentence and on to the end.
do: Review a cut beat by beat and ask what compels the viewer to the next beat; if nothing does, add a pull or cut the beat.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: If a reader gets through the first quarter of an ad they will likely finish it, and the Magic Stat ad earned that by tearing apart its own product.
do: Put your best curiosity into the first quarter of the runtime, for instance by openly criticising the product before revealing why it won you over.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A flip, sceptical tone and the question 'what's the gimmick?' kept readers going, and a joke callback ended the ad.
do: Try a sceptical voiceover that pretends not to like the product, and end with a joke that calls back to the opening complaint.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The 'stealing' hook for Consumers Hero is a shocking claim that is then honestly reframed, compelling the reader to continue.
do: Open with a provocative claim that sounds wrong, and resolve it within a few lines with a truthful twist.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Axiom 6: readers should be unable to stop until the end, and an offbeat story or news item is a strong way to start the copy.
do: Start a reel with a short, odd true story or news item, then pivot to the product.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A story with no real connection to the product can still start the slide, as long as you admit the liberty later.
do: Use a quirky story as a cold open, and own up to the tangent with a humorous line before the pitch.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Keep a collection of offbeat news clippings and open an ad with one that loosely relates to the product.
do: Keep a swipe file of odd stats and headlines and use one as the first line for a product with a loose link.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: An interesting article tied to the product starts the slide, and magazines use large type at the start to ease the reader into the copy.
do: Make the opening on-screen text larger and easier to read, then shrink it as the viewer settles in.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: End paragraphs with a short line giving a reason to read on, and promise a payoff early that is only delivered at the end.
do: Close each beat with a short pull line like 'But there's more' and tease the payoff in the hook so viewers stay to the end.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: By halfway through, readers should be helplessly caught, and curiosity (Axiom 8) is what keeps the copy moving.
do: Seed a new open question every few seconds through the middle of a reel, not only in the hook.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: People buy on emotion and then justify the purchase with logic, as Mercedes buyers cite engineering while really wanting prestige.
do: Build the script around the feeling the buyer wants, then add the practical features as the line they can repeat to justify the purchase.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Mercedes ads sell on emotion but speak in logical features, and music works like the harmony that gets the audience ready to receive the words.
do: Pick music and tone first to put the viewer in the right mood, then deliver the feature lines over it.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A phrase can persuade through its feeling even when it makes no logical sense, and that often works better than the logical version.
do: Write the guarantee or returns line for its warmth ("prompt and courteous refund" style), not as a legal sentence.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Competitors failed by explaining technical features, while a scene of the buyer in a stressful moment, then pulling out the gadget to everyone's surprise, sold the same kind of product.
do: Open a gadget or utility product script on a short, felt moment the buyer is in, then show the product solving it, and leave specs for later.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Sell on the emotional appeal and bring in facts and technology later and lightly; a rough first draft is fine if it holds all your feelings about the product.
do: Draft the script as a rough emotional dump first, then edit; put the logic justification after the emotional hook.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Every word carries its own emotion, like a short story, so word choice shapes how the message feels.
do: In the script pass, swap flat words for ones with the feeling you want (e.g. "farmer" brings honesty, earthiness) before recording.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A single word change (motel to cottage, repair to fix) can lift the emotional feel and response without changing the facts.
do: Test one-word swaps on hook lines and captions, such as fix for repair, as cheap A/B variants.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Do not sell the product itself; sell a concept or big idea around it, unless the product is so new that it is the concept.
do: Before writing, state the one concept (e.g. 'the first pocket directory') and build the hook around it, not around product features.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A concept can sit right in the name or headline (Pocket CB, Nose, Winners), and several products can be grouped under one concept.
do: Give the product a vivid nickname in the first line, or bundle several SKUs under a single concept like 'Winners'.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Selling the challenge against a famous rival, rather than the chess computer, gave a staid product an emotional story that carried the whole campaign.
do: Find a story or challenge the brand can run (a dare, a rival, a stunt) and let the product enter through it.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Concept ads outsold plain product ads, and the price alone changed how the same product was perceived (serious tool, walkie-talkie, toy).
do: Check that the price point matches the category the script positions the product in; reframe the copy if price signals a different one.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Copy is never too long if the reader takes the action, but it must be compelling enough to be read from start to finish.
do: Check each line of a script asks 'does this make them want the next line?' and cut any line that fails.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: People read everything when the piece is about them, so personal relevance holds attention through a very long text.
do: Make the hook speak directly to the viewer's own situation, street or problem, not to the product.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: People read in depth only about subjects they care about intensely, and that intensity fades as a market matures.
do: Judge how hot the category is: for a hot topic go deeper and more detailed, for a cooled market lean on a fresh angle.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Copy should be exactly as long as the pitch needs to create the environment, build interest, relate to needs and close, no longer and no shorter.
do: Set the reel length from what the sale needs to cover, not a house default.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Higher prices and unusual products need more copy, while a perceived bargain or low price needs less.
do: Give high-ticket or unfamiliar products a 45-60s cut with more explanation, and keep cheap, familiar ones to 15s.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Short copy can work when photography sets the buying mood and prices are low, so visuals do the work words would do.
do: On low-price items let styled, beautiful footage create the mood and trim voiceover.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Write as one person talking to one person, using I, you and me, instead of a company addressing a crowd.
do: Rewrite voiceover and captions from 'we at Brand' to 'I' and 'you', as if speaking to one viewer.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A thank-you letter feels warm when it includes a specific human detail (I showed your order to our president) instead of generic gratitude.
do: Add one concrete, human detail to thank-you and UGC scripts so they don't sound like a template.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Even in print ads you are talking to one reader, so put a named person behind the message and write from them to that one person.
do: Put a named founder or team member on camera presenting the offer in first person.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The BluBlocker opener used a personal first-person promise ('If you believe me, you will be well rewarded') to start the slippery slide.
do: Open with a first-person claim plus a promise, such as 'I'm about to tell you something true.'

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A visible personality makes people feel close and more comfortable parting with money.
do: Keep one recognisable voice or face across a brand's videos so viewers build a relationship.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Copy must flow so each sentence answers the question the previous one raises, since you cannot hear the prospect's questions.
do: After drafting, check each beat is the answer to what the viewer is thinking after the previous beat.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: An eight-year-old's guinea pig ad opened with a benefit question, then answered the obvious follow-up questions in order.
do: Open with a benefit question ('a pet that doesn't shed?') and answer the next questions in plain order.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The pinball ad ran in blocks: excitement, drama, how it differs, build quality, then logic to justify the purchase.
do: Structure a long script as blocks (feel, difference, quality, justification) and place justification after the emotional hook.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Each block anticipates the next buyer question (will I tire of it, what if it breaks) and flows down to the order request.
do: List the buyer's next-question objections in order and give each one a beat before the call to action.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Sequence the copy by the questions a salesperson would be asked face to face, in the order a buyer asks them.
do: Write the likely buyer questions as a list, order them, and make each one a beat in the script.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Restate the problem several ways, list concepts, pick the best, then write a short hook and first line.
do: Restate the brief three ways until it sounds like a fun, easy buy, and write the hook from that version.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Pattern your ad on a similar admired ad's format and feel without copying its layout.
do: Pick a high-performing reel in the category and mirror its structure and pacing, but not its look or lines.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Editing means expressing exactly what you meant in the fewest words while keeping the same emotional feel.
do: On each edit pass, shorten lines until nothing can go, then reread to check the feeling survived.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Cutting a paragraph from 59 to 36 words kept the meaning and made the copy less imposing and faster to read.
do: Aim to cut about 40% of words from a first-draft script and reorder it so the pleasure comes first.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Concrete edit rules: drop 'that' lead-ins, vary sentence length, merge sentences, and trim small words.
do: On the edit pass, strike lead-ins like 'you know that' and alternate short and long lines in the voiceover.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Reordering so the emotional pleasure comes before the explanation makes copy more emotional and flow better.
do: Put the felt payoff before the reason why in the line order.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Errors in copy make readers doubt the whole business, and readers do notice and write in about them.
do: Proofread on-screen captions and price text before posting, since typos undercut trust.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Legibility beats style (serif type gave 5 to 1 better comprehension), and the first sentence must be short and compelling.
do: Choose caption typefaces for legibility first, and keep the first spoken line short.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The second sentence must also pull the reader on, and early lines should build momentum, not carry facts or features.
do: Keep the first two lines of a script free of features and use them only to build momentum.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Explain complicated products very simply and simple products in surprising detail.
do: For a familiar product, add a mechanism or story about what's inside; for a complex one, show one plain use.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A simple, familiar smoke detector sold at a higher price by telling a detailed story of its inner workings.
do: For a commodity item, show the unseen detail (materials, parts, how it works) to justify the price.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Test whether readers understand the product, show what is new, and use technical explanation to build trust.
do: Ask a non-team viewer to describe the product after the cut, and add every question they raise.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A technical explanation the reader may not fully understand still signals real expertise and builds confidence.
do: Include one specific technical callout, backed by real research, to signal expertise.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Showing specific things you reject, like a grapefruit's wind scars, proves your standards better than claiming quality.
do: Show what you reject or test (the grading, rejected batches, QC check) on screen with a specific detail.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Raise the buyer's likely objection yourself, even an ugly design, before they do, then justify the product.
do: Name the obvious objection (price, looks, install, fit) early in the script and answer it right after.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Resolve each objection honestly with a solution, as Gillette did by stating the battery question and its answer together.
do: Pair every objection beat with a one-line answer, such as 'battery lasts six months.'

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Keep copy clear, short and simple, and avoid clichés that signal nothing real to say.
do: Cut stock phrases ('game-changer', 'you won't believe') from scripts and replace them with specifics.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Copy needs a varied rhythm of short, long and medium sentences, and lists of three give a pleasing cadence.
do: Mark sentence lengths in the VO and break any run of same-length lines; use lists of three.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: For expensive or hard-to-return items, address service head-on with a frank, specific paragraph.
do: Add a plain 'what if it breaks' beat that explains how repair or replacement works.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Where the category had reliability problems, a strong warranty with pickup and a loaner watch turned the problem into an advantage.
do: If the category has a known weakness, lead with the guarantee that answers it.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Addressing service up front melts resistance, and delivering on it made customers into a strong repeat list.
do: Repeat the service promise in the offer recap and honour it so the customer buys again.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: List all physical facts (weight, size, limits) because any missing fact is an excuse not to buy.
do: Put size, weight and dimensions in the video or its caption.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Missing facts make people call and ask, and many more simply don't order, so state them all; mail order also needs a trial period.
do: Check each script for unanswered practical questions (size, weight, what's in the box) and answer them in the video.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A longer trial period (one to two months) lowers returns and raises buyer confidence, because people stop feeling pressure to decide.
do: If the brand can, state the longest return window available on screen and in the offer line.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Price comparisons establish value, but they must be fair and accurate, and a celebrity testimonial must fit the product.
do: Compare against a named, real alternative's price and confirm the facts before publishing.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A mismatched celebrity can backfire, while a reverse testimonial that contrasts your plain spokesperson with a competitor's expensive one makes a value case.
do: Use the competitor's costly endorsement or marketing as the contrast for your lower price.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Testimonials must be authentic, and price should be large when it is a bargain and underplayed when not, answering when the reader asks.
do: Show price big on screen when it's a selling point and small when it isn't, but never hide it.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Summarise the offer near the end, and cut copy hard because it can often shrink 50 to 80 percent and say the same thing.
do: End with one line restating what they get and the price, and trim the script by half on the edit pass.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Make ordering easy, and always ask for the order at the end after summarising the offer.
do: Close every video with a direct ask and one clear way to buy.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The best salesman spotted buyers by who touched the product, and ads can get the same involvement by making viewers imagine handling it.
do: Get the viewer physically or mentally touching the product in the first seconds.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Take the reader on a sensory mental journey of holding and using the product, so they feel they are already experiencing it.
do: Script and shoot in second person with sensory detail ('feel how light it is') over hands-on close shots.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Involvement devices, even silly ones, often double or triple response, and TV and the internet involve people naturally.
do: Give viewers a small action in the video, such as a comment, pause or spot-it task.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: An ad with deliberate misspellings that earned a discount per word found made readers study it for over an hour and lifted revenue.
do: Try a spot-the-mistake or find-the-detail game that unlocks a discount.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The feeling of ownership comes from describing what it will be like once they already have the product.
do: Add a future-tense walk-through ('when yours arrives, open it, adjust it...') before the close.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Honesty is the most important point because consumers are smart and sense dishonesty even when they skim.
do: Strip any claim you can't back up and keep the ones that are true and specific.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Naming the product's flaws up front, then explaining why they matter little, made buyers trust the message and respond more.
do: Put one honest drawback in the first half of the script, such as slow shipping, a size limit or a plain look, then answer it in a line.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Credibility means explaining why a low price is real and raising every obvious objection yourself, then resolving it.
do: List the three doubts a viewer has, such as why the price is so low, whether it is hard to set up, or whether it is real. Give each a one-line answer on screen before the close.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Answer the viewer's next question as it forms, and borrow credibility from the place or channel the offer appears in.
do: Show a trusted stockist, press mention or marketplace badge near the offer, and answer the next likely question straight after each claim.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A known brand name, a fitting celebrity and a credible company name each raise believability, and comparing your price with similar products proves value.
do: Use a side-by-side price comparison with a known alternative, and put the brand name and logo on screen early.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: People buy on emotion and then need logic to justify it, so teaching them the product's value works like lowering the price.
do: After the emotional beat, give one rational reason the buyer can repeat to themselves, such as materials, lasting value or cost per use.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The higher the price, the more you must justify the purchase, with reasons like savings, health, recognition or simply deserving it.
do: For pricier products, add a justification line that fits the buyer, such as saving, looking good or a reward they have earned.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A real price rise with a short window at the old price beat a larger ad, because bargains and deadlines pull buyers in.
do: Close with a true deadline, like the old price ending on a stated date, and say it plainly. Never invent one.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Find something true that shows your size, specialty or position and keep using it in every ad, because new viewers always need the reassurance.
do: Pick one authority line, such as the founder's years in the craft or a South African first, and put it in the opening or close of each cut.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Buyers look for reassurance before and after buying, and telling them a product is popular confirms their choice.
do: Use best-seller and sold-count lines, and add a post-purchase reassurance line in the close.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A guarantee that goes beyond a basic trial period signals conviction, and changing only that element doubled response in a test.
do: Write a guarantee that goes past the standard return window and say it in the close as a bold promise.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A strong guarantee at the very end of the ad removed the last resistance, even after the reader had read everything.
do: Keep the guarantee for the final beat right before the call to action.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The best guarantee raises the buyer's last doubt and answers it beyond expectation, and every product has one nature that sets how to present it.
do: Name the buyer's final doubt out loud, then answer it with a guarantee that fits that exact doubt.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Each product has its own nature, such as fun for a toy or serious for a safety device, and the presentation should play to it.
do: Set the tone, music and pace of the cut to the product's nature: playful and fast for fun items, calm and steady for serious ones.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Match the product's nature to the prospect's emotional needs, because emotion is the core of their motivation.
do: Before writing, state in one line the emotional need the buyer has and open the script on it, not on the product.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Linking ties your product to something already in public attention, like Pocket CB, but the link must not be illegal or toxic.
do: Hook a reel to a current trend or familiar term the viewer already knows, and check it is safe before using it.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Comparing a new product to a familiar thing, like a nose on the ceiling for a smoke detector, makes it instantly understood.
do: Open with a one-line metaphor from the viewer's daily life, such as vitamins for your car, and show it visually.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A link must be one the viewer can easily identify with, and links from past campaigns can go stale or turn offensive.
do: Test your metaphor on someone cold, and do not reuse an old winning angle without checking if it still fits today.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: For hard-to-believe products, short links like tuneup in a pill help the viewer grasp them.
do: Write two or three one-line comparisons for the product and pick the clearest as the hook line.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Once someone commits to a small purchase, they tend to stay consistent and accept add-ons.
do: Keep the first offer one clear product, then offer a bundle or add-on after the click, for example on the thank-you page.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Keep the first offer extremely simple, then offer extras while the buyer is ordering, which sold more over half the time.
do: Advertise one product at one price in the reel, and handle extras after the order.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Pattern yourself on what already works in the marketplace first, and take your own ideas later.
do: Borrow the structure of the top-performing ads in the category before experimenting with a new style.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: People often buy a brand to belong to the group that owns it.
do: Show who uses the product, including real customers, and let the viewer see themselves in that group.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Identifying with a group is a strong motive, and people with one item often want more of the same kind.
do: Target existing buyers with a new colour or style in the same range.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Past buyers are the best list for similar items because many people collect.
do: Make a separate reel for repeat buyers showing the full range or a matching set.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Collectors respond to series and holders, and mail order buyers cannot touch the product, so curiosity does the selling.
do: Show part of the series and give the starter holder or box free to push the next purchase.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Showing people reacting to the sunglasses but never the view through them created curiosity that sold millions.
do: Show strong reactions first and hold the reveal or result back until late in the reel.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Curiosity is the strongest buying motive when the viewer cannot touch the product, so holding back part of the story helps.
do: Cut the product reveal later, and do not explain every feature in the first seconds.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: When a prospect says they will think about it they usually do not buy, so give a true reason to buy now and never a false one.
do: End with a reason to act now that is true, such as a real end date or a limited run.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Real urgency comes from limited editions, price rises or closeouts, but leaving out key information gives the buyer an excuse to delay.
do: Make sure price, shipping and returns are all in the reel or caption, and add one true urgency line.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Urgency lines go at the end, because the beginning and the end are the two critical places in an ad.
do: Spend the most care on the first three seconds and the last five, and put the deadline or fast shipping line in the close.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Fear of losing out or of a real danger motivates action, and fear of missing the price drives buying.
do: Name the specific loss, such as missing the sale price or running out of stock, once and without drama.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Fear works in response to a perceived danger, and mail order should offset waiting by promising prompt delivery.
do: State delivery speed in the reel, for example delivered in a few days.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Faster delivery beats retail's main advantage, and limited editions make buyers feel special.
do: Lead with fast delivery if you have it, and show a limited run with the real number made.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A specific scarcity fact, six sold in the state and two allocated here, made him buy something he did not need.
do: Give the actual quantity left or allocated, not just limited stock.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Keep the offer, words and layout simple, because fancy words, colour bars and hard-to-read type hurt comprehension.
do: Use plain words, one idea per beat, and clean readable captions without decorative clutter.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The watch company wanted to show nine styles, but he insisted on testing one because too many choices are dangerous.
do: Feature one hero product or colour in each reel.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: In a split test, the ad showing one watch outsold the ad showing nine by three to one.
do: Run a one-product cut against a range cut and expect the single product to win; show the range later to qualified buyers.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Show the full range only after people are qualified as buyers, and a complicated dosing offer worried him.
do: Send the full range on the website or in follow-up, not in the first ad.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A simple one-price offer beat the complicated dosing offer by a large margin even though it cost him product.
do: Reduce the offer to one line, such as one price and one thing, even if you give up some margin.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Every element should resonate with the viewer so they keep nodding yes, and a first-person conversational voice and light humour help.
do: Write the script in first person in a conversational voice and make each beat something the viewer agrees with.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A hand holding a small product shows size and adds a human element, and attractive people help viewers relate.
do: Show the product in a hand for scale, and avoid faces that could create a negative reaction.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Stories hold attention and create a bond, and the most interesting salespeople always have a story.
do: Open with a short true story about how the product was found or made.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The best ad opened with a true story told conversationally, and the story built curiosity so people read to the final pitch.
do: Open with a friend's surprising reaction in first-person speech, and hold the product reveal until later.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Start with a story that fits the product, either about a discovery or about yourself, because it grabs attention and builds a bond.
do: Choose a founder or customer moment for the opening beat.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The more the viewer's mind works to reach a conclusion, the more enjoyable it is, so copy that is too obvious bores.
do: Leave one beat for the viewer to figure out instead of spelling out everything.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Leaving the obvious conclusion unsaid, that jewellers profit hugely, was more powerful than stating it.
do: Show the price comparison and let the viewer draw the conclusion rather than adding the line yourself.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Vague descriptions let the viewer imagine, and making your intentions too obvious patronises them.
do: Do not over-explain; show the result and let the viewer fill in the rest.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A precise figure like ninety-two percent sounds believable, while a general claim sounds like puffery.
do: Replace every vague claim in the script with a specific number, such as a percentage, count or price.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Specific reasons and exact figures make the speaker sound like an expert, and that builds trust.
do: Give the exact mechanism or number, such as 72,000 nerve endings, instead of a lot.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Familiar brand names and familiar selling places create trust, and advertisers drop campaigns before the public tires of them.
do: Keep a consistent look, logo and format across reels so viewers recognise the brand.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Keep running an ad until sales stop, not until you are bored or a focus group complains, and tweak it to improve.
do: Do not retire a creative while it still sells; iterate on hook and cut instead.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A specific measurable promise kills hope when it fails, so imply results through testimonials instead.
do: Let customers describe how they feel in their own words, and avoid promising an exact result or timeline.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: People pay far more for a cure of a problem they have than for prevention of one they might have.
do: Frame the product as the fix for a problem the viewer already feels, not a way to avoid a future one.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: People assume they will never get the problem a preventive guards against, so it is a hard sell, but once they have the problem they will pay far more for the cure.
do: Open the script on the person who already has the problem (the sore, the leak, the stain), not on the risk of getting it, and show the product as the fix.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Cures can be priced much higher than preventives, so ask whether your product can be positioned as a cure or whether the market is already shifting it that way.
do: Before writing, state the product as a fix for something the viewer already has, and price and frame the offer on that basis.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: When a product is both preventive and cure, lead with the curative results and underplay the prevention, and remember that belief decides whether people act at all.
do: Write the hook and first benefit as the problem it fixes now (knock, ping, failed test), and put prevention in a single late line.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Selling a cure is easier than selling a preventive unless the preventive is perceived as a cure or its curative side is emphasized.
do: Check each brief: is the product a cure or a preventive, and if preventive, rewrite the angle around the cure.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: An opening of about 9 words per sentence and few long words scored fifth grade and the ad was understandable to a very large market, with later blocks drifting only slightly higher.
do: Keep spoken lines in the first ten seconds to around nine words and avoid three-syllable words; check a few blocks, not just the opening.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Greater clarity gave broader appeal and more response, but sentence length should still vary and hard words are fine when needed.
do: Cut voiceover down to short plain sentences, then deliberately vary a few lengths so it does not drone.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Great copy comes from product expertise and knowing the prospect, then a short headline and subheadline that create curiosity, then dumping a draft, editing, and leaving it overnight before a final look.
do: Write the on-screen hook as a few curious words, draft the full script without editing, then edit and re-read it the next day.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A provocative headline, short first sentences and identifying with the prospect's frustration pull the reader into the copy.
do: Open with a very short first line that names the viewer's frustrating situation in their own terms.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Karbo builds curiosity and trust by saying plainly that the ad took two hours and that he is selling for $10 something that costs him 50 cents.
do: Try an honest opening admission about the economics or the odds before the pitch, to disarm and make viewers keep watching.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Offering to not cash the check for 31 days is a guarantee so bold it makes readers wonder how he avoids being ripped off, and it comes early.
do: State the risk-reversal early in the script as an unusually generous term rather than a closing footnote.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Karbo keeps his success relatable (a Cadillac, a mortgage) and sells the sizzle, ending the list on time with family.
do: Show aspirational results that are within the viewer's reach, and finish with the emotional payoff.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Listing the lack of need for education, capital and luck, with varied examples like a widow or an older woman, widens the appeal so more people see themselves in it.
do: Run a quick line of varied customers (age, background) so different viewers can see themselves.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The close restates the guarantee, uses a wise quote, and ends on a question: what if I'm right?
do: End on a reversal line that sets the tiny cost of trying against the upside.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: An accountant's sworn statement and a bank reference, which no one had used before, gave credibility to a skeptical buyer.
do: Put a verifiable third-party fact on screen near the order point, such as a named reviewer, certifier or order count.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Schultz's ad opened with a short claim that he is a farmer telling the truth, and Sugarman cut a clichéd line and fixed the headline.
do: Open with who you are in one plain identity word that carries trust, and cut any generic slogan line.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The word farmer implies honesty and hard work, and the second sentence creates curiosity, then a discovery story follows.
do: Use a founder or maker role as a trust shortcut in the first line, followed straight away by a curious story moment.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A fairy-tale discovery story makes the product feel rare, and the rarity claim is built by narrowing it further.
do: Tell the origin as a short story with a surprising moment, and make scarcity believable with a specific narrowing figure.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Schultz made fruit rare by narrowing its grade, made it personal by showing himself in the grove, and used taste as the involvement device.
do: Write one rarity line with a real percentage, then describe the sensory experience so viewers can almost taste it.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Specific, fussy rejection rules (the picking ring, wind scars, sheep nose) make the viewer picture the founder in the grove and believe the quality.
do: Shoot or describe the maker's strict rejection standards in concrete visible detail, like testing and discarding product on camera.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A simple product should be made complex by showing its details and selection process, while a complex one should be made simple, and a small personal company voice sells one-to-one.
do: For a simple product, build a script on the hidden detail of how it is chosen or made; speak as a small team.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A low-priced no-risk sample with the reader judging for themselves feels so generous that it creates a satisfaction conviction.
do: Make the trial offer the viewer's own test, with specific instructions such as chill four and cut them, rather than a pitch.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Homey phrasing like right quick was kept deliberately, and the offer billed after the trial so nothing is paid up front.
do: Keep natural spoken phrasing in the call to action instead of polishing it into corporate English.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The Lingerie for Men ad uses a short headline, a story opening, and a question the reader would ask, answered at that exact moment.
do: Say the viewer's likely objection out loud as a question right where it would form, then answer it.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Raising an objection (embarrassment) and answering it honestly makes the copy truthful, and the answer then widens the market.
do: List the viewer's top two objections and write each as a plain question followed by an honest answer inside the script.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The ad missed a return policy at the critical end, where a credit toward a first order would have helped.
do: Always put the return policy or a credit-toward-purchase incentive in the final lines.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The end of an ad is where the buying decision happens, so a good ad can fail by missing important things there.
do: Audit the last five seconds of every cut for offer, risk-removal and one clear action.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Sugarman would open the DC-10 ad by naming the crash and bad publicity directly before the reassuring copy.
do: When a brand has a known doubt (bad reviews, past issue), open the script by naming it plainly, then resolve it.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Addressing the problem first makes the same reassuring copy sincere rather than defensive.
do: Prove the fix with specific changes made, such as inspections doubled, not general assurances.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Leaving out the real issue makes good copy read as covering up, whereas raising the objection however embarrassing wins appreciation for candor.
do: Do not skip the obvious doubt; state it first and answer it, even when it feels risky.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A boring theme executed in a boring way fails because few will read a boring ad, so you must grab attention with story.
do: Never open on a category description; open on a story of someone who switched and got a result.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A very long, abstract first sentence full of lists loses the reader, and non-professionals applying these principles can beat professional agencies.
do: Cut any opener that lists generic problems; start with a short concrete line.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The Magic Stat ad starts by attacking the product's worst traits, then resolves each one, putting the biggest buyer worry (installation) early and building the company's credibility near the end.
do: Open with the product's biggest flaw or objection said candidly, then turn each one around, and put the buyer's number one worry first.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The ad confesses the hated name, cheap case and missing readout, then finds one good feature that leads to a discovery, using a light playful tone.
do: Write a hook that says what the team disliked at first and what changed their mind.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The features are shown through a concrete day (70 degrees at wake up, 54 at work) and anticipates the reader's what's so great about that.
do: Demonstrate a feature through one specific day timeline in the viewer's life, and answer the so-what out loud.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The ad answers the trust doubt by checking the company, then makes the offer irresistible with a one-year buy-back and a price tier.
do: Make the guarantee tied to a result, such as a refund if you have not saved the cost in a year.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Vision Breakthrough was sold as an educational breakthrough rather than sunglasses, with a story of discovery and strong curiosity that could only be satisfied by trying them.
do: Reposition the product as a discovery with an education angle and make trying it the only way to satisfy the curiosity.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The ad opens with a promise about a true story, a friend's excitement, and a first-person reaction of taking the glasses on and off to test it.
do: Show a person testing the product repeatedly, on and off, to prove the difference visibly.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The ad explains why it works and reveals a danger in ordinary sunglasses, then guarantees performance exactly as described.
do: Explain the mechanism in two plain sentences and reveal a surprising danger in the usual alternative.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The close invites a side-by-side comparison with old sunglasses and offers a 30-day refund if the difference is not immediately noticeable.
do: Close with a side-by-side test the viewer does at home and a 30-day refund tied to that test.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The Consumers Hero ad used a shocking headline and the language of the consumer, so the reader couldn't stop once started.
do: Pick a shocking, slightly taboo word for the hook, then explain it in the viewer's everyday words.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The ad explains the economics with a concrete example, an Uncle Henry figure and real numbers, to make the strange offer plausible.
do: Walk through the cost chain with real figures and a named everyday person so the price logic is clear.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Step-by-step numbers show why the manufacturer sells cheap and how the guarantee of looking new makes it safe.
do: Show the margin story on screen in three numbers so the low price feels earned.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The offer lists reasons the consumer is glad (better product, half the price, longer warranty), plus fair rationing and a two-week trial.
do: Stack the offer as a short numbered list of reasons ending in the guarantee.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A refundable five-dollar membership with interest removes the risk, and a good copywriter can write to fit any market by using its jargon.
do: Write each client's script in the exact words their customers use, and make a small entry step fully refundable.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Facing a price restriction, Sugarman invented a game of finding misspelled words for $10 off each, turning a constraint into the hook.
do: When a price or claim restriction blocks a discount, make the viewer earn it through a simple challenge.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The spelling ad states the rules and a sliding prize plainly, with deliberate mistakes and humor, then explains the reason for the generosity.
do: State the playful rule and the biggest prize in the first lines, then give the reason.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Planting deliberate misspellings for readers to find made the ad an involving game, and people spent hours with it and sold out the stock.
do: Hide one small, findable oddity in a reel and invite viewers to spot it, so they rewatch and comment.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A catalog needs a personal letter from a real, reachable person, and every salient fact must be given because one missing detail hands the buyer an excuse to delay.
do: State the practical facts (size, weight, material, delivery, returns) in the script or on-screen so no small question is left to stall the buyer.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The look of the piece should match the price point, and a single product wins in an ad while variations belong in a catalog.
do: Advertise one product or one hero variant per reel and keep the production polish in line with the price of what is sold.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Write in the first person, as a friendly person chatting with enthusiasm, and put an easy ordering route on every page.
do: Script voiceover in I/my founder voice with a story opener, and show the shop link or handle on every video.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Direct mail copy should say I rather than we and talk about my team, with the first page strong enough to carry the reader on.
do: Write brand scripts as one person talking ("my team") rather than a corporate "we".

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The postscript is often the most-read line, so use it to clinch the decision or repeat the key point, and unusual objects keep prospects looking forward to the mail.
do: Make the final line or end card restate the single strongest reason to buy and the offer.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A restaurant special with a playful catch (bring a Brinks armored car top) spoke to students in their own spirit and drew a line around the block.
do: Give an offer a quirky, audience-specific catch or challenge that viewers can act out and share.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Keeping the same format week after week built community trust, and advertisers benefited by keeping the format and changing only the copy.
do: Run a repeatable series format for organic and paid, with the structure fixed and only the product or message changing.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A billboard needs one headline and one graphic so simple it lands in a few seconds, and a teaser can build curiosity before the reveal.
do: Make the first frame carry one idea, one image and at most a few words that can be grasped instantly.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Linking a product to a current trend with a provocative headline can make a minor offering national news.
do: Tie a hook to a live trend or conversation, with a bold premise that is cleanly connected to the product.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A radio spot should carry only one core message, delivered linearly one statement after the next, and listeners fill in the picture themselves.
do: Pick one core message per reel and cut anything that does not serve it.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A direct response spot must open with a curiosity or news-style trigger to keep people listening, and the response handle must be easy to remember and cover likely misspellings.
do: Open with a news-style curiosity line, and use a short memorable URL or code, with common misspellings redirected.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Making a message sound like news fits radio, and humour works when it grabs attention and humanises a single clear core message.
do: Use humour or a story only as the carrier for one plainly stated core message, such as lowest price.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Short-form TV works for impulse-priced products with almost-too-good-to-be-true value and one simple offer with no choices, adding extras only near the end.
do: Build the reel around one offer with no colour or size choices, stack the added value in the final seconds, and leave variants for the checkout.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Urgency and a time limit stop people from noting the number down for later, and the product must appeal to a mass market to justify TV.
do: Put a real deadline or limited stock into the call to action so the viewer buys in the moment.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: In a short spot every word and visual must be counted and aimed at the buying conclusion, with props that fit the buyer's world and a bonus the whole audience would want.
do: Audit each line and shot of a script against the core message and cut any that do not lead to the purchase, and set scenes in the product's real use environment.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A free bonus that part of the audience does not want can lower sales of the main offer, so test gift versus no gift.
do: When adding a bonus to an offer, test the reel with and without it and choose a bonus that every viewer wants.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Present the show in a format audiences already know, such as the candid street interview where strangers react with surprise to the product.
do: Use a familiar native format, like street interviews with real reactions on trying the product, as the frame for a reel.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Build relationships by giving useful information before selling anything, because money is made only at the last of push, pull and dangle.
do: Run organic content that teaches or helps first, and put the product pitch only after trust is earned.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Long web copy needs buy buttons throughout, and testimonials are more believable with true names and hometowns and become stronger as audio and video.
do: Show video testimonials captioned with the person's real name and town, and place them through the reel and not only at the end.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: A presenter on video must speak naturally without sounding scripted, since looks and delivery can provoke bad emotional responses, so test with and without video.
do: Pick on-camera talent for natural delivery and trust, direct them off a loose script, and A/B test with and without presenter.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Web viewers leave more easily than TV viewers, so longer pieces suit pricier products but must keep a fast-moving, interesting pace with an easy order button.
do: Keep the cut fast with a new beat or visual change often, and add a tap-to-buy prompt wherever the call to action lands.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: Product pages fail when they only give colour, size and texture, so describe materials, origin, construction and what makes the item better.
do: In a product reel, show and say the specific material, where it was made and how it is built, not only the colour and size.

title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook
author: Joseph Sugarman
says: The more clicks needed to buy, the less likely the purchase, so keep the steps to a minimum.
do: Send the viewer by link straight to the product or checkout page and cut every extra tap between the reel and payment.
